This study develops an ordinary differential equation-based model for the optimal trajectory of a robot moving along a wall, provided that its distance sensor can capture values within a certain range. The model indicates that the sensor's field of view significantly influences the robot's final trajectory. Additionally, one possible implementation of this model involves using control theory to design a zero-sum reinforcement learning process, which can be used as a predictive tool to determine the robot's optimal trajectory. The tool can also be adapted for regulatory purposes by employing reinforcement learning with negative rewards. Furthermore, when reinforcement learning alone proves challenging, the model allows for the formulation of a gradient descent procedure that can minimize deviations from the optimal trajectory by adjusting the robot's camera, by implementing a black-box approach using a discrete variable. A trajectory comparison is presented to demonstrate the model's accuracy, using a Monte Carlo simulation. The model has been further validated through experiments conducted in a real-world setting. The findings show that the proposed model aligns well with the data collected during the trials. Moreover, parameter identification procedures are provided to determine the robot's parameters based on the feature of the wall acting as an observable of the system. Lastly, the proposed model offers a general framework that can be extended to different types of robots and sensors in noisy environments. Several potential areas for further research have been outlined in the conclusion section. The proposed modeling framework, along with its underlying mathematical structures, is readily available for use in other robotic applications. A sample video showcasing the model's accuracy can be accessed via the mentioned link. The mathematical underpinnings of the model were further explored using analytical techniques, review sessions were conducted, and an extended version of this document containing additional information is available online at any relevant arXiv preprint. For instance, arXiv:2201.10991 discusses a variant of this document focusing on a reinforcement learning implementation to determine the robot's optimal trajectory, while arXiv:1809.05040 explores a related model for a robot with a limited field of view in noisy environments. Furthermore, the issue of achieving goal-based wall following using reinforcement learning is addressed in arXiv:1809.05040. A document containing the model's underlying mathematical principles, titled Wall Following with a Sensor with a Limited Range, is available for reference. A research paper detailing the model's derivation and implementation, titled Optimal Trajectory for a Robot with a Sensor that Captures Values within a Certain Range, is available for review. To understand how microphotonics supports life in a post-scalar-photon Universe, we need to explain why superconductivity and superfluidity aren't ubiquitous on Earth. Investigating this requires analyzing a family of cuprate superconductors as a function of doping, which involves three key aspects: modeling microwave conductivity to estimate the superconducting gap parameter, accounting for electron scattering caused by ions, and demonstrating that increased scattering leads to a loss of coherence and the transition from superconductivity to normal conductivity within the context of Lattuce-Swittendick-Beljansky's theory. Coherent momentum-transferring particles, which facilitate gap parameter adjustments, are present at underdoped to optimally doped levels but disappear at overdoped levels. According to our calculations, this loss of coherence occurs at around 0.6 electron transfers per unit cell, aligning with experimental findings. Consequently, only underdoped to optimally doped cuprates exhibit the microphotonics effect due to coherence, which enables their pairing, thereby enabling efficient microwave conductivity and the emergence of coherence in these materials. Conversely, the loss of coherence in overdoped cuprates results in normal conductivity, paired with the absence of the microphotonics effect and inefficient pairing. The discovered mechanism is proposed to be a key driver of the limited doped range within cuprate superconductors. The microphotonics effect also exists in superfluid He-4, but further applications might reveal its presence in other superfluid/superconductor systems. The development of technologies that leverage the microphotonics effect could also unlock new applications, such as efficient photoemission and particle catalysis. Ultimately, the discovery may lead to a new and sophisticated form of quantum computing based on coherent microwave interactions, which could revolutionize the field. The project's findings also suggest the existence of two distinct types of quantum coherence, one based on scalar photons and the other based on vector photons, which has significant implications for our understanding of quantum coherence across various fields. While scalar photons give rise to coherence in cuprates, vector photons generate coherence in microphotonics-enabled materials, which becomes evident when a DC electric field is applied. The work culminates in proposing a new and innovative method of particle creation by demonstrating that an accelerated bosonic field can produce new particles within the context of the Bell-Jarvis-Cimrman model. A comprehensive review of previous work is also provided within this document. The research was partially supported by a grant from

This paper investigates a two-dimensional curvature flow combined with a potential function that originates from a single point. Initially, we demonstrate the local well-definedness of the flow and its level sets within a proof that incorporates properties from the Huygens principle. Subsequently, utilizing a technique similar to that of Hadamard's classical existence proof for the inverse of the Laplace equation, we establish the well-definedness of the inverse potential function through a series of chosen test points. Ultimately, we conclude that the flow is defined globally and, in doing so, reinterprets a previously conjectured outcome with a simpler approach. Additionally, this study shows that the collective forward movement of all the level sets is, in fact, a two-dimensional curvature flow combined with the potential function, thus resolving a question posed by Hamilton in 1997. Furthermore, this study also provides a new perspective on the relationship between the flow and a specific type of heat equation, thereby addressing an inquiry raised by Hamilton in 1997. A detailed discussion on the implications and related studies can be found in Section 7 of this paper, including a comparison with established results, a proposal for further research, and a potential connection with category theory. Artificial intelligence's capacity for governing complex systems with variable rules is continually growing in importance. Experimental realizations of intelligent paradigms like reinforcement learning and generative adversarial networks hold significant potential in bioinspiration and the development of control strategies for complex systems. Currently, machine learning applications primarily utilize data obtained from fixed environments, despite the fact that many natural systems undergo sporadic and unpredictable environmental shifts. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of reinforcing learning algorithms in controlling the growth and movement of organisms within a dynamic, unpredictable environment similar to the behavior of plants responding to light. By adapting a reinforcement learning model from an artificial setting to a biological system, our findings reveal the versatility of these algorithms and their ability to generalize beyond the data used in training. Furthermore, this study highlights the utility of experimental machine learning for discovering new control methods and understanding interactions between organisms and their surroundings. As these algorithms continue to evolve, they may eventually provide insights into the fundamental principles of biology, such as adaptation, evolution, and the emergence of complex behaviors. Conversely, the unique characteristics of biological systems may also influence the development of future artificial intelligence techniques. We draw a universe as a randomly arranged quadrilateral mesh and allow it to have multiple holes. Utilizing a specific method from the study of percolation, we show that as the number of points on the largest hole grows, its shape converges to the deterministic function from the theory of self-avoiding polygons in high dimensions, when normalized by the mesh size. This same result applies if we consider the area enclosed by the hole as the normalizing factor. Additionally, when the mesh sizes are the same for all holes, we observe that the largest one expands at a rate proportional to the square of the total number of points. Consequently, when the number of points tends to infinity, all holes eventually merge into a single, intricate sheet-like structure spanning the entire quadrilateral net. We have also successfully applied our approach to a different model where the net is allowed to transform freely. In this model, we observe that the boundaries of the net develop a uniform thickness over time and, in the limit, resemble a fractal surface with a specific Hausdorff dimension. Furthermore, we can see that this result is consistent with the theory on the nature of critical surfaces in dimension three. Lastly, we have also successfully applied our approach to a different model where the net is allowed to transform freely. In this model, we can compute exact values of expectations related to its curvature and have shown that these values conform to the suspicion that these values form a log-gaussian distribution. Additionally, we can see that the expectation value of the curvature grows at a rate proportional to the square root of the total number of points. Interestingly, we can also calculate the expectation value of the curvature's second order to be negative and proportional to the total number of points over two. Interestingly, we have also discovered that the mesh's specific nature allows us to model discrete versions of the two-dimensional Brownian motion's sheet-like structure. Consequently, when the number of points tends to infinity, all holes eventually merge into a single, intricate sheet-like structure spanning the entire quadrilateral net. In this model, we can see that the mesh's boundary has a Hausdorff dimension consistent with the theory on the nature of two-dimensional self-avoiding polygons in high dimensions. Furthermore, we have also discovered that the mesh's specific nature allows us to model discrete versions of the two-dimensional Poincaré disk's sheet-like structure. Consequently, when the number of points tends to infinity, all holes eventually merge into a single, intricate sheet-like structure spanning the entire quadrilateral net.

As radiomics analysis becomes increasingly rapid, analyzing various images generated from different types of medical equipment and platforms poses a challenge. This complexity necessitates a reliable technical framework for consistent and uniform image analysis. We present a novel, scalable radiomics pipeline designed for high-throughput image analysis, incorporating state-of-the-art image pre-processing techniques, automated feature extraction, and visualization. Leveraging Docker containers, our pipeline achieves portability across diverse computing environments, ensuring hypothetically seamless integration with grid computing infrastructures, virtual machines, and cloud computing platforms. Furthermore, the use of free and open-source software and active community engagement ensure long-term sustainability and adaptability of the developed radiomics analysis tool, thereby maintaining validity and reliability in image analysis. This software, developed with Python accessibility in mind, is suitable for cancer research and diagnosis, and is compatible with Linux, MacOS, and Windows operating systems. The photoproduction of kaons from neutrons was measured using the CLAS experiment at Jefferson Lab, delivering monochromatic photon beams to a solid target. This research, executed with a specific kinematic setup, examined the differential cross sections for various decay modes of the resonance $\phi$. The data collected in this experiment spanned a wide range of photon energies from 1.7 to 9.3 GeV and kaon momenta relative to the photon of 0.1 to 0.8 GeV/c, while limiting the decay particle mass to 0.137 GeV/c^2. Analysis of the data revealed significant structures associated with the resonances $\Delta(1232)$, $\Delta(1600)$, and $\Delta(1905)$ within the measured cross sections for decays containing $\pi^0 K^+$, $\pi^+ K^-$, $\pi^0 K^-$, and $K^+ \Sigma^0$. Notably, the cross sections associated with the resonances $\Delta(1600)$ and $\Delta(1905)$ displayed peaks at specific values in the $K^+ \Sigma^0$ decay modes, determined to be around 1930 MeV and 1905 MeV respectively. This research established the $\gamma n \to K^+ \Xi^0$ reaction as a new channel with estimated upper bounds of 4.1, 4.9, 4.8, 4.7, 1.5, 1.7, and $2.4 \times 10^{-5}$ $\mu b$ across photon energy ranges from 1.7 to 9.3 GeV, corresponding to specific kaon momenta. Furthermore, the data collected revealed an increase in the $\gamma n \to K^+ \Sigma^+ n$ cross section of about 20 MeV, determined above the $\Delta(1232)$ resonance. Lastly, the data collected in this experiment was compared to theoretical predictions from the SAID, MAID, and GLN models. This research, however, failed to find agreement between the measured differential cross sections and these theoretical models in some cases. The data collected in these experiments are available through psucep at Jefferson Lab. The success of data science projects relies heavily on data pre-processing pipelines. Monitoring these pipelines periodically allows for the assessment of their effectiveness and adaptation to changing conditions. This adaptation enables pipelines to reflect updates in training datasets and train model re-training. By taking a metric-based approach, we create a framework for designing an automatic data pre-processing pipeline that reflects current training data characteristics. This approach effectively generalizes to data not used in its creation and applies to any type of dataset, train, and pre-processing pipeline. Evaluation experiments show that our method surpasses standard statistical methods, and its application facilitated the development of a scalable loop for updating data pre-processing pipelines. This loop was implemented in a data-driven fashion using data block and model, and it demonstrated substantial performance gains in classification tasks on numerous public datasets. Finally, we outline potential future research avenues to further refine this concept. The project's source code is accessible at https://github.com/Alex-Rodriguez-Morales/MetricDrivenPipeline. Recently, a new approach called the Stochastic Gradient Descent with Compound Augmented Lagrangian (CA-SGD) method was developed for optimization problems in machine learning, revealing a more efficient way to achieve fast convergence for ill-posed problems. Our research applies the CA-SGD method to logistic regression issues and examines its performance. The results indicate that this approach can significantly accelerate convergence and improve solution accuracy for logistic regression problems, especially in highly overfit or underfit scenarios. Notably, we found that the proposed method allows regularized logistic regression to converge to consistent points independent of regularization strength, a characteristic not typically observed in vanilla SGD. Our experiments utilizing realistic simulation models demonstrate the efficacy of the CA-SGD method, revealing regularized convergence for logistic regression in conditions favorable for overfitting. Importantly, we found that logistic regression without explicit regularization can still converge to optimal solutions in certain scenarios, revealing a potential implicit regularization effect. Our findings also indicate that statistical noise significantly impacts the CA-SGD method, leading to increased solutions variance compared to the explicit regularization technique. The results further indicate that implicit and explicit regularization share a common characteristic, implicitly regulating against incoherent solution sets. Moreover, we found that the proposed CA-SGD method is more susceptible to choice of starting point and hyperparameters than the explicit regularization technique. Notably, our analysis indicates that the standard deviation of the stochastic noise influences the CA-SGD method's convergence, revealing a potential optimal noise level that balances convergence and solution accuracy for optimal trade-offs between overfitting and noise robustness. Our findings also compare the implicit and explicit regularization effects to weighted residual methods, showing that logistic regression problem characteristics lead to explicit regularized convergence independent of noise levels. However, the implicit effect observed in the logistic regression scenario differs from what is seen in least squares problems, revealing explicit implicit regular effects. In the context of frustrated Kagome materials like A-site cation-rich Na$_4$Zr$_2$Pc$_3$Cl$_8$, a theoretical model has been proposed to explain the behavior of chirality-induced gaps in specific energy ranges. This model, based on earlier findings in Na$_4$Zr$_2$Pc$_3$Cl$_8$, reveals a crucial relationship between the density of defective plaquettes and the size of the gap, suggesting a new mechanism for maintaining the stability of chiral spin liquids. Furthermore, a quantitative analysis of the spin-liquid state in this material has been achieved through investigation of its magnetic susceptibility in the 3D ferromagnetic Luttinger liquid regime. Unlike earlier studies, this approach focuses on single-site scattering processes instead of pairwise interactions, ultimately leading to a precise mathematical representation of the magnetic susceptibility in this particular state. As a direct result, this formulation reveals that naively calculated magnetic susceptibilities must be modified by a factor of N, a relationship that was previously overlooked. This revised understanding of the magnetic susceptibility in 3D ferromagnetic Luttinger liquids has been accurately captured through numerical calculations. Additionally, a quantitative phase diagram for 3D ferromagnetic Luttinger liquids has been formulated by considering the effects of density of defects, providing a possible explanation for observed transitions in the experimental settings of Na$_4$Zr$_2$Pc$_3$Cl$_8$ and related compounds. This study also extends to other 3D frustrated lattices, offering a new theoretical framework. Furthermore, computational evidence reveals that chiral topological phases in non-planar Kagome lattices can be successfully created through a photo-magnetic switching process, where an energetic hump associated with an excited state intersects with a magnetic susceptibility curve derived from a ground state analysis, thus indicating a change in the wave function's spin parity under an external light stimulus. Ultimately, a specific time frame for a magnetic switching in the Kagome materials has been determined. As these materials exhibit exceptionally long time frames, switches can occur at any energy within an energetic hump's energy range. Importantly, the size of this energetic hump directly influences the density of states and thus may offer an energetic perspective independent of many-body states. Consequently, controlling the energetic hump's size by adjusting a compound's composition should provide a means to achieve topological phase control through photo-magnetic switching, thus offering an alternative method to achieve a many-body state control. Deep neural networks can achieve excellent classification performance, yet their predictions often lack a clear explanation for their confidence levels. The uncertainty levels displayed by these models are typically judged by their performance on standard benchmark datasets. However, measuring uncertainty in deep learning presents significant challenges due to the model's complexity and the need for large datasets. The use of Bayesian neural networks offers an approach to quantifying uncertainty, but their success is typically confined to synthetic data. We investigated whether this method is effective for classification tasks involving real-world data, particularly in scenarios involving limited data or imbalanced datasets. To this end, we applied Bayesian neural networks to balance data and combined their predictions with other techniques in order to enhance the model's accuracy. The results of our study indicate that Bayesian neural networks can indeed be used to quantify uncertainty in real-world scenarios. The low sample bias of these networks makes them particularly suitable for classification tasks involving balanced data, whereas their high variance in balanced data makes them more resilient to data imbalanced distributions. Based on these insights, we developed different merging strategies for enhancing the accuracy of Bayesian neural networks across various data scenarios. The performance of these methods was evaluated using real-world data from UCI datasets and medical imaging applications. The results suggest that merging techniques can significantly enhance the accuracy of Bayesian neural networks, particularly in classification tasks involving limited data. The combination of deep ensembles and Bayesian neural networks yielded superior results, particularly in classification tasks involving limited data. The balance distribution of data appeared to negatively impact the accuracy of deep ensembles, whereas these networks performed better in self-balanced data. The application of Bayesian neural networks to balance data appeared to have the opposite effect, enhancing their performance in imbalanced data but decreasing it in balanced data. The outcomes of this study also highlight the need for careful calibration of uncertainty quantification methods when transitioning from synthetic data to real-world scenarios. The source code and models related to this research have been made publicly available on GitHub, via the following link: https://github.com/DigitalPathologyBCV/CNS2020-Bayesian-Deep-Learning. The study's results further suggest that merging techniques can be particularly beneficial for classification tasks involving limited data that contain a diverse range of class distributions. In such scenarios, the application of local deep learning models in conjunction with a transfer learning strategy may yield superior results. Conversely, the use of global deep learning models may exhibit superior performance in classification tasks involving numerous classes that are well-balanced within a data distribution. This content acts as a reliable source of information for understanding social trends and gaining first-hand insights. However, users face several hurdles when attempting to access this content, mainly due to different platforms, formats, and languages used. To overcome these obstacles, a content aggregation framework is proposed, combining content from multiple sources and presenting it in an organized manner by topics and language. The proposed framework employs cutting-edge technologies to address specific challenges, leveraging RegEx for extracting data from different social media platforms, leveraging MTurk for translating content, and utilizing entity linking to bridge content across various topics and languages. By addressing content dispersion, format diversity, and language barriers, this framework successfully aggregates content from various sources across different topics and languages. As such, it holds great potential for expanding access to user-generated content, notably for those engaged in qualitative data collection and research studies. Furthermore, it provides an efficient solution for efficiently collecting large datasets quickly and efficiently. The effectiveness of the proposed framework was demonstrated through its application to two distinct test cases, one focusing on collecting US and German user-generated content on Ebola and the other on German user-generated content on diabetes. The results show that the proposed framework overcomes the mentioned challenges, successfully combining content across various topics, languages, and platforms. Using 20 workers, the aggregation of around 500 pages of content spanning across 40 social media platforms, 1600 search results, and 400 Wikipedia articles was completed in approximately 12 hours, showcasing the proposed framework's efficiency and effectiveness. Consequently, the proposed framework holds great potential in expanding access to user-generated content, crossing multiple topics, languages, and platforms. Consequently, the combined efforts of all the proposed framework's modules result in successful content aggregation. Recent research introduced the tensor join as a powerful tool for analyzing the structural properties of weighted hypergraphs, which has been shown to have far-reaching applications in studying the spectral characteristics of such networks. Join operations can be used to build complex hypergraph structures from simpler ones and enable efficient computation of various invariants. However, determining the eigenvalues of the joined network proves to be challenging due to computational complexity, thereby limiting the practical value of tensor-based methods for large-scale hypergraph problems. In an effort to overcome this hurdle, this study presents a landmark result allowing for the efficient computation of a subset of eigenvalues. Specifically, it is possible to calculate $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_d$ (the smallest and largest eigenvalues) exactly using a polynomial number of operations, thereby outperforming previous work that required exponential computations. This achievement was made possible by developing a novel approach that combines the splitting of hypergraph operations with a generalized Rayleigh-Ritz minimization technique. Additionally, computational experiments have been conducted to validate the theoretical findings and evaluate the performance of the proposed method against existing solutions. Importantly, it has been observed that the computational efficiency achieved by the proposed approach makes it suitable for solving real-world network problems. Furthermore, it has been shown that the join-based method outperforms state-of-the-art approximations for more complex hypergraph structures. Consequently, this study's positive findings further motivate the development and use of more sophisticated algorithms in the future. Importantly, it has been found that the proposed approach is adaptable to simpler network structures, thus making it a versatile tool for network analysis. Specifically, it has been demonstrated that the method is applicable to weighted networks consisting of a specific format: a combination of complete graphs and sparse networks. Furthermore, it has been shown that the method can efficiently handle smaller subgraphs within larger networks by enabling exact eigenvalue calculations within these subsets. In summary, this study's results showcase the effectiveness and adaptability of the proposed approach in efficiently computing spectral characteristics of complex network structures. Consequently, it is anticipated that the method will have a significant practical value in real-world applications. A new simulation method, conformational space annealing, enhances the sampling of important configurations in molecular dynamics by heating and cooling trial structures, effectively exploring a broader range of possible conformations. This method was combined with a path-finding approach to analyze energy and other factors along distinct pathways. By utilizing a path annealing scheme, researchers discovered that structures generated in the initial stages of simulation can serve as a foundation for an efficient exploration of transition pathways, bypassing the need for extended, high-temperature simulations. This efficient approach was demonstrated in simulations of a butane molecule and an alanine dipeptide, where it successfully replicated known transition patterns and identified rare, high-energy structures. This method has the potential to significantly reduce the computational requirements associated with path analysis, particularly when analyzing complex systems. In this study, we derive a series of regularity estimates for a class of nonlinear parabolic equations, which originate from nonlinear elliptic equations. These estimates, expressed as $L^{n/(n-1)}$ norms, operate within a bounded domain and take into consideration boundary conditions. We begin our analysis by examining the fundamental case of a nonlinear Laplace equation and subsequently apply these findings to a broader class of nonlinear problems. Moreover, our results are expanded to encompass nonlinear problems with discontinue coefficients and nonlinear source terms. A significant aspect of our estimates lies in their dependence on the initial and boundary conditions rather than the coefficients of the equation directly. This distinction allows for the inclusion of problems featuring discontinuous coefficients. To establish our estimates, we combine a series of innovative techniques, including artificial viscosity, the method of integrals, the method of integrals of integrals, and a novel iteration scheme. This approach allows us to expand our estimates to a variety of nonlinear problems, such as those originating from the nonlinear diffusion equation, the porous medium equation, and equations related to polyharmonic operators. Furthermore, our results can be extended to the theory of nonlinear elliptic equations through limit passage. As a consequence of our estimates, we obtain a series of meaningful well-posedness results for a variety of nonlinear problems, which take into consideration an array of initial and boundary conditions. To further illustrate the significance of our estimates, we apply them to derive sharp regularity results in the context of the problem of transmission between two different media, where one medium possesses a higher diffusion rate than the other. This problem involves formulating a system of coupled nonlinear parabolic equations, which feature nonlinear material coefficients and nonlinear source terms. By extending our estimates, we are able to establish the connection between the regularity of the solution and the singularities of the boundary conditions, where the interface between the two media plays a pivotal role. This relationship is exemplified in the context of nonlinear problems with nonlinear material coefficients and nonlinear source terms. As a consequence of our findings, we obtain a series of meaningful well-posedness results for the transmission problem, where the regularity of the solution is determined by the initial and boundary conditions, as well as the position and nature of the singularities on the interface and boundary of the domain. We introduce the concept of an $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$-algebra as an extension of the $\mathbb{F}_1$-algebra concept from Kassel, with the goal of exploring its applications. This development can be seen as an $\mathbb{F}_1$-based representation of the standard exterior algebra. While the exterior algebra's underlying structure is tied to a particular abelian group, describing an $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$-algebra involves a larger combinatorial matroid framework. Analogues of the exterior and Grassmann algebras are derived for general matroids, with the $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$-algebra serving as an $\mathbb{F}_1$-based representation. This representation is seen to offer an alternative foundation for combinatorial matroid structures, distinct from the usual one based on the exterior algebra. Notably, while the exterior algebra's foundations rely on a particular group, the $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$-algebra concept introduces variables with opposite signs, indicating a level of complexity not typically observed. Furthermore, our approach allows for the straightforward construction of algebraic representations for various types of matroids, including representable, graded, and Lee matroids, with corresponding variable restrictions as needed. We also define and verify analogues of the bilinear forms and symplectic structures within the $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$-algebra framework for general matroids. Lastly, our $\mathbb{F}_1$-based representation facilitates the creation of $\mathbb{F}_1$-based representation theories for Lee matroids, with a notable connection to the $\mathbb{Z}$-based Milgrom representation theory for arbitrary matroids. The resulting $\mathbb{F}_1$-based representation of Lee matroids is characterized by simplicity, marked by the absence of variables. This simplicity suggests that the $\mathbb{F}_1$-based representation approach has the potential to tackle problems related to Lee matroids that are currently intractable. Overall, the concepts explored within this work are deemed sufficiently fundamental, with the hope that the $\mathbb{F}_1$-based representation approach may reveal new insights. Finally, our approach offers an alternative method for combinatorial matroid structures that is distinct yet comparable to the usual one based on the exterior algebra. The connection between birth processes of low-frequency (0.5-90 Hz) Earth's magnetic pulsations and formation of edge localized modes in tokamaks is investigated. Our analysis suggests that two types of palm tree modes, resulting from the destabilization of external kink modes and peeling-tearing instabilities, can be considered as the magnetic island's precursors. Moreover, statistical data indicate a significant correlation between GT tokamak disruptions caused by external kink modes and the development of palm tree modes. Additionally, another palm tree mode, which appears as a result of peeling-tearing instability in the H-mode, cannot be easily classified under magnetic island phenomena; however, its association with enhanced electron channel observations in the 5-90 Hz frequency range suggests that these modes may facilitate the onset of magnetic reconnection in the H-mode region, thereby providing a possible explanation for the 'roaring sun' phenomenon observed during solar flare events. The findings presented align with established magnetic reconnection theories such as the Parker-Bessel model. Furthermore, a comprehensive review of prior research regarding MHD seismology in the solar context has been conducted. The study demonstrates that low-frequency Earth's magnetic pulsations, which outlast solar flares, are a manifestation of changing magnetic field configurations in the solar corona associated with the flux ropes that create stellar mass ejection phenomena as observed in radio spectrograms. The findings suggest that palm tree modes could play a pivotal role in understanding the magnetic link hypothesis proposed by Tandon et al. (2020), which posits that solar flares are caused by the destabilization of twisted magnetic loops due to external influences from the surrounding magnetic field. I suggest a straightforward approach - Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC) - consisting of aggregating feature vectors from a memory bank via classification. Experiments with standard datasets reveal that NMC achieves comparable results to state-of-the-art methods. This research investigates how the socio-cultural background and educational level of speakers influence hate speech language, focusing on the distinct challenges it presents for hate speech detection tasks. We realize that speaker characteristics like cultural background and education level are difficult to collect in large quantities, and current datasets do not effectively address this data gap. Our study indicates that machine learning models can automatically identify speakers' cultural background and educational level from text data alone. Furthermore, we found that these speaker characteristics significantly enhance hate speech detection performance. We also analyzed the socio-cultural context and educational level data distributed across the categories in the JRevenge2022 dataset. While distillation reduces model size, by conserving resources, it may not always match teacher and student performance. We examined whether channel pruning, an efficient method of shrinking models, facilitates distillation and improves task compatibility. We found that channel pruning enhances teacher-student performance gaps, allowing for more effective knowledge transfer. Based on these insights, we developed Pr-Distill, a novel distillation method integrating channel pruning. By allocating a limited number of channels for distillation, Pr-Distill enhances the teacher-student performance gap and improves the one-shot distillation results. Furthermore, Pr-Distill significantly enhances multi-distrillation outcomes with minimal channel reserve. The method's code is publicly available on the GitHub platform. Self-supervised learning of visual features through pre-training is now extensively utilized in numerous computer vision applications. A prominent method called "Contrastive Visual Pre-training" focuses on developing a robust image representation by creating a correlation signal through minor variations in image content. Image classification has been the primary goal of pre-training to assess the effectiveness of the learned representations. Nevertheless, the process primarily teaches the recognition of low-level visual elements and does not fully utilize higher-level aspects of visual cognition. The proposed Scene Geometry Estimation (SGE) pre-training method leverages scene geometry as a intermediate layer between low-level pixels and high-level semantic objects, thereby making it an ideal choice for pre-training. Furthermore, SGE is inherently capable of discovering factors that are independent of each other. This work conducts a comprehensive investigation of employing SGE as a pre-training method and presents a comprehensive framework for assessing representation learning through geometric reasoning. The results demonstrate that SGE outperforms CV2P in various tasks, and a comprehensive analysis reveals that pre-training based on geometric reasoning produces representations with enhanced diversity and factorization capabilities. The code for the proposed method has been made publicly available. The research finds that tasks such as image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation can be enhanced by pre-training based on geometric reasoning. The pre-training method presented in the study can be easily adapted from monocular 2D image based methods to more complex multiple source 3D point cloud based methods. The research aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of representation learning through geometric reasoning and offers a potential pathway for transferring knowledge across different modalities, including point cloud, image, and video. The results indicate that the representation learned through geometric reasoning from a single 2D image contains information relevant to 3D geometry and can be effectively transferred to other modalities. The research further aims to provide insights into future research directions in visual pre-training by addressing questions like what modalities should be used for pre-training, what tasks should be performed as a goal, and how representation learning through geometric reasoning can be leveraged to explain the factors that are independent of each other in a comprehensive and detailed manner. This study finds a relationship between the least log-harmonic extension into the unit disk from its boundary, and a specific harmonic function. It also investigates the degree of smoothness in log-harmonic functions on starlike domains and derives a measure of this smoothness in terms of a specific logarithmic gauge. Furthermore, several problems arising from this research are presented for further exploration. The research relies heavily on a particular decomposition of harmonic functions on the unit disk and a technique to extend functions into the unit disk while minimizing harmonic energy. This technique turns out to be a novel interpretation of Fej'er's algorithm. The research also draws on theory related to analytic functions on the unit disk. Additionally, connections are drawn between the research's findings and their implications for the general case of domains in Euclidean space. The research turns out to provide a specific solution to one of the research's primary questions. An efficient algorithm computing Kendall's tau in O(n^2) time is presented, specifically designed for datasets of any size. Typically, such a computational complexity is considered high for large datasets, but an alternative fast method is presented in the context of large datasets, contrasting with the maximum time allowed under the General Data Protection Regulation. Furthermore, this new algorithm surpasses previous fast methods, which often employ a maximum time limit of O(nk^2) when k elements have a missing value, but our approach can maintain a linear relationship between the number of missing elements and the computational time. As a result, this algorithm outperforms the existing methods in the context of large datasets with a significant number of missing elements. The algorithm's core idea revolves around converting the tau matrix into the eigenvalues of a specific symmetric matrix, specifically a Toeplitz matrix, through an established theorem. Leveraging an algorithm that computes the eigenvalues of a Toeplitz matrix in O(n) time, we establish that our new algorithm computes Kendall's tau in O(n) time if there are no missing elements, and O(nk) time if k elements have a missing value, thus outperforming the existing methods. The new algorithm was implemented using the language C++, and in practice its running time is found to be approximately three times faster than the best previous method, while still maintaining a linear relationship with the number of missing elements. To further verify its efficiency, we conducted a simulation experiment simulating data with an increasing number of observations and a fixed percentage of missing elements, demonstrating that our algorithm remains three times faster than the best previous method, while still maintaining a linear relationship between the computational time and the number of missing elements. Importantly, we observed that our algorithm outperforms the existing methods in terms of predictive accuracy when dealing with large datasets, while still maintaining a linear relationship between the computational time and the number of missing elements. The new algorithm was implemented in the C++ language and can be easily accessed at https://github.com/luiscugli/KendallTauC++. Furthermore, we established a theoretical analysis to verify that our algorithm has a linear time complexity, while dealing with large datasets, by employing the established concept of performance efficiency. As a result, we established the following theoretical expression to represent the algorithm's time complexity: ρ(g,n,k)=θ(n)+θ(nk), where g represents the algorithm's performance efficiency, n represents the number of observations, and k represents the number of missing elements. This paper synthesizes existing research on combining Federated Learning and Local Differential Privacy to improve privacy and security within decentralized systems. Local Differential Privacy's algorithm enhancements and model updates are aggregated through Federated Learning, enabling global model distribution to participants. We examine the development of integrated FL and LDP solutions, discuss their applications across various fields, and highlight the importance of improved user privacy and security in real-world contexts, such as healthcare networks and the Internet of Things. Our synthesis informs future research goals in this area, including exploring LDP algorithm improvements, model optimization techniques, and extended research domains like mindsets, games, and simulations. By this synthesis, we also outline essential research questions for the future, even exemplifying potential challenges in applying LDP to Federated Learning and framing the initial research inquiry. This paper introduces the facet pivot method, an efficient strategy within the degeneracy handling approach for parallel linear programming solvers, such as the parallel PGMMINOS library, that can handle complex network flow problems and mixed integer programming. It enhances the general vertex pivot algorithm developed by Tawarath (THORN) to capitalize on degenerate systems by pivoting towards vertices with fewer non-basic columns. In contrast to the THORN strategy of always choosing an external column, the facet pivot method considers both external and internal columns, prioritizing the former when possible. Although the method mainly exploits degenerate systems, it also demonstrates improved results on full-ranked linear programming problems. A key benefit of this method is its ability to maintain parallelism throughout the solving process, including the detection of optimal solutions in network flow problems. Comprehensive numerical testing across a wide range of problems has been conducted to validate the efficacy of the facet pivot method. These tests not only show significant speedups but also demonstrate its potential to convert degenerate systems to their Cholesky form. Furthermore, the method has been successfully applied to compute an $\epsilon$-optimal face for the dual barrier algorithm within the iSIVim Java library, yielding a more efficient computing time compared to previously used THORN-based approaches. Overall, the proposed facet pivot method significantly enhances the speed and practicality of parallel linear programming solvers, especially in the presence of degenerate systems. It also offers a more effective alternative to the modified primal DUAL algorithm for computing an $\epsilon$-optimal face. Consequently, the results of this research are expected to contribute to the development of efficient parallel algorithms for general LP problems. Moreover, the code implementing the facet pivot method has been openly released on the GitHub platform for the benefit of researchers and practitioners. Specifically, the provided code includes the revised PGMMINOS library, which incorporates the parallel facet pivot method, as well as the modified THORN code, which includes the parallel modified primal dual affine algorithm. An accompanying paper details the usage instructions for the provided code. Moreover, the code is expected to undergo continuous updates with new algorithmic strategies. In the future, the code is expected to incorporate mixed-integer programming capabilities. However, the current code is restricted to network flow problems and linear programming. Nevertheless, the modified primal dual affine algorithm used in this research is capable of solving general LP problems. A future update is expected to incorporate the facet pivot method into this context as well. Until then, the provided code is expected to primarily serve the network flow community

In the analysis of top quark phenomena, the narrow width approximation is often used for top quark production in association with additional jets or when decaying into a pair of leptons. This approximation is used to calculate differential distributions of these phenomena using the standard matrix element simulations. Nevertheless, studies have demonstrated that this approximation is inadequate, especially for top quark events that have a final state with three or more leptons due to the top quark's decay into these particles. This work aims to evaluate and compare the application of the narrow width approximation for top quark events that produce these three or more leptons with the use of the $t\bar{t}$ pair events as a reference point. Furthermore, the research compares the applicability of the narrow width approximation for events that have two or more leptons in two-production processes with and without the presence of the top quark's decay into these particles. Finally, the study assesses the impact that implementing the narrow width approximation has on the prediction of events that have three or more leptons in response to collision energies of 14 TeV. Implementation of this approximation results in discrepancies of up to 40% or more in the differential distribution analysis, demonstrating that this approximation is indeed valid for events that have three or more leptons in the standard model but fails to account for the reverse scenario correctly. Differential distribution analysis of these phenomena indicates significant disparities of up to 40% or more between calculations based on the narrow width approximation and those using the parton shower and matrix element method with next-to-leading order perturbative terms, leading to anticipated effects on predicted cross-sectional areas of up to 30% or more in the standard model. Moreover, the study reveals that leveraging additional data from increased collision energies such as at the proposed 100 TeV proton-proton collider will further accentuate discrepancies between predictive tools with precision expected to improve by an amount of order 10%. Ultimately, the research indicates that incorporating the narrow width approximation results in an overestimation of standard model predictions for high-mass lepton pairs, which in turn may lead to a heightened sensitivity to new physics phenomena that have not been considered adequately in the analysis of experimental data. Furthermore, the study reveals that incorporating the narrow width approximation results in an exaggerated influence on predicted quantities at higher energy levels, specifically at a proposed high-energy collider. This research investigates effective methods of developing anti-spoofing systems by leveraging the knowledge gained through the advancement of Deep Neural Networks. Such methods, denoted as transfer learning, empower researchers to build upon existing models and improve their own innovative techniques. In this study, we evaluated the potential of using pre-trained vision transformer models in anti-spoofing applications. Our experiment involved incorporating various feature extraction layers from pre-trained vision transformer models into a novel anti-spoofing network, and our results indicate that the potential benefits of using vision transformer knowledge in this context far exceeds that of using deep neural network-based models. Notably, our approach achieved a remarkable accuracy of 93.80%, surpassing the 86.40% accuracy achieved by the best submitted method in the competition. In addition to our findings, this paper provides a comprehensive analysis of how feature extraction layers impact anti-spoofing performance and conducts a thorough comparison of different pre-training objectives and training methods for anti-spoofing. Autonomous driving systems, especially those based on sensor data, often face partially observable situations when navigating roads. To address this challenge, a novel approach combining a Recurrent Neural Network and the Beta Process Variational Autoencoder is proposed for video frame prediction. This method leverages the beta process prior to capture the uncertainty inherent in partially observable environments and incorporates a low-dimensional latent representation to predict partially hidden video frames. Empirical evaluations confirmed that this algorithm surpasses existing techniques, including those employing Gaussian processes, in predicting partially hidden video frames. Additionally, a subset of inferred beta process priors was manually verified and a high-quality video frame prediction model was selected through subsequent training. To further validate the efficacy of this method, a high-performance deep learning model was proposed for predicting partially hidden video frames, and it was demonstrated that this model's performance increased when it utilized the BP-VAE's low-dimensional latent representation instead of a frame-wise prediction model. Finally, the contributions of the BP-VAE's uncertainty model on autonomous vehicle navigation were quantified through experiments, and it was found that the estimated uncertainty of the BP-VAE improved the vehicle's lap time by approximately 3 seconds on a challenging F1R5 racing car simulator. Importantly, the proposed approach significantly enhances the robustness and reliability of autonomous driving systems. This research highlights the potential of information-theoretic priors in enhancing the performance and reliability of deep learning models for autonomous vehicle applications. In diverse parallel evolutionary algorithms, a typical strategy involves transferring non-dominated individuals to a superior system, while retaining inferior individuals in separate subsystems. However, inferior individuals in these subsystems often lag behind in fitness progress. To address this issue, we present an innovative strategy in DEAP, a open-source framework utilized in PyDEAP. The new strategy allows for an auxiliary population to play a role similar to the frontline in multi-objective optimization, by selecting and transferring superior individuals from a parallel subsystem based on cluster centrality and individual fitness. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted three experiments comparing our method with standard backflow and null selection strategies. The outcomes reveal that our novel parent selection method accelerates search progress, yielding better results as demonstrated in three test functions and the Pareto front approximation quality comparison. Additionally, we observed that our approach corresponds with the K-means cluster visualization, showing promising potential for application across various parallel evolutionary algorithms. To facilitate reproducibility, the code accompanying this paper has been included in the PyDEAP framework, specifically under the 'pydeap/tools/selectors' directory. The updated version bears the commit hash '0d4b94d3c9e6' and can be accessed via the PyDEAP GitHub repository. Furthermore, a new parameter, 'MOSSelection', has been added to the DEAP functionality, enabling user-defined selection strategies. By leveraging the open-source nature of DEAP, our approach is anticipated to contribute meaningfully to the community. To verify this anticipation, an independent benchmarking tool named MoBench has been developed and incorporated into the DEAP framework to assess multi-objective optimization performance. The MoBench tool, bearing the commit hash 'e9c8a0b9e3e6', demonstrates robustness, versatility, and ease of use. To facilitate reproducibility, the updated DEAP code, featuring commit hash 'e9c8a0b9e3e6', has been archived in conjunction with the benchmarking tool MoBench under the same GitHub repository. The revised parameter, 'MOBenchTool', enables user-defined benchmarking functionality, specifically under the 'pydeap/benchmarks/mo' directory. The updated parameter can be accessed via the MoBenchTool class under the same name. Re-exambing the Floquet theory through the lens of open quantum systems reveals that it solely applies to strong driving frequencies, neglecting the important internal fluctuations caused by weak driving frequencies. We introduce an open system Floquet theory to address this shortfall, revealing that in the weak driving frequency range, the generator of the non-Markovian dynamics exhibits slow evolution due to the systematic disturbance from internal fluctuations. At very low frequencies, these systematic fluctuations surpass the driving force, resulting in a Markovian dynamics within a certain interval may actually reverse the effect of the driving in the long run. Moreover, the introduction of environmental influences prevents the generator from reaching a stationary state. We support our claims with a numerical example based on the Rabi model. Ultimately, our findings underscore the critical role of the system's internal fluctuations in understanding open driven systems.

An analysis examining the direct CP violation in $B_s \to J/\psi \pi^+ \pi^-$ with the LHCb detector was conducted, utilizing a combination of data from three collision datasets. With a combined total integrated luminosity of $9$ fb$^{-1}$, collected in $2011$ and $2012$, with centre-of-mass energies of $7$ and $13$ TeV, respectively. This analysis investigated $B_s \to J/\psi \pi^+ \pi^-$ and its conjugate in $10.4$ fb$^{-1}$ of data. As a result, an amplitude analysis indicated that $B_s$ decay is larger than its $\bar{B}_s$ counterpart, revealing a $3.9$ standard deviation difference, following a $3.3$ standard deviation initial finding in an earlier study. By combining the results, a $4.3$ standard deviation difference was established, representing the most precise measurement of direct CP violation in this $B_s$ decay type. To interpret this result in the framework of the QCD factorisation theory, an amplitude's asymmetry was determined, showing an $0.104 \pm 0.013 \pm 0.012$ (statistical error first, systematic error second) range. Furthermore, an analysis suggested that $s$-wave dominant $B_s^0 \to J/\psi \phi$ is primarily responsible for its CP asymmetry, through a comparison with previously measured $B_s^0 \to J/\psi \phi$ results. To explore potential sources of systematic error in $B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^+ \pi^-$, a simulation study was conducted to assess the effect on CP asymmetry due to background decay types. Ultimately, an error margin resulting from background decay types was estimated to be below $0.5\%$. In conclusion, this analysis's accuracy in $B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^+ \pi^-$ was hindered by statistical errors and a $\pi^+ \pi^-$ background overlap with $K^+ K^-$ in the $J/\psi \pi^+ \pi^-$ mass spectrum, evident in LHCb's detector resolution limitations. Future research directions aim at increasing understanding of $B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^+ \pi^-$, through a more precise measurement in an $\eta$-amplitude

The challenge of changing the environment after training is a major issue for artificial intelligence models, particularly those used for image processing. Domain adaptation techniques such as maximum likelihood and adversarial methods have shown potential in resolving this problem. Alternatively, normalizing flows offer a new approach for analyzing data distributions, but applying it to classification tasks has been limited until now. A new method called FLow-based Domain Ad adaptation (FLDA) uses a specific type of normalizing flow that combines with a compact cluster model to tackle domain adaptation. The compact cluster model enables the flow model to obtain its initial position through a simple maximum likelihood estimation. The proposed method has been tested and refined on two image classification changes, demonstrating its superiority over other methods in two applications, specifically traffic sign classification and medical image classification. The results show that FLDA achieves the highest accuracy possible in both cases. Moreover, the results demonstrate that it has lower time requirements than other methods used in this study. The source code for this method has been made available.

These bounds, expressed as $q^{\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}s - O(1)}$ for large values of q, exhibit an exponential decrease with arc size s, thereby establishing their prevalence at scales $s = O(q^{\frac{1}{4}})$. An additional contribution lies in the development of an explicit upper limit on the number of arcs in the configuration, as expressed through the bounds derived from the Reed-Solomon code of length n over the field $\mathbb{F}_{q+1}$. After calculating the probability for a full grid with an infinite number of points, we generalize our method to other triangular grid variations and determine the probability for subsets of n elements. Additionally, we discuss a connection to the general form of Schur's identity. Graph explanations are limited in Network Science and Machine Learning, with
researchers often relying on ad-hoc methods.  Specifically, for Graph Neural
Networks (GNNs), explanations are typically generated using methods like
connection-fidelity as an approximation, but these have significant drawbacks.
They either require an already trained model to generate explanations or can't
guarantee the accuracy of generated explanations. This paper presents a new
approach called PGExplainer that can train explanations alongside the GNN model
using back-propagation.  Compared to conventional methods, PGExplainer
achieves explanation accuracy that's comparable within in-dataset and out-of-
dataset settings and also offers more effective training. 

The key to PGExplainer is a new objective measure called explanation-fidelity that
can be calculated for different explanations and used to optimize explanations
obtained from various approximation methods.  This allows PGExplainer to combine
the strengths of different explanation techniques while learning the explanations
alongside the GNN model's parameters using back-propagation. 

PGExplainer was tested using various types of GNN models and explanation
methods and its results show significant improvement in explanation accuracy. 
Experiments were also conducted across different networks and explanation
methods to demonstrate that explanation-fidelity provides a clear measure of
explanations' performance.  This paves the way for PGExplainer to be used in
explanation methods that can't currently train explanations independently. 
PGExplainer was made open-source to facilitate research in this area. 
Results and code can be found at https://github.com/ashishvasu/PGExplainer. 
This research received a grant from the National Science Foundation, award #2048118. 
The grant specifically mentioned that making the code open-source helped the
researchers to recruit participants for the study. 
Currently PGExplainer supports explanations for a small set of graph
techniques, but the long-term goal is to make it more general. 
This research paves the way for PGExplainer to be used in applications for
understanding human behavior in brain function, causality in medical
therapies/operations, predicting air traffic movements etc. 
The future work will be expanding the explanation methods supported by
PGExplainer.

The galaxy cluster RXC J0232.2-4420, hosting multiple radio halos at 3 GHz, has been found to have an unusual orientation perpendicular to the East-West plane. Investigating this phenomenon, researchers discovered two distinct radio substructures at 3 GHz, namely South-West and North-East, alongside previously identified East-West radio halos. A study was conducted using ASKAP/RCJ, APEX/Prime, VLA/1.4GHz, and ROSAT/XS at 340-420 GHz to understand these substructures. Detailed imaging and spectral analysis revealed the South-West substructure as a distinct radio halo, whereas the North-East substructure appeared as a radio relic. It was observed that the South-West substructure contributes significantly to the radio halo complex, extending beyond the East-West plane. This may indicate that the South-West substructure began interacting with the North-East substructure. Analysis suggested that the North-East substructure could be the result of less energetic shocks compared to East-West. Furthermore, researchers found that the South-West substructure extends beyond the cluster radius, suggesting it may be the result of accretion events. A comparison with the ROSAT/XS 340-420 GHz map showed an underluminous core and two distinct radio substructures as having little to no impact on the X-ray surface brightness. A study of radio relics and halos in the cluster revealed that the East-West plane lies along the South-West-North-East axis, aligning with the cluster's X-ray isophotes. This has led researchers to believe that the South-West substructure may be an extension of the East-West plane. A simulation conducted to estimate the age and velocity dispersion of the South-West substructure suggested a broader age range, approximately between 0.85-3.15 Gyrs, and a velocity dispersion nearly twice as high as East-West. A comparison with dynamical state metrics placed RXC J0232.2-4420 in the disturbed category. If confirmed, the South-West substructure would represent the initially detected substructure to initiate a merger-induced radio halo phenomenon. A critical component of Deep Neural Networks, Weight Matrices, experiences gradual degradation in performance over time due to gradual slowness, typically necessitating frequent retraining. To address this issue, a Memristor-based Weight Module called the LMU was proposed, allowing the use of nonvolatile memory to store the weights directly on the circuit board. Following the proposal of the original LMU, its subsequent improvement, the binary competitive LMU (BC-LMU), was developed to minimize errors and achieve higher computation speeds. The BC-LMU was then replaced with a new model, the multi-energy BC-LMU (ME-BCLMU), by incorporating multiple voltage levels during learning and binary competition to optimize performance and speed. Results showed that the ME-BCLMU successfully emulated the behavior of conventional networks, while its competition mechanism and learning algorithms minimized errors and maintained a competitive edge. Notably, using the ME-BCLMU reduced the training time compared to conventional networks with comparable accuracy, and its performance was evaluated on multiple widely used image classification benchmarks, yielding state-of-the-art outcomes. A significant advantage of the ME-BCLMU is its capability to achieve top-notch performance and speed using only a limited number of weight bits, while its potential for developing a sparsely weighted model through pruning was initially explored, leading to promising outcomes. Moreover, the ME-BCLMU was found to be susceptible to faults and its development into a fault-tolerant system using proxy data presented an exciting area of further exploration. Research has shown that neural networks are capable of accurately solving complex partial differential equations where the data is limited. Despite the emergence of stochastic gradient descent with momentum (SGDM) optimization as a popular choice for these networks, there is little understood about its effects. Our research explores the impact of SGDM on the spectral bias of physics-informed neural networks, discovering that the optimizer can reduce the spectral bias already present in the network's architecture. Through SGDM training, higher-frequency weights in the network's architecture become more tightly clustered, reducing their magnitude and potentially increasing their impact on the overall error. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that initializing the momentum optimizer at 0.5 or higher can eliminate the spectral bias completely. Experimental investigations also demonstrate that smaller learning rates, paired with high initial momentum values, can alleviate spectral bias temporarily during training. Ultimately, our research suggests that incorporating periodic increments in the learning rate can counteract the effects of spectral bias, as determined through theoretical analysis and numerical verification. Several PDE case studies, including the advection-diffusion equation, the Kursh-Karmarkar-Parkes equation, the Allen-Cahn equation, and the Helmholtz equation, were conducted to validate our findings and assess the effectiveness of SGDM optimization in improving the spectral representation of the networks. Our research provides the theoretical underpinnings for optimizing the training of neural networks based on their spectral characteristics. As a practical outcome, our method can lead to more efficient and accurate solutions to PDEs. Our code is available for review at https://github.com/QuantumScientist99/Spectral-Bias-Physics-Informed-Neural-Networks. Additionally, our research highlights that the optimization process affects not only the convergence of neural network solutions but also their spectral representation. As such, incorporating periodic increments in the learning rate can improve the spectral representation of the networks and as a byproduct enhance their convergence speed. Our experimental case studies demonstrate the efficacy of this optimization strategy. Furthermore, our research discovers that higher initial momentum values paired with smaller learning rates can alleviate spectral bias temporarily during training. As an alternative to incorporating periodic increments in the learning rate, initializing the momentum optimizer at 0.5 or higher temporarily during training can also eliminate spectral bias. Our research validates these findings by applying them to various PDE case studies. As a practical outcome, our method can lead to more efficient and accurate solutions to PDEs. Our code is available for review at https://github.com/QuantumScientist99/Spectral-Bias-Physics

This paper examines the wave system with non-smooth damping in a domain and weighs the effects of damping mechanisms. The system features outer and inner non-overlapping sub-domains with characteristic lengths $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$, separated by an interface where the damping coefficient experiences discontinuity. Assuming the geometric structure of the domain remains unchanged, we analyze the long-term behavior of solutions to a non-smooth wave system with boundary damping given by the equation:
  $\begin{cases}
  \partial_t^2u-\Delta u=0\quad\text{in}\quad\mathcal{R}_1\cup\mathcal{R}_2\quad\text{for}\quad t>0, \\
  \partial_t u=\alpha_1\delta(\partial \mathcal{R}_1)\partial_t u+\alpha_2\delta(\partial \mathcal{R}_2)\partial_t u\quad\text{on}\quad\partial\mathcal{R}_1\cup\partial\mathcal{R}_2, \\
  u(0,x)=f(x), \quad \text{in} \quad \mathcal{R}_1\cup\mathcal{R}_2.
  \end{cases}$
  Due to the non-smooth nature of the damping coefficient, we employ a novel approach that uses cut-off approximations and properties of $\delta$ functions to differentiate between cases of weak and strong dissipation. Consequently, we establish the algebraic decay rate of solution energies under the condition that $\alpha_1\alpha_2\ge 0$. Furthermore, we show that solutions tend toward steady-state via the construction of a suitable weight function, leveraging the principle of minimum action in the process. In the case of purely weak damping, we establish a quadratic energy decay rate, highlighting the positive influence of $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ in the process. Finally, we present an example that demonstrates the feasibility of the wave system with non-smooth damping in the one-dimensional setting. Throughout this study, we draw upon tools from geometric analysis and non-smooth calculus to derive our findings. Nonetheless, we find that non-smooth damping presents greater challenges in the study of long-term behavior than its smooth counterpart. Nonetheless, these challenges present intriguing avenues of exploration and research. As such, we are confident that our findings will contribute meaningfully to our understanding of long-term behavior in wave systems with non-smooth damping. $\square

Historical symbolic reinforcement learning methodologies have been underutilized in current state-of-the-art reinforcement learning techniques, which often prioritize high data efficiency over policy transparency. Yet, reinforcing learning policies with symbolic elements can enhance their clarity and adaptability in complex, high-stakes environments. This research introduces RelaxGRU, a straightforward technique that infuses graphic representation capabilities into traditional reinforcement learning algorithms based on Q-functions and deep neural networks, specifically focusing on GridWorld scenarios. We demonstrate that graph-based information significantly impacts the predicted actions in these scenarios. Additionally, we propose SymbolicQ, a symbolic reinforcement learning method that extracts and utilizes action-oriented subgraphs from policies trained using Q-functions via deep reinforcement learning. By integrating these subgraphs into logical rules, SymbolicQ can directly generate near-optimal policies in environments where we have prior knowledge of their dynamics. We evaluate these methodologies on a variety of settings, including partial observations, discrete action spaces, and partial observability in GridWorld scenarios. We compare the action-oriented subgraphs extracted by various symbolic reinforcement learning methods from multiple original reinforcement learning baselines and highlight their distinct strengths in terms of transparency, data efficiency, sample efficiency, adaptability, and scalability. While the extracted subgraphs may not surpass the performance of the original reinforcement learning baselines in most cases, they have the potential to improve several crucial aspects of reinforcement learning. For instance, they can enhance data efficiency by reducing the required number of samples, as well as promote policy transparency, flexibility, and adaptability. This research indicates that the integration of symbolic elements from prior knowledge or from automated extraction from demonstrated policies has the potential to improve the overall performance of reinforcement learning in certain scenarios. Furthermore, the extracted subgraphs can facilitate the explanation of learned policies. In some cases, the subgraphs have predictive information that complements the original reinforcement learning baselines, while in other instances, they possess information that directly improves the original reinforcement learning baselines. Overall, the results suggest that the incorporation of symbolic elements from prior knowledge or from automated extraction from prior experience or demonstrated policies has the potential to improve the overall performance of reinforcement learning in certain scenarios. In some cases, the subgraphs have predictive information that complements the original reinforcement learning baselines, while in other instances, they can directly improve the original reinforcement learning baselines. This methodology leverages a collection of point spread functions, which describes the blur kernels, to recover high-resolution images from their low-resolution counterparts. Notably, by imposing a structure on these kernels, the process of image deblurring becomes more robust and effective. In this research, a novel kernel regularization technique is introduced, which enhances the precision of the deblurring process. Furthermore, a GPU-based implementation was developed to facilitate the kernel shrinkage process. Using a large dataset of images, the efficacy of the proposed technique was demonstrated through comprehensive testing on various datasets. Interestingly, the approach yielded significantly better outcomes when compared to other advanced deblurring techniques, even when the data on blur kernels was incomplete or inaccurate. Notably, the highest level of image enhancement was achieved for datasets with highly regulated structures, which in turn significantly contributed to the overall performance. Crucially, the proposed technique outperformed current state-of-the-art methods by achieving a notable 63% increase in SSIM scores, 33% increase in PSNR, and 81% increase in MSI scores. Accurate representation of uncertainty in object detection is challenging due to potential errors in training data, object masks, and object detection algorithms themselves. While standard approaches cannot fully address this challenge, we introduce BayesOD, an object detection framework that leverages an occupancy grid to represent uncertainty and assess detection reliability. By utilizing an occupancy grid, BayesOD enables the refinement of its own weights through Bayesian estimation, enabling the incorporation of prior knowledge and initial object detection results. This innovative framework also incorporates an object mask that contributes to the refinement of object detection under uncertain conditions. Experimental evaluations conducted on the BDD100K and KITTI datasets reveal that BayesOD outperforms other approaches in terms of object detection accuracy, especially in cases of uncertain environment, missing data, and object occlusion. Moreover, BayesOD's uncertainty estimates prove effective in object tracking applications, while further enhancements to BayesOD's performance can be achieved through the incorporation of an object tracking module. BayesOD's source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/hi-gaochang/BayesOD. This research is a significant advancement in object detection uncertainty analysis and has significant potential for real-world applications. Furthermore, our analysis of the BDD100K dataset uncovers biases in object detection, particularly towards minoritiy groups. This finding is presented in the paper's supplementary material. BayesOD's innovative approach has the potential to be expanded to other applications, such as semantic segmentation. Private data processing often employs a mechanism to protect privacy by adding noise to the data. This study focuses on mechanisms for quadratic optimization problems, specifically those that minimize differential privacy's overhead. An improved mechanism, based on the Huber mechanism, is developed, which meets differential privacy guarantees, has a more flexible range than the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, and provides quantitative guarantees on its utility. This new mechanism outperforms its alternatives in terms of mean-squared error. A thorough examination of its performance, including its ability to handle varying data dimensions and sizes, is also conducted. Experimental results show that the proposed mechanism's performance is largely unaffected by dimensionality but can benefit from data growth. This study's findings, code repository at https://github.com/quantum-privacy/Huber_Mechanism_Diff_Priv, and open-source implementations at https://github.com/quantum-privacy/Laplace_Mechanism_Diff_Priv and https://github.com/quantum-privacy/Gaussian_Mechanism_Diff_Priv confirm that quantitative utility guarantees are feasible to obtain. Furthermore, the proposed mechanism's development and utilization involve minimal additional overhead. Open-source implementations of the proposed mechanism are made available at https://github.com/quantum-privacy/Huber_Mechanism_Diff_Priv.
