At data sizes of 1000 and above, its performance is largely similar to that of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, demonstrating its scalability. When data dimensions are extensive, its performance approaches that of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, demonstrating its relative insensitivity to data dimensions. Notably, the proposed mechanism's performance is largely independent of the number of parameters in the quadratic loss function. Overall, the proposed mechanism's performance is largely consistent with that of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, while offering improved privacy and more flexible differential privacy guarantees. The models suggest that to accurately explain the observed polarization patterns in nearby molecular clouds, dust particles must be aligned in a specific way. If these particles were cap-shaped, the patterns would appear different, but the observed alignment would still be possible. EMCCIs (extinction features) in its HST-F160W images reveal spiral arms caused by material depressed by the planet. By correlating these EMCCIs with VLA-CMWA dust emission maps, researchers discovered linked features, suggesting the spiral arms originate from underlying gas structures. Analyzing the features, they found the spiral arms rotate in sync with the disk's overall rotation, but with varying patterns in their eastern and western branches. What's more, the ratio of light to gas density in the observed spiral features is significantly higher than in the rest of the disk. These findings indicate the planet not only impacts dust distribution but also greatly influences gas distribution. Consequently, the spiral arms generated by the planet have profound effects on disk structures and may provide crucial insights into planet formation and evolution. As such, using near-infrared extinction measures like those in the HST-F160W band, offers a promising avenue for identifying and studying massive planets through disk observations. Further research is needed to understand how massive planets affect disk structures, especially in determining how these objects influence the evolution of their parent disks and the accompanying increase in planet mass. In addition, investigating the relationship between planet mass and the impact it has on disk structures may help set an upper limit on the number of massive planets that can exist in a given disk. In the near future, the WFIRST-SPIRALS program may find SPITE-like disks through an intermediate band at 4700 Angstroms with high sensitivity, leading to the detection of spiral arms generated by massive planets. The operation of the telescope in an all-sky survey will provide researchers with a complete understanding of the demographics of such disks, whether they host single or multiple massive planets. The combination of all these factors highlights the remarkable potential of operating near-infrared space-based observatories to study planetary formation. The reuse of the LUVOIR-A 122nm channel with zoom modes, especially when paired with its polarization analysis, may allow researchers to directly detect massive planets themselves by analyzing polarization in their vicinity and relationship to their depression effect in dust emission, providing insight into their orientation. The family of abstract interpreations in programming languages has achieved significant precision, yet its potential for improvement remains largely unexplored. Researchers have overlooked analyzing different approximations simultaneously during interpretation, considering them as distinct approaches. This paper presents a modified interpretation called abstract values with attributes, combining multiple approximations concurrently. This new model enables the incorporation of various attributes for each abstract value, allowing the specification of intricate, attribute-dependent data flow relationships. To facilitate the implementation of complex attributes, a abstract domain based on zones has been designed to efficiently manage extensive state descriptions. A description of ZZA, a language used for demonstrating the proposed approach's benefits, is provided. Furthermore, we illustrate how to apply this new abstract domain to analyze a function from the CompCert C compiler verification project. Initial results suggest a significant increase, up to 50%, in accuracy over more conservative approaches. This research shows that pairing multiple attributes can lead to substantial gains in accuracy without additional complexity. The proposed abstract domain and its implementation are available online at https://github.com/abstract-values/zzza. All demonstrations and evaluations can be accessed at https://zzza.lang.cea.fr. A brief demonstration of the tool is also presented at the Steganography Workshop 2020 (virtual event), following this presentation's schedule. MRPG's data processing is based on hierarchical clustering of shared data across nodes, ensuring optimal data distribution. Two types of proximity graphs, APG and DP, are proposed to accommodate data that needs to be aggregated as well as data with individual records. Experimental results confirm the superiority of MRPG over traditional approaches in outlier detection, with benefits including reduced data transmission, improved data quality, increased efficiency, and a more general applicable algorithm. MRPG's scalability and effectiveness were validated through experiments using real-world data sets, producing high-quality outputs and minimizing the number of generated graph nodes. MRPG's proposed distance metrics and graph structures can be used as a standalone technique or integrated with other data mining methods to enhance their functionality. MRPG's effectiveness in real-world applications extends beyond outlier detection to encompass various data analysis tasks, including data alignment, association analysis, and parallel visualization, making it a versatile and essential tool for data miners. MRPG can be applied to various types of data, including data sets with complex structures as well as simple numerical data. To promote in-depth research in this area, MRPG serves as an ideal teaching tool in various data analysis courses. MRPG's proposed proxy nodes optimize its functionality and improve its performance. Enforcing neighborhood fairness in graph representation learning through graph neural networks is crucial as it greatly impacts both the accuracy and generalizability of the models. While there's a common technique to weight updates based on the distance between nodes, it has limitations and becomes less effective for larger graphs. We introduce a new approach that guarantees fairness in the neighborhood for all graphs regardless of size, by assigning a weighted edge between neighboring nodes based on the similarity between their respective node features. This is achieved through a novel edge weighting method combining random walks with feature matching, and can be trained using an adversarial approach or through a regularization method based on the edge weights. In our experiments, we find that this approach outperforms existing distance-based techniques, and achieves better results than state-of-the-art models that don't enforce neighborhood fairness, on tasks such as node classification and link prediction. We also show that this technique is useful for understanding human behavior in social processes within graphs, and provide additional insights by analyzing the edge weights in larger graphs. All code and datasets used in this research are available on GitHub under https://github.com/graphlearning/NEF-GNN. We open-source the code to facilitate replication and enable others to apply the NEF-GNN method to various graph-based tasks. Furthermore, a new benchmark dataset titled FAIR-Bench can be found at https://github.com/graphlearning/FAIR-Bench, that measures the fairness of different graph neural network models after training. The datasets demonstrate that widely-used graph neural network models exhibit significant and sometimes severe fairness issues, and there's substantial room for improvement over current baseline models on tasks such as node classification and link prediction. The datasets are contributed in partnership with the graphnetX organization, aiming to provide a framework for the graph machine learning community to prioritize fairness when developing new models. We hope that implementing a framework for measuring and evaluating fairness will prompt the development of more fair and responsible graph neural network models. As an additional contribution, a new dataset titled Growth-Fair-Bench at https://github.com/graphlearning/Growth-Fair-Bench provides a quantitative measurement of fairness during the training process, and demonstrates that edge weighting based on the novel method NEF-GNN achieves growth-fairness without compromising accuracy, and highlights the potential of incorporating fairness constraints during the training phase to facilitate robustness, accuracy, and generalizability. Investigating the dynamics of complex systems like financial bubbles is essential to understanding their nature and potential downfall. Our research focuses on a discrete-time market model that incorporates an automatic correction mechanism, thereby giving rise to binary or ternary systems with random phase cycles. The existence of this mechanism, along with asymmetry, is crucial in explaining the sudden collapse of bubbles. By analyzing the inherent properties of these systems, we've been able to categorize the potential outcomes of market transactions in terms of feedback strength and asymmetry levels. Given that binary systems exhibit unique behaviors, we've identified distinct transition patterns between different orbits within a specific parameter range. Moreover, our findings suggest that the set of feasible solutions is vast and diverse. To further validate our research, we've carried out numerous market simulations, yielding results that align with theoretical predictions. Specifically, our simulations indicate that in markets with dominant players, a distinct pattern of transaction activity can emerge, characterized by a high frequency of sales during the initial phase of the cycle. Moreover, our results show that in markets with relatively small asymmetry, a reversible process can occur, caused by a shift in cycle direction. These outcomes highlight the significant role of non-linear feedback mechanisms in understanding and modeling the sudden collapse of financial bubbles and other similar phenomena. Ultimately, our research provides valuable insights into diversification and investment strategies, drawing from the analysis of these market models. A supplementary code is available for replication purposes at this link: https://github.com/Adolfo-Chavez/Critical-Systems-with-Feedback. Additionally, we present a new model for analyzing the sudden collapse of financial bubbles, founded on a fundamental principle: that speculation can give rise to a distinct pattern of transaction activity, distinct from other mechanisms driving the phenomenon. The underlying idea stems from a simple observation: when the price of a good rises, buyers are willing to pay more, yet sellers, being more rational and informed, take advantage of this situation, thereby explaining the phenomenon in terms of feedback mechanisms. Inspired by a previous study on critical systems without feedback, we've developed a new model for analyzing the feasible solutions set and simulated market transactions within this framework. The outcomes of these simulations have allowed us to quantify the significant role of non-linear feedback mechanisms, along with asymmetry, in determining the sudden collapse of financial bubbles and other similar events. While human reviews contain valuable insights that guide people in making informed decisions, most recommender systems have not effectively utilized this information due to lacking techniques to process interactive elements. To address this, our work focuses on uncovering the significance of reviews containing interactive features and develops a new model that efficiently incorporates such features. The interactions within reviews indicate how various items are connected. Therefore, our review-based recommender system constructs a bipartite graph from review data and uses a convolutional neural network to encode the interactive features into latent vectors. By incorporating these features into a neural network, our model generates more accurate rating predictions. Empirical tests conducted using the Yelp and IMDB datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms other methods, with a notable improvement of over 13% in rating prediction accuracy when training and testing data come from the same source, and a notable improvement of 15% when testing data is unknown in advance. Our research shows that interactive elements in reviews have a substantial impact on people's final ratings. As a result, our approach yields around a 1% increase in the accuracy of rating predictions compared to other methods. Moreover, our work has the potential to be extended to other applications, such as natural language processing and computer vision. Furthermore, our approach can be used to recommend items based on reviews containing text and mixed media in the future. Two supplementary methods have also been developed to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach under different conditions. First, a training data augmentation strategy is implemented to handle situations where limited data is available. Second, a transfer learning technique is developed to leverage data from a related task under the assumption that data is unknown in advance. Both techniques yield satisfying results and provide a basis for further research in the field. Overall, our work provides valuable insights into how interactive features within reviews contribute to rating predictions and has the potential to be a cornerstone in many areas of recommender systems. The expansion of our approach to mixed media is inevitable given the widespread use of text-based reviews and mixed media feedback. Furthermore, our approach offers a more comprehensive understanding of how interactive elements within reviews influence people's final ratings and provides a basis for further research in the field. Ultimately, our work serves as a fundamental component in many areas of recommender systems. Currently, synthetic data is widely utilized in the research of code-switching, particularly for addressed queries and generation tasks, as it permits the creation of considerable amounts within restricted natural language scenarios. Prior studies have successfully utilized copied or modified individual words from existing datasets with satisfactory results. We hypothesize that altering segments rather than single words could lead to more effective data enhancement. Consequently, we have developed a Search-Based Synthesis algorithm that rearranges segments in existing texts by identifying the most suitable orders using a learned transformer model. Our results also reveal that the synthesized data is often indistinguishable from human-generated code-switching data, with 90% of its sentences scored as perfect by humans. A mesh's accuracy depends on the quality of its individual elements. Mesh quality metrics are utilized to evaluate and improve meshes. However, a major challenge arises when employing these metrics on unstructured meshes, often resulting in data sparsity and irregularity. Mesh decomposition is used to overcome this issue by dividing a mesh into local regions, each associated with a mesh element, and assigning a quality metric value to a point within each area. Previous methods for decomposing meshes focused either on linear functions or completely avoided sparse regions. This paper presents an efficient and robust mesh decomposition approach that overcomes these limitations by employing generalized gradient fields to fill in sparse areas and account for non-linear element quality metrics. This method is flexible and can be adapted to multiple mesh quality metrics. Its performance is demonstrated using several test cases involving different quality metrics, two types of mesh decomposition schemes, and various input meshes. The results show that this method significantly outperforms existing mesh decomposition approaches in terms of result precision. Furthermore, this method's applicability is extended to boundary representation meshes, allowing for the decomposition of surfaces as well. This method is versatile and adaptable, enabling the utilization of different mesh quality metrics for specific applications. Knowledge graph link prediction focuses on forecasting links that are missing between well-known entities and their relations on extensive knowledge graphs like NELL and TREC.  Link prediction on these graphs leverages information from extracted data gathered through various methods like NLP and human-guided input over TREC.  Recent studies have shown that connection-based models, which base their decisions on the surrounding link connections, perform much better than attribute-based models.  However, the top-performing connection-based models for TREC, which relies on node embeddings, experience significant decreases in their accuracy during the forecasting process due to loss of memory during subsequent forecasting stages.  To overcome this limitation, researchers proposed an attentional model called NetARC that employs connection attention to process connections layer-wise while remembering key connections in a short-term memory module for enhanced relationship forecasting, resulting in NetARC achieving 0.3308 MRR on TREC-9 and TREC-11 datasets in single-step forecasting and 0.3309 and 0.3152 on TREC-9 and TREC-11 in multi-step, outperforming the then-current top models by approximately 5% and 10%.  NetARC's design also enabled it to serve as a connection filter to process connections in knowledge graphs in conjunction with existing graph-based models for further improved forecasting performance.  NetARC's design offers a unique short-term memory module called NetARC-MEM to retain information from extracted data gathered through human-guided input over TREC, resulting in NetARC-MEM achieving 0.3366 MRR on TREC-9 and 0.3179 MRR on TREC-11.  NetARC and its variants significantly outperformed the then-current top models by approximately 10% on TREC-9 and 15% on TREC-11 in single-step forecasting and 0.3309 MRR on TREC-9 and 0.3152 MRR on TREC-11 in multi-step, outperforming the then-current top models by approximately 10% on TREC-9 and 15% on TREC-11 in single-step and 0.5174 S@10 on TREC-9 and 0.4942 S@10 on TREC-11 in top-K prediction.  NetARC's design also enabled it to compete with the then-current top models in top-K prediction on TREC-9 and TREC-11 by achieving S@10 of 0.5174 and 0.4942.

Offline reinforcement learning presents a significant challenge in large complex state-space scenarios. In our research, we introduce a new criterion for evaluating the smoothness of policies, which targets reducing noise in observations and actions. Since our criterion is based on differences in policy outputs at closely adjacent states, it effectively handles noisy action inputs. Furthermore, we develop a new offline policy distillation framework, which incorporates the smoothed policy gradient approximation. To improve learning efficiency, we modify the distillation loss function and leverage a dynamic threshold to filter out unstable data samples. Theoretical analysis confirms that the distillation loss converges to zero. Experimental results show that the proposed method distills more stable policies than traditional loss minimization, and outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on visual planning tasks. The methods introduced in this work are implemented in code available at: \begin{code} https://github.com/ziyi-chen/Offline Policy Distillation\end{code}. All evaluated datasets are from publicly accessible sources. 

Please note that a prior discussion on this topic can be found at: \begin{code} https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.14260\end{code}.

We've developed a novel filter that maintains consistency when solving PDE-based problems with polynomial approximations. Inconsistent results have been an issue for previous polynomial-based methods due to low-order terms being overshadowed by high-order terms. Our proposed filter is structured in a way that it doesn't have a non-zero threshold, yet it's still capable of removing numerical oscillations that occur during the Runge-Kutta based spatial polynomial approximation of first-order PDEs. This is achieved by identifying and removing low-order components that aren't contributing to the solution, effectively reducing computational costs. We show through theoretical analysis and numerical testing that this filter is suitable for various applications and maintains the smoothness of the solution with minimal error. One notable benefit is that it allows for the preservation of essential structural properties that are critical for many real-world PDE-based problems, including incompressible fluid dynamics, where preserving div-free velocity vectors is crucial, for example. This is problematic for previous polynomial-based methods as they can't guarantee div-free velocity vectors. We demonstrate through numerical testing how our proposed filter successfully preserves structural properties, while significantly reducing error at the same time, outperforming other approximation techniques such as Gaussian processes and radial basis functions in the process. This is particularly notable in the simulation of incompressible fluid dynamics, where preserving structural properties is critical. We also show through numerical testing how our proposed filter successfully reduces error and preserves structural properties in the simulation of elliptic PDEs with constraints, without the need for additional regularization in the process. This is an additional benefit of the proposed filter in this context. Additionally, we've successfully applied the proposed filter in the simulation of more complex PDE-based problems, such as nonlinear transport equations, where reducing error and preserving structural properties is critical. Our proposed filter is compatible with existing polynomial-based methods, which means it can be easily integrated into existing systems with minimal disruption to performance, for example. One of the main obstacles to applying Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning to real-world scenarios is achieving a high level of coordination among collaborative agents. To enhance the quality of interactions within these environments, we focus on increasing the 'empowerment' - the common benefit gained by agents working together - during the training process. This goal is achieved through the introduction of a new transfer learning mechanism, where the knowledge gained from a source domain is optimized to yield maximum empowerment in a target domain. By implementing this innovation in the MAXIMILE algorithm, which integrates inter-action and intra-action maximization to promote coordination, we show empirically that the resulting algorithm, transfer MAXIMILE (tMAXIMILE), enhances empowerment levels in varied transfer scenarios across different benchmark scenarios. Additionally, the model's capacity to adapt knowledge can be controlled dynamically via a new measure of transfer empowerment, facilitating smarter allocation of knowledge resources. This new transfer empowerment measure also provides valuable, domain-independent performance gauges for assessing empowerment in various contexts. Overall, the incorporation of the tMAXIMILE algorithm leads to notable improvements in coordination and convergence rates compared to other approaches, underscoring its potential to enhance multi-agent reinforcement learning systems. The shape of a magnetic active region plays a crucial role in various atmospheric processes, but it is often overlooked in observations and data analysis. To address this gap, fill fraction maps based on 2-D magnetic field data can be created. These maps, however, typically only account for magnetic polarity and overestimate the actual shape of the active region. To develop a more accurate representation, we introduce a new approach that utilizes three-dimensional magnetic field data to determine the shape of active regions. By doing so, we can generate more precise polygon maps with improved completeness. Our findings reveal that incorporating fill fraction based on three-dimensional magnetic field data can reduce errors by a factor of two, with average errors less than one pixel. Furthermore, we find that utilizing complete 3D magnetic field data can precisely define the shape of active regions with an accuracy of better than one pixel. This new method will enable the creation of more accurate polygon data, facilitating better mapping and statistical analysis of active regions on the solar surface. In particular, we can leverage this technology to develop larger, high-resolution active region polygon datasets, allowing for the study of region statistics, evolution, and classification. In the near future, high-resolution, three-dimensional magnetic field data for both the Western Hemisphere Active Region Label Catalog and the Global Dynamic Sun Catalog will become available, enabling more precise active region shape data. Consequently, we can derive more accurate statistical insights from this data, enhancing our understanding of active region evolution and shape. To illustrate this, we demonstrate that a three-dimensional reconstruction of active region 11942 can significantly improve the accuracy of its shape when compared to single atmospheric layer observations. By leveraging modern computational capabilities and advanced machine learning algorithms, we can achieve even greater speed and efficiency in this data analysis. In the long term, we can expand upon the concept of active region shape data by developing three-dimensional reconstructions of entire active regions, active region groups, and even solar belts, enabling a more comprehensive and accurate understanding of the shape of three-dimensional magnetic fields and their impact on the solar atmosphere and heliosphere. This is achieved by investigating the speed of convergence for averages of a polynomial $P(\sum_{t=1}^k T_{t_j})$ with real coefficients over various time sums $\sum_{t=1}^k t_{j}$. A prior hypothesis that a spectral gap is needed for such convergence is thus invalidated. For specific, broad families of polynomials, particularly those with increasing or decreasing coefficient values, the speed of convergence for averages $\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m P(\sum_{t=1}^k t_{i})$ is precisely determined as $O(1)$ plus a universally minimum estimate of $\frac{1}{\sum_{t=1}^k t_j}$ multiplied by a particular weighted sum, specifically $\sum_{j=1}^k \frac{t_j}{\sum_{s=1}^{t_j} (t_s - 1)}$. Additionally, broader bounds applicable to any polynomial are formulated. The objective of this research is to achieve greater insight into the inner accretion disk of cygnus A through high-resolution spectroscopy using the ALMA system. We specifically aim to identify specific spectral lines that can help measure pressure and the temperature conditions within the disk. We analyzed the 1mm continuum spectrum of cygnus A to find out if its emission can provide the pressure and temperature information we need. We also examined the emission from several atomic species, including Fe, Si, and O, to see how it correlates with the emission from a primary gas, such as H2. Using the emission from these species in their ground state, we were able to determine the pressure and temperature conditions in the disk, but the results were not consistent. Furthermore, we were able to see the emission from Fe, specifically its transition at rest, but were unable to measure its higher energy transitions. This led to the development of a new method to determine iron abundance by comparing the emission from Fe to that of a primary gas, such as H2. By using this new method and a model of a parabolic disk, we were able to see how iron abundance at different points on the disk correlated with its emission at 545.09 nm. We were specifically able to see a negative correlation between iron abundance and the emission from a region about 0.1 parsecs from the center of cygnus A. Our findings also showed that metallicity can be determined from the emission from a region about 0 to 0.5 parsecs from the center of cygnus A. By using iron abundance and a pressure estimate derived from the emission of a primary gas, such as molecular hydrogen, we were able to see a negative correlation with the emission from a region about 0.5 parsecs from the center of cygnus A. Analysis of Greece's aerial imagery to track wildfires has become more automated thanks to a developed method. By utilizing Google Cloud Vision API to process images, the number of flames in each image can be estimated in near real-time. Though the model trains on images from specific regions, its application is not limited to those areas. By testing the model during the 2020 and 2021 fire seasons, it was found that certain areas showed an increase in active fires. Specifically, the Peloponnese and Crete regions, which have experienced a higher number of active fires in recent years, were identified. Furthermore, there was a positive correlation between the model's estimates and data from Hellenic National Meteorological Service regarding temperature and precipitation. While the model can provide rapid estimates, it may be less accurate compared to more resource-intensive statistics from Hellenic National Meteorological Service. The model requires both image data and label data to improve its performance in detecting flames. Additionally, there was a discrepancy in the model's estimates during the 2021 fire season due to its training data limitations. Therefore, the model is most effective when used in specific geographic areas with adequate training data. We utilized typological variables from the World Atlas of Language Structures to represent a language's properties, such as word order, sentence structure, and word morphology. We computed other complexity metrics like word length, syntactic density, and morphological complexity from the Universal Dependencies treebank. We obtained these data for 59 languages from the Language Atlas of the Americas and the Eurotype databases, and for 104 languages from the WALS and UD repositories combined. We discovered significant correlations between typological variables and morphology-related complexity metrics. Notably, we found that the typological variable related to morphological complexity showed the strongest connection with another typological variable also indicating complexity. This association was however lower than one observed between a particular typological variable and another complexity metric that simply measures sentence density. We discussed these findings with existing research on language complexity and attempted to explain them through the nature of typological variables and their representative powers. We further supported our results from two case studies involving the Shuar and Portuguese languages. In these analyses, we found the typological variable related to morphological complexity was able to classify languages into their respective morphological types with 81% accuracy. We observed similar accuracy using the HLD for lexical typology in a classification experiment. We discovered hypotaxis consistently occurred in biclausal sentences in the data, while in most cases parataaxis occurred in monoclausal sentences, but with some exceptions. We argued that hypotaxis and parataxis have similar characteristics and properties, leading to confusion in their classification. This paper presents an event detection system that identifies significant occurrences, such as natural disasters and traffic congestion, within spatially aggregated social media data. The system acknowledges that different areas possess distinct resolutions of events and incorporates a novel approach to capture these events at various granularities. We achieve this by modeling the relationships between social media posts and events within a specified area, as well as their associations with neighboring regions. The proposed method is scalable and adaptable, allowing it to be applied efficiently and repeatedly to multiple geographic areas without capturing events at coarser resolutions. We test the system's effectiveness in three areas - a 5km radius in Singapore, a 10km radius in Singapore, and a 1 mile radius in Philadelphia - using actual data and a baseline method. The results show that the proposed approach surpasses the baseline method in detecting events in the 5km and 10km Singapore scenarios and the 1-mile Philadelphia scenario. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/ChengChiehChou/EventText. Additionally, the relevant data can be accessed at https://data.scienss.org/eventdetect. We intend for this dataset to facilitate further research in spatio-temporal event detection. The proposed approach has been successfully implemented as a cloud-based application, accessible via http://eventdetect.cloud. We also provide access to interactive visualizations of our results at http://socialmartools.cloud. Finally, the project's source code can be found at https://github.com/ChengChiehChou/SocialMart. We intend for this code to serve as a foundation for reproducing our findings and developing new techniques. Bidding algorithms play a crucial role in the Digital Market, with researchers increasingly focusing on modeling risk tendency to optimize online pricing strategies. This study proposes an expert knowledge-based framework for modeling risk tendency and outlines the key characteristics of this approach, which is grounded in statistical analysis and probabilistic modeling. The formulation is compatible with a wide range of distribution models, can be used in both continuous and discrete bidding processes, and allows for the incorporation of uncertainty through stochastic processes. The framework encompasses various stochastic models of risk tendency, each with a range of attributes tailored to specific bidding algorithms, such as auction types and pricing frequencies. To facilitate easy integration with bidding algorithms, stochastic risk tendency models are presented as deterministic functions, and a comprehensive catalog of these models is provided for future reference. The thesis includes an empirical validation of one such stochastic risk tendency model, which demonstrates a notable improvement in performance and stability metrics, including Mean Absolute Error, Standard Deviation, and Coefficient of Variation. Additionally, this model outperforms a naive approach in real-world simulations of online bidding processes. The study concludes by outlining key challenges and potential research directions associated with modeling risk tendency for bidding algorithms. These challenges include addressing uncertainty in probabilistic models, overcoming issues of limited historical data, and striking an balance between conservative pricing and optimal revenue. The proposed framework is a foundational step in modeling risk tendency for a diverse range of bidding algorithms, which are increasingly employed by market makers and are soon to be widely available as a pre-configured default on market making platforms. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the development of a Market Simulator, which will enable researchers to investigate the interplay between market mechanisms, stochastic risk tendency, and bidding algorithm behavior in a holistic system. As another significant outcome of this study, this Market Simulator will serve as a tool for synthetic data generation, which is currently scarce and difficult to procure in the field of Digital Markets. The research is now poised to explore the reverse problem of feature selection and design, which involves identifying the most relevant attributes of stochastic risk tendency models to optimize. In the final section of this thesis, we describe an initial implementation of this concept, which is known as Feature Engineering for Stochastic Risk Tendency Models. The study concludes by outlining its current status, highlighting that the field of Feature Engineering has received relatively limited attention, and that this work represents an innovative application of this concept to modeling risk tendency for a diverse range of bidding algorithms. The implementation of BCHF in existing reinforcement learning systems provides a straightforward way to integrate human feedback in a variety of applications. Given its ease of use and capacity to accelerate the learning process across diverse tasks, we suggest that BCHF is an ideal choice for reinforcement learning tasks requiring human feedback. We examine the properties of this discrete distribution, particularly as m is increased, to show that it converges to the original Extreme Value Type I distribution. We then compare the posterior distributions of the estimated parameters using Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations for different values of m. The results indicate that the chosen Bayesian model achieves convergence to the correct distribution as m is increased, but may be sensitive to the initial choice of m. To resolve this issue, we propose the use of a "bridging" technique, effectively selecting m=1 and then increasing it in a second analysis, which was found to enhance convergence and provide accurate parameter estimates. Furthermore, we investigated model comparisons using posterior model probabilities and Bayes factors, showing that the proposed Bayesian model outperforms competing models and suggests that parameter estimates from these models can be refined using the Bayes factor method. We performed similar investigations for the generalized extreme value distribution, reaching analogous conclusions. To validate these findings, we tested the Bayesian model on real-world datasets, specifically the annual maxima of significant daily precipitation in Toronto, Canada, and daily extremes of sugar-lacounty lobster prices in South Africa, applying both a distribution-free approach and a more informative one with prior knowledge. The results from the distribution-free approach matched those of the discrete Bayesian model, while the informative prior yielded estimates that varied depending on the chosen parameters, with some estimates suggesting a non-zero shape parameter for the generalized extreme value distribution. Consequently, the distribution-free approach appeared to provide the most reliable results in this case. To facilitate future research, we have made our code available for replication purposes. We focus on the impact of systemic financial shocks on real economies. We develop a quantitative model that captures the prevalent view among economists: small shocks have limited effects, but severe shocks lead to significant declines in output and employment. Our model indicates this narrative holds true when considering widespread negative evidence. We reveal the differential effects of shocks on employment and output are a direct result of the combined outcomes of employment and output declines. Notably, while multi-factor shocks result in greater variations in outcomes, when accounting for these variations, there is no notable disparity in the impact of multi-factor versus binary directional shocks. Furthermore, in the context of the recent Great Recession, our model outperforms existing DSGE models. Its capabilities can be extended to analyze the effects of anticipated and coordinated fiscal policies intended to mitigate the consequences of multi-directional financial shocks, providing evidence that such policies could reduce unemployment. Finally, using regression-based discrete choice procedures, we derive a probabilistic framework for characterizing the likelihood of events, including the direction and size of financial shocks. We discover a notable pattern where, during the 2007 Great Recession, the frequency of negative equity wealth loss increased in response to increasing home prices. This counterintuitive result can be attributed to greater multi-factor shock probability, which was prevalent during the recession. We also find that the likelihood of job destruction was greater during the recession when home prices fell and job destruction was more frequent in states with higher home prices. In contrast, the frequency of job destruction when home prices rose did not exhibit a notable relationship. The results can be extended to other contexts, such as a analysis of Great Recession data that shows the states with the highest home prices experienced greater unemployment. However, the direction of the association between home prices and unemployment in other contexts is inconsistent with the results. The model's probabilistic framework can be utilized to determine the potential benefits and costs of multi-directional fiscal policy interventions. For illustration purposes, we can determine the approximate number of jobs that could be saved through a multi-directional fiscal policy in 2009, which had a probability of occurrence of about 25%. We find such a policy could yield a net benefit of $12 billion if implemented, with an 80% likelihood of reduced unemployment, but with a 60% likelihood if it led to increased unemployment. In the NER domain, entity typing has garnered significant attention, with a primary goal of categorizing entities within a corpus into precise subsets. Although existing approaches have made notable strides, they often rely on limited, hand-crafted rules for entity descriptions. To overcome this limitation, the FGNET-RH framework introduces a novel rule-based model that utilizes pre-trained BERT vectors as input. This model refines the accuracy of entity descriptions through a series of transformer-based operations, ultimately facilitating precise typing predictions. Furthermore, the proposed framework enables seamless integration with various existing models, thereby allowing comprehensive evaluation against over a dozen state-of-the-art baselines. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed FGNET-RH framework achieves superior performance on TAC 2006 and 2007 datasets, with notable typing accuracy improvements of 2.0% and 4.2%. Moreover, the combined framework yields superior performance across all metrics on TAC 2008 and 2009 datasets, with notable improvements of 3.1%, 2.3%, and 2.1%. Overall, the proposed FGNET-RH framework offers a simple, adaptable solution for accurate entity typing. The framework's code and trained models are publicly available for download at the repository address: https://github.com/GuGuHu/FGNET-RH. Additionally, the framework's execution time is substantially faster, with a notable improvement of 2.3 times, and average memory usage that is 3.2 times lower, when compared to other combined models. A key issue with training Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) is finding the optimal balance between matching the true distribution and retaining a compact latent space. However, current VAE training methods often fail to monitor this balance during training. As a result, they can't adjust the trade-off between matching the true distribution and model complexity. Our proposed method, the Distribution Regulated VAE (DR-VAE), addresses this issue. It introduces a metric to measure the distribution mismatch after each training step and incorporates this metric as a balance factor to adjust the trade-off between matching the true distribution and model complexity. Our experiments demonstrate that DR-VAE remains focused on matching the true distribution throughout training. Additionally, DR-VAE's impact on sample quality can be fine-tuned by adjusting its sensitivity to distribution mismatch. Our method provides a systematic way to monitor VAE training progress and offer manual adjustments if needed. The DR-VAE method can be applied to any standard VAE model, as seen in our code open-source repository dr-vae, which also includes experiments with the CIFAR10, CelebA, and MNIST datasets. Furthermore, our research shows that DR-VAE's control mechanism can be used to investigate the cause of failure in VAEs when generating images. Our findings indicate that subpar image generation is often caused by poor fit to the true distribution, especially in early training stages. Utilizing DR-VAE's control mechanism may help identify potential improvements to VAE design or training strategies to overcome this limitation. As an alternative use case, DR-VAE can be employed to develop a "best effort" VAE model prioritizing latent space compactness even at the expense of distribution mismatch. Our proposed method expands the scope of interpretability in VAE training by monitoring learning progress and offering manual adjustments to achieve optimal balance between matching the true distribution and model complexity. Deep neural networks are highly sensitive to data labeling errors and often encounter situations where labels are incomplete or missing. To mitigate labeling issues, we explore the application of ensemble modeling to neural networks, particularly in a classification task. We developed an ensemble model that incorporates various architectures to improve accuracy in the presence of missing labels. Our proposed model demonstrates superior performance compared to the traditional mean model and achieves a high variance-reducing effect. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate the benefits of ensemble modeling when dealing with incomplete data, label noise, and a limited training dataset. Notably, the results suggest that the ensemble model performs well even with a training dataset comprising only 35 samples. To assess the ensemble model's performance under varying training data conditions, we employed the bootstrap resampling method and established confidence intervals for the model's performance. Our analysis reveals that the ensemble model's performance exhibits minimal variation when compared to other methods. In conclusion, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of ensemble modeling in improving the accuracy of deep neural networks when confronted with data labeling uncertainties. Furthermore, our use of bootstrap resampling to evaluate model performance accommodates uncertainty and prevents overconfidence, making the ensemble model a reliable choice for real-world applications. The proposed model's adaptability to multiple architectures and ability to mitigate labeling uncertainties and incomplete data make it a highly versatile deep learning framework. A general covering array, extended from the uniform covering array concept, allows its entries to be colored with different values and still maintain its covering property. We have developed an approach to directly construct a general covering array, which bypasses the requirement for a uniform one. By minimizing the group size and maximizing the groups counts in an optimal general covering array, we have also identified key factors to be considered during its construction. Additionally, this methodology has been applied to a real-world problem, covering the 20 distinct features listed in the Google Data Catalog. Our method allows for varying numbers of unique values across these 20 features. In the worst case, we have determined that a uniform general covering array can be constructed with a group size of 2 and specific group counts. We have also investigated the Berlekamp-Nietzche problem recharacterized as a general covering array problem and established a criterion for its solvability. Moreover, we have solved the Berlekamp-Nietzche problem for all prime numbers up to 37. Although a uniform solution to the Berlekamp-Nietzche problem is computationally feasible, a non-uniform solution is significantly more challenging. In the case of general numbers, we have found that a direct approach to the extended van der Loon problem, which involves finding a general covering array with a small number of colors, is more efficient than a method based on the van der Loon inverse. We have further proposed a generalization of the van der Loon problem to multidimensional matrices and developed an algorithm to address this problem. We utilize machine learning to analyze BPT diagrams for galaxy spectra, providing an objective method to distinguish between genuine and fake galaxies based on their emission properties. We train a BPT diagram recognition system using machine learning algorithms for a control sample with known genuine and fake labels. The system is then tested with an unlabeled dataset of BPT diagrams, with the goal of identifying those that are unlikely to belong to genuine galaxies. We evaluate the performance of this approach using accuracy, precision, and recall as key metrics. The results demonstrate that this system is capable of accurately distinguishing between genuine and fake galaxies, with an accuracy of 90% and a precision of 80%. Furthermore, we apply this framework to a large unlabeled dataset of MEGALODI galaxy spectra, identifying a subset of unlabeled galaxies with exceptional BPT diagram characteristics. We subsequently examine the BPT diagrams of these high-risk galaxies, revealing a substantial number with extreme values that are likely the result of non-physical processes in mock data or real galaxies with specific anomalies due to aging or hot massive black holes. Notably, a substantial number of these high-risk galaxies (40%) are actually genuine, underscoring the need to carefully assess the BPT diagrams of all unlabeled galaxies to prevent mistakenly eliminating genuine galaxies. We also compare the performance of this systematic approach with a random classifier in multiple experiments, with the results indicating that it is superior in most cases, particularly when evaluating samples with predominantly genuine data. However, the outcomes also show that a random classifier surpasses the systematic approach in scenarios with predominantly fake samples. Current action segmentation techniques rely heavily on video data containing clear labels of actions, making broad inference possible. However, these methods often fall short when dealing with novel and unseen actions, as they cannot draw on existing knowledge for classification. Our proposed Co-occurrence Action Parsing (CAP) algorithm overcomes this limitation by introducing a co-occurrence constraint to efficiently model complex action interactions. This extension empowers CAP to accurately identify and classify actions, even in the absence of explicit action labels in videos. As a result, CAP exhibits superior performance compared to contemporary action parsing methods, according to comprehensive experimental findings on the Kinetics400 and ActivityNet datasets. Furthermore, CAP remains computationally efficient, with its processing time comparable to existing approaches. Providing automated feedback to students is a potential strategy to enhance learning outcomes when taking online programming courses. This research investigates the impact of the specificity of feedback on the performance of students in a MongoDB course. The study divided students into three groups, providing one group with general feedback (such as "Correct!" or "Incorrect"), another with feedback explaining right and wrong answers (including "Code is correct/incorrect"), and a third group with detailed feedback (including "Code is correct/incorrect and here's why"). The study measured student performance by self-reported code coverage and exam scores in a multiple-choice exam. The results indicate that students receiving detailed feedback demonstrated higher code coverage and exam grades compared to those receiving general or partial feedback. This study demonstrates the value of providing detailed automated feedback to students to improve their performance. The data also suggests that students who receive general feedback may be less motivated to submit more trials, although this requires further validation. Overall, the data indicates a positive net benefit from providing detailed versus general or partial feedback. This benefit is estimated at 2.6% for code coverage and 4% for exam grades. Based on the actual number of submissions in the detailed group, the calculated net benefit is equivalent to around 65-95 additional submissions. In an actual course, this benefit would translate to around 370-570 additional submission trials compared to providing general or partial feedback. In light of these findings, course instructors may consider providing detailed automated feedback to improve student performance when teaching online programming courses. We developed a novel numerical approach based on the random vortex dynamics method and a lattice Boltzmann solver for the continuity equation to efficiently model three-dimensional fluid flow. By integrating vorticity-constrained methods, our algorithm ensures that the continuity equation is satisfied. The newly designed method overcomes the limitations of traditional random vortex dynamics by allowing large time steps without losing precision. The efficiency of our algorithm was evaluated in different scenarios by comparing it to experimental results when the exact solution was unknown. Additionally, the numerical results were validated by comparing them to the well-established methods of lattice Boltzmann and random vortex dynamics. Our approach was found to be comparable in accuracy to random vortex dynamics for flows with well-defined vorticity, but significantly faster for turbulent and complex flows. The newly developed method shows a significant potential for modeling complex three-dimensional fluid flows in practical applications. The associated C++ code to implement this new method is also made publicly available for further studies and evaluations. Further details can be found at the following repository: https://github.com/AMilani/rd-dyn. By publicly sharing our code, we aim to facilitate future research into the topic. In finite-horizon, partially-observable optimal control problems, where the environment's future optimal states of action are predicted using a recurrent neural network (RNN). The RNN's hidden states converge to a stationary distribution that reflects optimal state variable beliefs. Building on this, we developed two RNN-based policies, augmenting the RNN's hidden states with additional beliefs, which converge to estimates of the optimal state variable beliefs. The first policy uses a single neural network to capture the distribution of the system's state and the control variables. The second policy uses two neural networks to separately learn the system state and control beliefs. We tested these methods against models with known distributions and found that the methods effectively learn the distributions. Notably, we discovered that our methods yield significantly improved performance compared to a benchmark method when the environment's optimal policy is non-stationary. The experiments also highlight the benefits of factorizing the state variable distribution into multiple neural networks to achieve better performance. The results suggest that neural networks can be an effective tool for approximating the distributions of state variables in optimal control problems. Our approach to action detection in video analysis combines self-attention and Graph Convolutional Networks to identify temporal actions within video data. 

We utilize a video representation consisting of semantic actions and temporal relationships between them via the Long Short-Term Memory neural network. 

The integration of self-attention allows for the selective use of relationship information based on action duration lengths, while Graph Convolutional Networks convert this information into dense dense temporal action matrices.

Subsequent transformation of these matrices into diagonal binary binary forms enables the retrieval of their original corresponding action durations through inverse square root transformation. 

We demonstrate the efficacy of our novel diagonal binary transformation method over existing matrix decomposition techniques such as symmetric decomposition and Palter decomposition. 

We conduct a thorough evaluation of our method's performance on the UCF-101 and HMDB-51 datasets, achieving a mean average precision of 39.2 and 51.1, respectively. 

In comparison, other action detection algorithms like D2P-RCNN and TC-RNN, even with their significant increase in model complexity, were unable to match our results even under an equally resource-intensive training regime. 

Consequently, our research offers an innovative solution to the long-neglected problem of action duration lengths. As such, the generated human action duration lengths can serve as a supplementary input to other action detection models like RCNN. Our findings successfully establish a new high standard on the UCF-101 and HMDB-51 benchmark datasets. Our research code is publicly accessible at this GitHub repository. The far-ultraviolet regime is a valuable area of study for investigating the conditions within molecular clouds and the surrounding star-forming environments. Notably, the fluorescent emission from molecular hydrogen constitutes a considerable contributor to the overall intensity in this wavelength range within the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex. In this study, observations conducted with the Hubble Space Telescope's Goddard High Resolution Spectrograph across 160 square degrees of this complex revealed a total of 33 sources displaying intense far-ultraviolet radiation. These sources were determined to be young stellar objects based on their observations across multiple spectrographic settings. In contrast to earlier studies, the majority of these sources were found to be low-mass stars, and not photometrically detected prior to this observation. Furthermore, our analysis also revealed a correlation between the surface densities of dense molecular clouds and the intensity of far-ultraviolet radiation emanating from the young stellar objects. This relationship was specifically examined within specific filaments in Taurus. In addition to this, it was discovered that the fluorescent emission from the photodissociation regions within these filaments cannot adequately account for the observed far-ultraviolet intensity. Rather, it is proposed that the radiation from the young stellar objects themselves significantly contributes to the overall intensity in this wavelength range. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the far-ultraviolet regime is significantly influenced by the direct radiation from young stellar objects within molecular cloud complexes. Future studies should seek to leverage observations that are simultaneously obtained across optical and far-ultraviolet regimes in order to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the complex photodissociation processes occurring within molecular cloud environments. To improve the user experience, we propose several design modifications such as incorporating a 360-degree view and refining the joystick function. This research contributes to the understanding of telepresence robot usability, offering valuable insights for designing these robots for the future. Ultimately, our research goals are to inform design solutions from a user-centric perspective and foster more research on these robots from this user-centered research approach. Mafia is a multi-round, party-based game involving deception and social interaction. Its intricate dynamics, influenced by alignment, are relatively under-researched. This work utilizes an exploratory data analysis to shed light on the game's behavior. Our analysis, based on over 14,000 players from online Mafia games, reveals essential characteristics. We identify typical alignments for different roles, determine how effective each role is at eliminating opponents, and find the longest average lifespan for each role. By identifying frequent sequence combinations of role deaths, we gain a deeper understanding of the game's progression. These findings provide valuable insights for Mafia players. Furthermore, we discuss potential limitations and begin developing mathematical models to describe the game's behavior. Specifically, we derive an equation describing the average number of lives for each role. By establishing a mathematical framework, we set the stage for future research to transition from descriptive to predictive game analysis. Ultimately, our goal is to create a predictive model that can suggest roles and alignments during live Mafia games, an area we intend to explore in future works. The simulations revealed that multiple giant planets can emerge from a single disk by accreting material at different rates, which led to an expansion of their orbits due to interactions with the disk's pressure field. The cluster labels generated by Fuzzy k-means (FKM) are often considered a major drawback due to their unreliability in practical applications. To overcome this challenge, we present an innovative FKM optimization strategy. First, we alter the FKM objective function to minimize label uncertainty through the incorporation of entropy terms. Next, we frame this optimization problem in the context of the Lagrange multiplier method and apply the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to devise an efficient solution. The effectiveness of our approach is evaluated through comprehensive experiments and comparative analyses with established clustering methods. Notably, our proposed strategy outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in the accuracy of manual label assignment. Furthermore, with the incorporation of a knowledge-based regularization term, we modify the Adam algorithm to derive a learned attention mechanism for efficient label propagation, ultimately enhancing the accuracy of manual label assignment. The simplicity and adaptability of our attention mechanism make it easily integratable with various clustering algorithms. The resulting algorithm, dubbed ExFKM, significantly improves clustering performance over existing state-of-the-art methods, according to experimental results. The source code for this research is available online for public access. Ultimately, our research has the potential to accelerate future breakthroughs in the field of visual clustering. Containerization is now widespread, providing a virtual environment for processes to run in. The concept of resource limitation introduced the idea of constraining the resources available to processes. Building on these principles, virtualization and process management techniques enabled the development of application runtime environments. The next step was the orchestration of services, enabling the management of application lifecycle and resource allocation. Although service orchestration effectively manages resources, it lacks granular control over non-executable components, such as data. The Ozy container, a user-level virtualization solution, was developed to address this limitation by allowing for the deployment of functions that run on Ozy and interact with the filesystem through Unix sockets and filesystems. The Ozy Orchestration Container (OOC) was developed as a successor to service orchestration, enabling the deployment of multiple Ozy instances that engage in client-server interactions. The OOC provides benefits including reduced resource consumption, faster deployment times, improved security, and the ability to decouple functions at runtime. The OOC also enables the static analysis of code security during deployment time. The OOC prototype was implemented as a user-level daemon using Unix namespaces and the devio system to manage memory and processes. The OOC supports the creation, deployment, and management of Ozy instances and functions. Due to the limitations of user-space virtualization, the OOC does not support the untrusted execution of code in user-space. To showcase the OOC's capabilities, a deployment template called the Ozy template was developed to facilitate the deployment of functions on OpenTelemetry producers and consumers. The OOC and Ozy orchestration promise significant benefits in terms of resource management, security, and speed, with potential applications in the deployment of untrusted code on remote resources, the decoupling of in-transit data at runtime, and the development of hybrid orchestration frameworks that integrate multi-cloud and local resources. The OOC and Ozy orchestration can be used in the deployment of various use cases such as streaming data processing, the deployment of functions that run on hybrid and multi-cloud resources, the deployment of hybrid applications that integrate local and remote resources, the deployment of functions that run in hybrid multi-cloud and local resource environments and the deployment of functions that run in cross-domain cloud and local resource environments. Initially, we examined how pressure variations influence particle movement, emphasizing the unique conditions that must be met for pressure to affect particles in a stable environment. Pressure has the potential to significantly impact the growth of planets by influencing the dynamics of rings formed through gravitational clustering in protoplanetary discs. Pressure may enhance the development of rings in discs that experience low-level turbulence, but it likely has a minimal effect on rings formed in highly unstable environments. In the future, research into planet formation can benefit from considering the role of pressure in a comprehensive model of protoplanetary discs. Traditional machine learning methods make few model assumptions but offer no protection against data corruption, whereas robust learning techniques incorporate model assumptions to achieve resilience against various types of data corruption, typically using certificates or a designated corruption distribution. We contrast robust and non-robust learning by examining their dependence on model parameters. In a general analysis, we found that robust learning requires significantly more model parameter adjustments than non-robust learning, specifically an order of magnitude more in the polynomial regime and exponentially more in the Gaussian regime. To illustrate the relevance of our findings, we examined classification problems in deep learning and binary matrix multiplication in quantum learning, observing that robust learning tends to necessitate more model parameter adjustments across these different problem settings. These results show that robust learning techniques may suffer from slow convergence when applied to binary matrix multiplication, a problem known to be readily solvable in the non-robust case. Consequently, we developed a new approach to robust binary matrix multiplication and verified its effectiveness through empirical testing as well as an analysis of its sample and model complexity. Additionally, we explored an alternative method of robust learning, specifically mini-batch gradient descent with adversarial perturbations, and discovered that such an approach can be slow in the sample size relative to non-robust learning, specifically an exponential order of magnitude slower in the polynomial regime. To illustrate the slowness of this alternative method, we analyzed a simple binary classification task and computed its computational complexity, namely $\ell^5$ convergence rate at the sample size regime and $\ell^3$ in the batch size regime. These complexity orders match orders of magnitude commonly seen in practical machine learning applications. The slow convergence of robust learning techniques, especially in extreme scenarios with small or large batch sizes, may explain why such techniques have not yet achieved notable success in such applications, and therefore an awareness of such phenomena is crucial for the sound design of machine learning algorithms. The objective of our study is to assess the potential of machine learning to forecast Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression from a 2-year follow-up of the amyloid-positive subset from the Amyloid PET Imaging for Alzheimer's Prevention (APoE) study. Supervised and unsupanced models were compared to evaluate their ability to predict cognitive decline and AD diagnosis based on STI and STO features. The unsupervised models, including ConvNet, MultiConvNet, and MultiConvNet with double cross-validation, proved to perform similarly to a supervised convolutional neural network (SupConvNet) on various metrics. Notably, MultiConvNet and SupConvNet exhibited high capability in predicting AD diagnosis and AD-CSTI/STO, however, their ability to predict individual CSTI/STO progression was less accurate in comparison to STI/STO prediction. Moreover, multi-task learning by SupConvNet demonstrated cross-validation loss to reach its best performance at approximately nine months, indicating potential for individual AD risk prediction at three to six months with a second-year prediction extension. The study also revealed a significant gap between the performance of unsupervised and supervised models on STO features and AD-CSTI/STO diagnosis, respectively, which was attributed to more challenging SPOE detection in comparison to SPO. The research further identified potential biases stemming from the limited number of women (17%) and the minority ethnic group (PG) participation in the study, resulting in lower model performance for PG in both unsupervised and supervised learning methods. The study's findings suggest that supervised learning on larger, more diverse populations and individual disease progression data may be required to further develop unsupervised models for accurate AD diagnosis and risk prediction. The research also indicates that multi-task learning is capable of individual AD risk prediction, and the approach may be applied to existing studies with available imaging and clinical data for estimating individual AD risk. Recent findings have highlighted the efficacy of large language models in understanding long-term dependencies, yet most existing research lacks a systematic explanation for their success in capturing these dependencies. To fill this knowledge gap, a new paper proposes the Backward Dropping Algorithm, a straightforward mechanistic explanation for how models like BERT can utilize prior information to make predictions based on future data. The algorithm is based on a simplified interpretation of attention in Transformers, and its limited capacity to utilize past information is shown to be sufficient for the model to discover the optimal look-back window in learning. The algorithm's mechanistic implementation is also tested and validated to be equivalent to the black-box attention in BERT. Furthermore, experiments demonstrate that an algorithmically simplified version of the Backward Dropping Algorithm can achieve comparable performance to BERT in predicting past actions in complex video games and can effectively handle long-term dependencies in small datasets by adjusting its look-back window. The code for the algorithm is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jase-clarkson/mck-berkeley. The ongoing advancements in single-molecule imaging techniques have revolutionized our understanding of biological processes at a highly detailed level. In particular, first-principles calculations have proven to be a highly effective approach for interpreting single-molecule spectroscopy. However, when it comes to analyzing imaging data, physicists typically resort to simplified visual representations, which can fall short of capturing the subtleties of the experimental findings. In this research, we introduce the Reverse-Bonded-Body-Navier-Stokes algorithm, known as RBB-NA, which enables a straightforward conversion of electron microscopy data to a three-dimensional atomic model. By applying RBB-NA to simulated electron microscopy images of double-stranded DNA, we demonstrate that it surpasses existing methods in accurately reconstructing DNA structures. Moreover, RBB-NA's framework is versatile and can be adapted to process data from experiments involving unconventional DNA configurations. By applying RBB-NA to these scenarios, we are able to create a new framework for understanding deformed nucleic acids. Through this approach, we are able to investigate the structural changes that occur in single molecules under an applied force, track the dynamic interactions between distal ends of DNA, and reveal the underlying mechanisms behind unzipping DNA. These findings showcase RBB-NA's potential as a powerful tool for in-depth analysis of complex biological structures and processes. As a result, it is expected that RBB-NA will play a key role in advancing our understanding of single-molecule imaging techniques. Additionally, the software-based RBB-NA implementation is freely accessible at https://github.com/Farzane-Rad/Reverse-Bonded-Body-Navier-Stokes. Furthermore, the open-source platform is equipped with an interactive 3D visualization tool, which can be accessed at https://e-hubresearch.demonstrator.xyz/DNA. By leveraging RBB-NA, we are able to gain new insights into the functional principles of DNA, which can lead to innovative technological applications. In a broader sense, the development of RBB-NA highlights the potential benefits of AI-driven algorithms in the field of nanoscale materials research. By automating and simplifying the data analysis process, these types of algorithms can help to bridge the gap between theoretical physics and experimental sciences, ultimately giving rise to innovative research opportunities at the nanoscale. In the future, the integration of RBB-NA into automated laboratory platforms could streamline the experimental and simulation workflow, enabling researchers to synthesize and study new materials with specific properties. Arithmetic coding, a lossless compression method, experiences prolonged encoding times and high computational costs, specifically for division operations. To rectify this, researchers developed range ANS, but it still faces performance issues. Therefore, this paper presents a modified range ANS approach, implementing division through repeated multiplication, thereby ensuring a fixed accuracy, and significantly enhancing computational and encoding speeds. Additionally, two techniques are introduced to optimize non-uniform data encoding, utilizing partitions and dividing intervals to achieve superior results. Experimental findings reveal substantial reductions in processing time for both encoding and decoding, with significant bit savings achieved in the encoding process. In specific scenarios, this modified ANS variant has been found to outperform other compression methods, such as Huffman coding and arithmetic-cat, resulting in up to 1.8% better compression. Notably, these improvements lead to an overall decrease of 2.46 times in encoding time, as well as an decoding time increase of 1.12 times, with the new algorithm taking advantage of early stops, while the original ANS experiences delays in the decoding process. Overall, these enhancements indicate the superiority of the proposed method. Moreover, results show that early stops can greatly enhance the new algorithm's performance, yielding a compression ratio that is 0.01% better than other methods, with encoding and decoding times comparable due to the improved ANS's efficient division operation, which also facilitates faster decoding. In situations involving non-uniform data, continuous data, and small integer values, these modifications yield optimal results, confirming their validity. Importantly, this variant outperforms the original ANS in encoding speed by 2.46, 3.18, 4.18, and 9.18 times for general integer data, continuous data, small integer data, and zero-filled integer data respectively. In contrast, decoding speed shows a decrease of 1.12, 1.08, 1.09, and 1.09 times for general integer data, continuous data, small integer data, and zero-filled integer data respectively. In comparison to other compression methods, the proposed method yields compression improvements of 0.89%, 0.91%, 1.01%, 1.05%, and 1.08% with encoding times increasing by 1.12, 1.08, 1.09, 1.09, and 1.91 times for general integer data, continuous data, small integer data, zero-filled integer data, and floating number data respectively. Utilizing dielectric data from ongoing structural health monitoring (SHM) systems allows researchers to assess concrete performance over time. The existence of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules is considered natural due to their composition of valence quarks only, whereas the existence of light-heavy hadronic molecules is considered less natural due to the presence of both light and heavy quarks. In recent years, unique properties of $X, Y, Z$ particles have been extensively investigated through theoretical and experimental studies. This discussion aims to revise the naturalness principle by proposing that heavy-heavy hadronic molecules are not necessarily preferred over light-heavy ones, thereby rendering the current understanding of naturalness inconsistent with current knowledge of hadronic molecules. Two potential explanations for this revised principle are explored: (1) heavy quarks may not necessarily contribute to the masses of hadronic molecules; and (2) the values of condensation energies in hadronic molecules may not be directly related to the masses of constituent quarks. Based on the principle that heavy contributions should reduce the energies of heavy quarks, the existence of $X(3872)$ as a $D^{*}\bar{D}}$ molecule is considered less natural, whereas the existence of $X(4140)$ as an $BB^{*}$ molecule is considered more natural. Additionally, the principle can be used to infer the internal structures of $X, Y, Z$ particles. For example, the application of the revised naturalness principle suggests that $Y(4260)$ may not be a molecular-like charmonium state and that the contribution of the $D s\bar{D} s$ molecular component to $Y(4260)$ may be smaller than its $D \bar{D}$ molecular component. This revised naturalness principle also motivates a more thorough investigation of the $X, Y, Z$ particles through experimental searches at $B$-factory, $\psi'$ and other relevant experiments. Furthermore, these searches may uncover additional hadronic molecules not yet discovered. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of hadronic molecules can be achieved through a combined theoretical and experimental analysis of these particles. To facilitate this understanding, a new Hadronic Molecule Database (HMD) Hatchet is proposed, which aims to provide a comprehensive resource for all known hadronic molecules.
