A Boltzmann machine's dynamics and parameters affect the complexity of its underlying dynamics. In a state where energy is minimized, this complexity - measured as the entropy of a state probability distribution - increases. This increase in complexity is observed in various Boltzmann machine architectures, including those expanded to three dimensions. In these models, the complexity of dynamics reaches its highest in a symmetric phase where the probability of finding a neuron in an active state approaches one. The research investigates how the complexity of a Boltzmann machine's state distribution changes as its parameters shift from an ordered to a disordered state. This investigation involves numerical simulations in both small and large networks. In a large network of $L$ layers and $N$ neurons, the log base 10 of the entropy of the state distribution is found to increase by at least an order of magnitude as the network transitions from an ordered to an disordered state. To increase swarm robots' efficiency in diverse tasks, there is a need for adaptive robot movement that enables them to adjust their distance from one another. A novel algorithm has been introduced in this research, which enables 3D swarm robots to adjust their distance from one another. This algorithm makes use of an existing distance adjustment method designed for 2D robots and introduces a layer of depth consideration. As a result, swarm robots can effectively navigate and maintain a desired distance from one another, even in a 3D environment. The efficiency of the proposed algorithm was tested by simulating it in a computer program and studying its performance in a real-world experiment using a robotic cluster. The results of these evaluations confirm that the proposed algorithm contributes to improved swarm efficiency, precise robot movement, and minimal computation requirements. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for developing effective 3D swarm robots. The algorithm can be found in this repository: https://github.com/brapranil/3Dinterrobot. Automating the analysis of blood test results is crucial for hospitals, as it heavily impacts the efficiency of the healthcare system. For more accurate measurements, multiple blood samples need to be taken and analyzed. We have developed a deep learning model that can automatically analyze a set of two blood sample images taken at different points in time. Our approach utilizes a conditional mutual information maximization technique to distinguish between paired samples and can handle various types of blood tests. By training this model, we found that it can effectively determine if two blood samples belong to the same patient. Our model, trained on a large dataset of 102,000 samples, achieved impressive performance, rivaling that of a human technician. This technology has the potential for widespread use in healthcare facilities, saving precious resources and aiding healthcare professionals in patient diagnosis. Unadutterated enthusiasm for adiabatic perturbation theory drives the derivation of a variational approximation scheme for adiabatic gauge potentials, modeled after variational perturbation theory. The new scheme involves substituting the exact time-dependent vector potential with a variational approximation, with the variational parameters determined to minimize discrepancies between the exact and variational adiabatic connections, specifically with respect to nested commutators and their squared norms. An optimal set of parameters is derived at the $n$th iteration step. An analysis of the variational parameters reveals their physical significance in the context of the one-electron Aharonov-Bohm effect, as well as an extension of the variational approximation scheme to multi-electron systems, in which variational parameters are determined to optimize the exact adiabatic connection in the Liouville space. An numerical investigation of the variational parameters' optimal values at different $n$ for a CO interaction model is presented. Furthermore, an operator-based approach to the Floquet matrix is developed and demonstrated to be effective in calculating the periodic adiabatic connection for a harmonic Floquet valley state, in comparison to approaches based on Floquet-Wilson theorem. Ultimately, the variational approximation scheme may find utility in the development of simplified, user-friendly versions of adiabatic perturbation theory for various applications, while findings related to optimal parameters may encourage further numerical research and discovery. Two notable open questions in the field are proposed at the conclusion. The convergence of certain infinite series is investigated, involving terms related to $C^\infty$ functions. Specifically, we find that the series can converge to $C^\infty$ functions even when individual terms do not, given specific conditions. This discovery enables the representation of certain classes of $C^\infty$ functions via infinite series. Further, we define a $\sigma$-algebra on a set of $C^\infty$ functions through a specific type of measure and establish that certain classes of Borel sets on a topological space are equivalent to the $\sigma$-algebra defined on the set of $C^\infty$ functions. This connection allows us to embed a topological space into the set of $C^\infty$ functions over a closed unit cube in a specific dimension. Ultimately, this work leads to a finding that the set of $C^\infty$ functions on a closed unit cube in a specific dimension is a Borel set determined by its universe. In this research, the electron beam generated by a laser in a CH2 plasma was studied and the implications for the photon beam examined using betatron radiation.  The experiment utilized a laser with a 40 fs pulse duration and a 800 nm wavelength, which created an electron beam, producing shots similar to those from a synchrotron light source allowed for measurement of the electron beam's properties.  The experiment found the electron beam's energy, focusing angle, and electron dipole moment were: approximately 600 MeV, 4.8 mrad, and 0.13 nm, respectively.  The electron beam's radiation power was 0.56 GW.  The photon spectrum derived from betatron radiation matched the experiment's measurements.  The experiment compared simulations using a fully 3D particle-in-cell code (EPOCH) with the experiment's results, finding good correlation between the simulated and measured electron beam properties.  The experiment demonstrated how modifying the plasma's composition can be employed to control the electron beam's characteristics, which in turn allows for tuning of the photon spectrum generating a high-energy user-friendly photon beam. Deep neural networks have excelled in the field of speech recognition, with a major factor contributing to their success being the larger and more diverse training dataset available. However, including a comprehensive training dataset is costly and sometimes impractical, as it may encompass data that is irrelevant, unreliable, or hard to obtain. Moreover, it is feasible that some trained models are more capable than others due to their exposure to a wide range of diverse data. To address these concerns, this paper presents an innovative cost-effective solution that leverages data diversity for improving the robustness of speech models. Experimental findings confirm that models trained on a diverse dataset outperform those trained on a non-diverse dataset. Furthermore, by utilizing clustering algorithms, it is possible for the models to adapt to novel topics without undergoing retraining. This includes a unique analysis of adversarial example robustness in large NTK kernel datasets that highlights the benefits of weakly-supervised visual classification with NTK, including out-of-distribution generalisation and adversarial example robustness. Recent breakthroughs in theoretical chemistry and physics have driven the development of a generalized scaling law for viscosity, applicable to a broad range of molecular fluids. By examining complex interactions and movement within these fluids, researchers have found that density scaling allows them to consistently model viscosity levels across different molecular configurations. In particular, they observed that non-associating molecules follow a power-law model with a power of 1.333, whereas associating molecules exhibit a power of 1.67. Notably, this study reveals that only the 2.5 equation of state is sufficient to derive viscosity scalings with reasonable accuracy. Moreover, these viscosity scalings can be seamlessly integrated into existing statistical mechanics and thermodynamics frameworks, based on the 2.5 equation of state, to generate a comprehensive model of associating fluids. By applying these viscosity scalings, researchers can accurately predict viscosity levels and assess the applicability and limitations of power-law models. Moreover, incorporating the developed scaling laws into dynamic light scattering measurements will enable researchers to calculate power-law exponents in real-time. Furthermore, these viscosity scalings can be utilized in conjunction with existing values of diffusion coefficients and intermolecular potentials to generate complete material property profiles at varying densities. By building upon existing values of these properties, researchers can establish a comprehensive profile of material properties, spanning a broad range of densities from ambient pressure to extremely high pressures under ambient temperature conditions. By employing this approach, we have generated complete material property profiles at ambient temperature for 13 different fluids found in the NIST database. By building upon the developed theoretical framework, we have also demonstrated that it yields data corresponding to the correct temperature dependence. In addition to these findings, we have successfully applied the developed theoretical framework to two distinct experimental conditions: a high-temperature scenario and a 5% molar dilution experiment involving methane. By extending this approach to various dilution scenarios, we have consistently obtained accurate results. Therefore, this newly developed theoretical framework is expected to yield accurate results across different chemical compositions, temperature conditions, and density scales. In conclusion, this study significantly expands our understanding of how material properties at the molecular level scale with density, offering new insights and correction to previous assumptions about power-law models. This research explores a cosmological model where the Lambda-CDM phase has a limited lifespan and is succeeded by an inflationary phase, facilitated by a modified lambda parameter. Notably, the period of expansion fluctuations, determined by an oscillating lambda, controls the transient nature of the Lambda-CDM phase. In contrast to the steady, de-Sitter-like expansion of the Lambda-CDM phase, the transition to inflationary expansion yields higher and more variable values in terms of Hubble rate and deceleration parameter. As lambda transitions through the inflationary phase, the Universe undergoes a profound transformation from deceleration to acceleration, accompanied by a substantial increase in exponential growth. Although this exponential growth in this periodic cosmology model shares similarities with the Quintessence model, the model's past-potential history, which was initially dominated by matter-radiation combination, closely resembles the Lambda-CDM model's past-potential history. In the model's past-potension history, however, a substantial period of domination by matter-radiation combination is replaced by a substantial period of domination by inflation. This research also delves into the concept of particle mass inflation, proposing that as lambda transitions through the inflationary phase, ordinary particles morph into inflationary particles, which possess much higher masses. Consequently, the energy density of ordinary particles, which adheres to the Lambda-CDM model's energy requirements, decreases exponentially, while the energy requirements of inflationary particles, which dominates the energy requirements of the Universe during this period, increases exponentially. This research also delves into the concept of cosmic curvature inversion, proposing that as lambda transitions through the inflationary phase, the negative curvature inherent in the Universe during the Lambda-CDM phase, which was estimated to be in the order of -10^(-2) cm^(-2), reverses direction and increases exponentially, while the Universe' geometry undergoes a substantial period of positive curvature during the inflationary phase, which was estimated to be in the order of 10000 cm^(-2). Lastly, the research also delves into the concept of black hole mass diminution, proposing that as lambda transitions through the inflationary phase, the mass of ordinary black holes, which was estimated to be in the order of 10^11 kg, decreases exponentially, while the Universe' energy requirements during this period yields a substantial period of negative energy requirements for inflationary black holes, which possesses much higher masses, which was estimated to be in the order of 10^25 kg.

Quantum theories allow for discussions of nonlocality, which often arise from the trade-off between classical efficiency and quantum nonlocality in real-space measurements. The concept of locality, together with quantum nonlocality, prompts the question of measurement independence - the idea that real-space measurements should be made without relying on the prior knowledge of quantum systems. The concept of measurement independence, in turn, raises further questions regarding its practical application through a process called 'counter-factual measurement', which enables the determination of locality and nonlocality without violating quantum mechanics' principles. However, implementing counter-factory measurements raises concerns that they might be unachievable in reality. To address these concerns, researchers have developed a Bell-type test that utilizes real-space measurements to test the independence of counter-factory measurements from their actual counterparts. Using this test, we successfully demonstrated the independence of our novel counter-factory measurement from its corresponding prototype, thereby verifying the locality of the system under test and opening the door to applications in image processing. The code used in this research has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ShutaoW/quantum-communication-channels. The research findings have significant implications for the construction of quantum communication channels in real-space. Additionally, we performed an in-depth analysis of the distribution rules for classical and quantum communication channels, thereby gaining a deeper understanding of the relationship between locality and nonlocality. The results were validated using numerical simulations. The research findings highlight the value of counter-factory measurements in testing the independence of prototype and novel measurements without compromising quantum mechanics' principles. Importantly, the novel measurement developed in this research does not rely on entanglement - a feature that sets it apart from other real-space measurements. The researchers therefore conclude that the debate surrounding real-space measurements - a topic of ongoing discussion in quantum informatoin theories - is worth continuing. The research findings, code, and data are openly available at https://github.com/ShutaoW/quantum-communication-channels. The research findings have significant practical implications and contribute to advancements in quantum informatoin theories. Furthermore, the novel measurement developed in this research outperforms other real-space measurements in terms of computational efficiency and structural complexity. The research findings open the door to numerous potential applications across multiple disciplines. The researchers therefore anticipate that the novel measurement will find applications across data compression, image processing, quantum communication, information theory, and other related fields. The research findings will likely inspire further discussion and analysis of real-space measurements - a topic of ongoing debate in quantum informatoin theories.

However, the growing complexity of these networks has made them difficult to use, as they no longer fit within the devices' memory limits. We propose COMET, an open-source, open-access neural network that strikes a balance between being simple enough to fit within a device's memory and being powerful enough to process with modern hardware. COMET's success stems from its use of pointwise multiplications, minimizing the need for matrix multiplications. We have implemented COMET in TensorFlow and made it available for public use, alongside this paper's source code. We demonstrate COMET's capabilities through its application in acoustic event detection on the Google AI Dataset. We've shown that COMET requires less memory and computation than comparable neural networks, while achieving comparable accuracy. Specifically, COMET uses 2.5 times more memory and 2.2 times more computation steps than the ResNet-20, SincNet, and TukeyNet networks, but achieves accuracy within 10% of these networks. We measured the real-world computation latency of COMET on the Google AI Dataset and found that it takes approximately 130 milliseconds, largely due to the absence of accelerated commodity GPU support on these devices. We identified potential avenues for optimizing COMET's implementation to speed up its computation. In particular, developing commodity GPU support for COMET would reduce its computation latency to around 20-30 milliseconds. We believe this potential speedup, combined with the absence of other factors influencing latency, is notable. We also performed a cost-balance analysis of COMET's potential deployment on a smart speaker, weighing its power consumption during execution against the power saved by switching off the device after completion. However, for longer networks, switching off the device increases the overall power consumption due to the extra switch-off feature step. Interestingly, the deployment tests showed that the device's memory and computation footprint influenced its power consumption in execution and switch-off feature steps, with significant variability observed across different network types and sizes. The dimer model on isoradial graphs has a cluster expansion, and modern methods make it possible to match terms cluster by cluster in this expansion, matching the underlying graph's symmetry. This matching technique allows for the incorporation of additional weight functions associated with specific clusters, or "local weights." By applying this method to the dimer model on a particular class of graph called triangulations of the Aztec diamond, it's possible to compute exact partition functions when additional weights are introduced, and related quantities, known as multiple weights, are calculable. Furthermore, the method enables the computation of the dimer model's bulk critical exponents for any isoradial graph with a specific set of local weights. These findings build on earlier results from Knoerr and Louck, and the outcomes coincide with an earlier study by Cesi, Knoerr, and Louck when applied to triangulations of the Aztec diamond. This approach eliminates the need for admissible images captured from fixed vantage points, thereby making pano capture simpler and more reliable. We exploit the IMU data to align images and calculate the camera's position, while also using rendering to adjust for rendering differences between captured images. Additionally, our technique includes a novel method for optimizing camera positions that takes into account image alignment and rendering. While investigating this application is a broader research study, it is beyond the scope of this paper, which instead focuses on advancing the field of pano capture. We explore the dynamics of excess BMS (eBMS) charges in holography and the emergence of degenerate vacua leading to soft charges. By applying techniques from Chern-Simons theory and a deformation of Virasoro algebra, we derive a non-Linear Regge Trajectory (NLT) equation that describes eBMS primary fields. The degeneracies in the NLT are indicative of "soft news" and Schwarzian modes that arise from local deformations of NLTs. We develop a deformation of the NLT equation that is analogous to a Schrödinger equation and shows that its first eBMS charge decouples from the bulk problem, mirroring the behavior of the central charge in the original BMS framework. Additionally, we find a canonical transformation that reabsorbs all eBMS charges into the new gauge field, thereby reducing the number of new degrees of freedom in the deBMS framework. Recent observations of neutron skin thickness in isospin-sensitive nuclei have sparked renewed interest in the role of short-range correlations involving nucleons and light ions. This research utilizes precise calculations with the NORESA cluster Hamiltonian to analyze the impact of short-range correlations on the structure of light neutron-rich nuclei from $^16$O to $^{208}$polt. By comparing computed radii to those predicted by the no-correlation case, calculated correlations involving one, two, and three nucleons or light ions are demonstrated to significantly affect the structure of light nuclei. Notably, these correlations are found to enhance the nucleon triplet density by about one order of magnitude than that of single nucleons, while light-ion correlations result in a smaller increase. As a result, the calculated radius in the $^{208}$polt nucleus is found to be 3.7 fm higher than that predicted by the no-correlation scenario, indicating that single nucleon correlations underestimate the effect of short-range correlations on the radius in asymmetric nuclei. This finding has substantial implications for the determination of isospin terms in the meson-nucleon interaction based on measured nuclear radii. Furthermore, the proposed NORESA Hamiltonian is shown to deliver accurate descriptions of light neutron-rich nuclei from the $^16$O to $^{208}$polt range through a combination of computationally efficient and theoretically grounded calculations that incorporate Green's function techniques and an empirical cluster analysis. This computational framework is particularly well-suited for investigating the properties of very neutron-rich nuclei in the $p$-process, a area of ongoing research. The study also includes a detailed examination of how the structure of light neutron-rich nuclei is influenced by the quantum states of correlated nucleons and light ions. Their projected density distributions, which exhibit increased density in the $x$ direction and decreased density in the $y$, $z$ directions by about 20 percent compared to the free-particle case, are shown to control the radius in asymmetric nuclei. This study demonstrates that an accurate description of short-range correlations between single nucleons is insufficient for this task and additional consideration of light-ion correlations is required, which is facilitated through computationally grounded and efficient ab initio calculations enabled by the NORESA Hamiltonian. Such calculations may deliver significant precision and computational efficiency, thereby allowing the investigation of complex phenomena such as nuclear clustering and cluster-glass transitions in highly neutron-rich regions. Ultimately, the advancements in the computational methods and understanding of the structure of light neutron-rich nuclei discussed in this study have substantial implications

A comparison of these different gluon distributions reveals a unified pattern, in which the Q^2 inverse behavior is accompanied by a characteristic shift in Q^2. The observed trends from proton to uranium and to jet data are in line with theoretical predictions from the color glass condensate and gluon saturation models. These models' predictions are validated across the entire available range of gluon saturation scales, with the agreement being even better if the calculated values are adjusted to match the data. Consequently, the observed agreement suggests that all measured gluon distributions have reached the saturation phase. Furthermore, the agreement with theoretical predictions is enhanced when the data from proton to jet studies is corrected for higher order QCD corrections. The agreement with the theoretical predictions is also improved when the data from proton to jet studies is corrected for a small displacement in the energy scale, caused by higher order QCD corrections. This correction process can be used to detect potential discrepancies between the data and the SMC solution of the gluon distribution at high energies. Finally, the agreement with the theoretical predictions is also enhanced when the gluon distribution in jets is corrected for a small shift in the energy scale, similar to the correction observed in the data. This new finding opens the possibility to measure the gluon distribution in less conventional systems, such as jets, not only through TMD but also through the traditional DGLAP framework. Additionally, the detected discrepancy between the data and the SMC solution of the gluon distribution in jets may be used to enhance the sensitivity of future top jet studies to the less-conventional, saturation phase of the gluon distribution in small systems. Optimizing variational quantum models using a gradient method with matrix product states can be problematic due to the cost of computing the gradient. We address this issue by analyzing the impact of the output used to measure the circuit performance. By optimizing either the average or the standard deviation of these outcomes, which are influenced by different overlapping superpositions of weight distributions, we can significantly improve the computational efficiency of the gradient calculation. This gain in efficiency can be understood through the interpretation of the output measurements as being related to the variance of the weight, which itself has a more localized gradient. As a result, we have developed a new, efficient approach that combines an optimal variational quantum circuit with a target output that is either the average or standard deviation of the output distributions. Researchers using biased estimators to prepare CMB maps from small camera pictures can easily identify and remove large errors through simple mathematical processes. A previous study (Planck Int. Collaboration XV. 2015) assessed the accuracy of noise distribution in these estimators, but did not thoroughly examine how the influence of intense radiation sources distorts this distribution. Through simulations and analytical calculations, we examined how the presence of point sources significantly impacts the CMB maps generated with biased estimators. We found that intense radiation sources cause a concentration of underestimations near the source location, resulting in a non-normal error distribution with concentrated negative errors. We developed a method to correct the biased estimator in the vicinity of these sources, thereby improving the estimation of statistical properties. By applying this method before using deconvolution to remove large errors, we found that it minimizes the occurrence of overestimations, reduces the concentration of negative errors, and shifts the expected normal distribution towards a more realistic estimate. Both the conventional bias correction and our new method were compared to a more accurate but complex direct estimator, demonstrating that, although the conventional method occasionally introduces negative errors more concentrated than the real ones, our new method brings the estimated distribution closer to the real one, reducing the distinction between the two. As a result, we believe our new method is more suitable for processing CMB maps. Furthermore, we suggest that in the event of the presence of strong radiation sources, direct estimation methods should be prioritized over bias correction when obtaining accurate statistics. Overall, our new bias correction method offers several benefits. Firstly, it minimizes the concentration of negative errors, reducing their magnitude and concentration to a level comparable to the error distribution in the rest of the map. Secondly, it brings the estimated distribution, weighted by the square of errors, closer to the real one, similar to the conventional method but with reduced error concentration. Thirdly, it allows for the calculation of this real distribution in the vicinity of intense radiation sources, an ability not offered by the conventional method. Lastly, it enables the comparison to a more accurate but complex direct estimator, reducing the distinction between the two. The developed method can be applied to future data, such as those from the Simbolon experiment, to improve CMB maps. In addition to CMB, this technique can also be used for CMB-SDSS joint analysis, allowing for the estimation of statistical properties in the CMB-SDSS map, thereby improving data quality. Quantum state reconstruction via shadow tomography offers a cost-effective method (currently experimentally demonstrated with restricted shadows) that doesn't necessitate performing all shadow measurements. This work explores the maximum information gain achievable through shadow measurements, quantifying the bias in reconstructed density matrix estimates and assessing the probability that actual quantum state fidelity exceeds its estimated counterpart. When density matrix estimates become negative definite, we ask how far does the estimated logarithmic trace deviate from its true value and how often does this occur? Our analysis reveals that such deviations are Markov, following a specific pattern that can be predicted. This prediction may also extend to the fidelity estimate itself; further research is required to confirm this pattern in the fidelity case. In the process of these findings, a straightforward method to evaluate the trace of a positive semi-definite matrix from its Lanczos approximations is presented. Additionally, a modified version of the maximum likelihood reconstruction algorithm, designed to prevent negative divisibility when reconstructing the density matrix, is presented. This algorithm, referred to as logical reconstruction, has the desirable property that logical estimates always yield valid density matrices, specifically positive semi-definite matrices. Logical reconstruction offers another desirable characteristic in the context of shadow tomography when applied to an overcomplete set of shadows. Thus, logical reconstruction can be seen as a generalization of conventional quantum state tomography to the realm of shadow measurements. This algorithm, constructed by solving the semidefinite program SDP logical, is presented. Our numerical simulations demonstrate that logical reconstruction successfully recovers the positivity of the density matrix with high likelihood when the chosen number of shadows matches or slightly exceeds the rank of the density matrix. Logical reconstruction also achieves a high fidelity estimate when applied to shadows, specifically shadows of the Pauli group, currently experimentally demonstrated. Our study reveals that logical reconstruction's bias in the logarithmic trace has a hard limit, specifically 1/R, where R is the rank of the density matrix, which can be approached arbitrarily closely as the number of shadows grows. Furthermore, logical reconstruction's bias in the fidelity estimate also has a hard limit, specifically 1/R, which can be approached arbitrarily closely as the number of shadows grows. Current implementations of logical reconstruction have the limitation of only being applicable to complete density matrices and not permitting the estimation of logical matrices that have missing elements. However, further research is required to extend the logical reconstruction to the realm of matrix completion. In the process of these findings, a straightforward method to evaluate the trace of a positive semi-definite matrix from its Lanczos approximations is presented.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are likely to become vital tools in wireless network architecture, particularly for delivering services to users in hard-to-reach areas. The way UAVs move and position themselves over time is known as a trajectory. Developing effective trajectories for timing adjustment and optimal user service delivery is crucial. The inner workings of these timing adjustments resemble an orienteering problem, where UAVs need to hit specific points to maximize service delivery. However, optimizing these routes is an extremely challenging task for complex networks. Our research proposes a divide-and-conquer approach, using an upper-bound model to simplify this optimization problem into more manageable sub-problems. This strategy enables solutions to be found quickly. The proposed method was tested and validated through simulations, which showed that it could reduce computational time by 90% while achieving upper-bound optimal performance. The effectiveness of this approach was further confirmed by comparing it with other optimization techniques. Specifically, it was found that a trajectory designed using this divide-and-conquer approach could deliver up to 122% more data through the orthogonally combined signals from multiple UAVs compared to a single UAV. Furthermore, this strategy enabled a 21% improvement in data transmission rate over a similar optimization problem in a timing adjustment scenario. The way multiple UAVs can work together to deliver services has also been explored through two variations of the divide-and-conquer approach. It was found that combining the trajectories of multiple UAVs could enhance data transmission quality. The performance of this approach was found to provide near-optimal results. The proposed method was found to effectively reduce computational time and achieve optimal results. The results show that a trajectory design problem for multiple UAVs is similar to its single-UAV counterpart when the division of the problem is properly aligned. Based on this understanding, the problem for multiple UAVs can be simplified into more manageable sub-problems. The proposed method was found to effectively reduce computational time and achieve optimal results. The effectiveness of this approach was validated through simulations, which showed that it could bring about a 3.3% improvement in data transmission rate over a scenario with optimal timing adjustment. The near-optimal results achieved through this approach were found to be close enough to the optimal results. The problem for multiple UAVs was found to effectively converge to optimal results when the number of UAVs is increased. The results show that adding more UAVs can potentially improve data transmission rate by 2.1%.

The identification of significant nodes within networks plays a crucial role in understanding various systems' behavior. Currently, multiple centrality measures are available to identify critical nodes, but they tend to be path-dependent and only effective on specific types of networks. For example, degree-based centrality is useful on sparse networks while betweenness centrality is suitable for large networks. Furthermore, all current Gromov centrality variants require exact computation and are unable to handle small-world networks efficiently. In order to overcome these limitations, a new Gromov centrality variant, known as SGromov centrality, has been developed. By breaking down the network into smaller clusters and averaging the expected flux using Monte Carlo simulations, SGromov centrality is an efficient method for identifying critical nodes on various types of networks, including those that are complex and small-world in nature. In non-geometric string theory, continuous-trace algebra plays a key role in classifying states and BRST cohomology of Q-exponentials. Building upon this concept, we introduce a group-theoretic approach for constructing Q-exponentials associated with elements of continuous-trace algebras. This method has the potential to expand existing three-dimensional non-geometric flux backgrounds, and we demonstrate its applicability in creating classical T-duals even in the absence of geometric counterparts. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between the introduced Q-exponentials and elements of the deformation quantization algebra of a two-sphere, which has previously been studied by Bunce, Courtain, and Yerger. Their findings on the equivariant deformation quantization of a two-sphere provide additional classical Aspinwall conditions, thereby giving rise to elements of continuous-trace algebras. This work is compatible with, but does not rely on, the recent research by Doulgerakis, Yerger, and Yerger, which relates to the localization of the algebra. As a result, we locate the 3-2 Toric Q-exponentials within the continued-trace algebras, providing a classical T-dual construction in the process. Additionally, we demonstrate the invariance of the introduced Q-exponentials under a specific type of modular transformation, which has implications for the related flux backgrounds. Along the way, we derive the magnetic translation function by solving an element of continuous-trace algebra as its principal element changes, offering a geometric interpretation in terms of the related flux background twisting the 3-sphere. Lastly, we outline the potential for the introduced Q-exponentials to be generalized to higher-dimensional continuous-trace algebras, which could lead to the expansion of non-geometric string theory. By doing so, the predictions regarding the potential non-geometric classical T-duals of the four-form flux solutions on K3 could be refined. Furthermore, the developed approach in the geometric context may provide additional classical T-dual constructions in the Geometric Flux Engineering Database. A database supplement containing the corresponding elements of continuous-trace algebras, their magnetic translation functions, and related Q-exponentials can be found at the mentioned database. For a broad class of time-periodic parabolic equations, we establish the existence of a converging subsequence of solutions, which leads to a limiting periodic solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that nearly all solutions within a small interval converge to either a fully periodic solution or a solution exhibiting spatial translation symmetry. However, in the latter case, we show that additional small modifications can induce a transition to a fully periodic solution. Our results are achieved through novel analytical techniques, including a generalized approach to invariant manifolds and a compactness method for extracting limiting solutions, as well as a frequency analysis in cohomological equations. Additionally, we provide new estimates for the rates at which solutions converge to periodic solutions. Specifically, we bound the exponential decay rate in terms of spatial norms and prove that as small initial conditions are considered, the convergence rates become increasingly singular in time. Notably, our work addresses questions first introduced in papers including Heinz and Kowalski, Kowalski and Wolansky, and J.J. J. Hwang. Finally, we extend our findings to a model describing the dynamics of a dilute Bose gas subject to an oscillating external potential. While our model is not directly derived from quantum mechanical principles, it is an approximation to the one- and zero-sound modes within the Hartree-Fock approximation. We establish the existence of periodic solutions to this model through methods analogous to those in the first section of this article. Specifically, we prove the existence of periodic solutions that are bounded in the fast time variable and demonstrate their convergence to semi-periodic solutions. Furthermore, we show that semi-periodic solutions can be made fully periodic by introducing small modifications within the slow time variable. Our main analytical tool within this model is a generalization of the compactness method for extracting limiting solutions in the Bose gas context. While our work primarily focuses on the one-sound mode, we also derive analogous results for the zero-sound model under the assumption of a Bose condensate. In the process, we develop a novel approach to determining the zero-sound mode within the Hartree-Fock approximation. Ultimately, our work provides new insights into the dynamics of Bose-Einstein condensates and dilute quantum gases subject to external oscillating potentials. Our model can be seen as an effective mean-field approximation to the Gross-Pitaevskii equation with an oscillating magnetic field. A new direction in representation learning utilizes neural networks in a supervised setting to derive a feature space from data labels. However, the majority of methods in this area focus solely on labeled information. In contrast, we suggest that unlabelled data, readily accessible in numerous domains, can be utilized to further distinguish between network representations. To accomplish this goal, we introduce the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD), a neural network designed to map input data to their corresponding class-specific distribution represented in a latent space. When trained on labeled data, the DGD achieves class separation in its representation space, enhancing the effectiveness of multi-view spectral reinforcement learning in this space. Furthermore, the DGD's ability to accommodate diverse prior knowledge through its latent space enables it to outperform existing methods that utilize only labeled data. In addition, we demonstrate that the DGD's representation aligns with human knowledge, as analyzed through semantic space, before presenting prior knowledge to the network. As a result, the DGD achieves better performance than previous approaches that incorporate prior knowledge in a self-supervised setting. Through experiments on various classification tasks and datasets, as well as medical diagnosis based on multi-modal imaging data, we verify the DGD's efficacy in extracting meaningful representations from data with deep prior knowledge. These extracted representations can subsequently be utilized in subsequent learning processes, such as transfer learning, without prior knowledge. As the distance increased, emissions from other molecules decreased more rapidly than those from HCN. In the rapidly advancing field of neural speech synthesis, researchers have primarily focused on systems that learn from annotated data. Conversely, we present an unsupervised approach that leverages extensive, unlabeled speech data along with text-based hyperparameters. This approach demonstrates a remarkable similarity in speech quality to that of a highly optimised supervised model, surpassing previous best-in-class unsupervised models. Furthermore, our system produces speech that is both natural-sounding and easily understandable, even when operating under varying voice conditions. This achievement facilitates an in-depth analysis of the relative effectiveness of speech samples in learning an unsupervised model. Ultimately, our system yields high-quality speech output with minimal need for further refinement. Given sufficient data, this model outperforms others even in a supervised setting. Research indicates that the interaction strength influences the stability issue in the models. Although the canonical THDE case is well-studied, this work explores the interaction parameter's relationship with matters and dark energy. By integrating quantum-corrected modification to perimetric entropy and adding an interaction term to the THDE equation, two new interaction parameters, λq and λρ, are established. This study proposes an objective method for comparing solution effectiveness known as the Investment Ratio (IR), represented as C^2 making partial orders on the set of non-empty, bounded subsets of candidate solutions. IR has its origins in a researcher's quest for a suitable post-optimality performance evaluation metric, with the aim of assessing the relative effectiveness of various strategies in addressing large and complex optimization challenges. By utilizing the characteristics of partial orders, the study establishes theoretical concepts of lower/upper bounds, cuts, and fusion operations for C^2. Furthermore, IR is applied in two case studies, with the latter showcasing its potential for adaptive strategy adjustments based on performance assessment. IR is accessible and understandable, with the accompanying computational tool allowing for seamless solution sets analysis in any programming language. Available online are the implementation of IR, along with additional study materials, at https://github.com/FaBi0/IR-C2/tree/v1.0.0. Lastly, the study's outcomes are discussed in a pedagogical context, offering insights from an experimental analysis of approximately 75 million solution pairs. These results provide valuable lessons learned in applying IR, highlighting its potential in real-world applications and offering suggestions for incorporating it into educational curriculums. Recent research highlights the effectiveness of supervised pre-training for downstream tasks, but most approaches focus on label coexistence or independent labels. This method draws inspiration from the concept of co-occurrence in natural language, grouping labels by common themes to refine capture of subtle differences in sentiment. Individuals with weakened immune systems are more susceptible to contracting listeriosis, a serious illness, which can be triggered by consuming food contaminated with the bacterium Listeria monocytogenes. There is limited research available on the effect of low doses of this bacterium on immunocompromised individuals. Our study aims to fill this knowledge gap by exploring how using gastric acid suppressors, which increase the likelihood of developing a low-grade L. monocytogenes infection, affects the onset of listeriosis in individuals with reduced immunity. We have also investigated whether low-dose infections ever progress to a life-threatening illness and whether treatment options are available in such cases. Through a mathematical model, we analyzed the dynamic interactions between L. monocytogenes and the immune system of the host in three different scenarios of reduced immunity, as well as in situations where host treatment and absence of treatment were applied. Our study shows that reduced immunocompetency not only accelerates the progression of listeriosis but can also convert a low-grade infection into a life-threatening illness in certain circumstances. Moreover, in cases where treatment is effective, the model indicates that reduced immunocompetency prolongs the treatment period required to eliminate the bacterium. In instances where treatment failure occurs, the model suggests that extending the duration of treatment is an effective strategy for curing the illness. Overall, our study highlights the significance of low-grade infections in understanding and modeling the progression of listeriosis, particularly in individuals with weakened immunity, which may lead to the development of new diagnostic and therapeutic techniques. As an extension of our study, we investigated the economic implications of using gastric acid suppressors, considering the trade-off between the elevated costs of treating individuals with low-grade infections and the potential benefits of these individuals recovering quickly and returning to their normal productive state. Our economic analysis found that the trade-off between the two variables varies inversely, which may lead to a possible gain in some scenarios, albeit a limited one. This research investigates a reliable MIMO-based RIS-assisted UAV communication system in real-world conditions, taking into account the impact of transmission power loss, transmission and reception hardware impairments, and RIS phase shift noise. To optimize the system performance in the presence of these impairments, a two-stage optimization approach is proposed, which initially finds an optimal eigenchannel-related matrix and subsequently determines the optimal phase shift matrix to maximize the usable signal power in the uplink phase. However, implementing such an optimization strategy is computationally complex due to its increased search space compared to other methods. To overcome this limitation, the authors present an alternative method. First, the optimal eigenchannel-related matrix is found using the RIS as a passive reflector. Then, the authors developed a simpler and more efficient algorithm to find the optimal phase shift matrix. This new method reduces search spaces and is simpler to implement. To validate its efficiency, a comparison is made between the new method, the two-stage and other existing methods. The results indicate that the new method achieves comparable performance with lower computational complexity and is more suitable for practical implementations. This study showcases the effectiveness of optimization methods in improving communication quality in UAV systems. The findings also emphasize the importance of considering real-world transmission impairments in these systems. Furthermore, the use of RIS with passive reflection is a reliable technology to improve communication performance. However, its simplicity makes it a more feasible technology compared to other methods. Our investigation of $P$-points is driven by the goal of understanding their implications for the consistency of Woodin's predicate, which leads to the further examination of strong inequalities between cardinals of different sizes within the set theory universe. Interestingly, a fundamental question in this area remains unresolved: does there exist a model of set theory where the property of being a $P$-point only applies to cardinals that are limit numbers. Our research suggests that the answer to this question is yes, and to prove it, we use a unique blending of tools from forcing and dispersive partial orders, along with a novel reworking of the fundamental theorem on dense ordered cardinals that was initially proposed by Erdos and Tarski. Furthermore, our study of $P$-points' properties leads to the conclusion that their presence is essential in ensuring the feasibility of strong cardinal inequalities, which sheds light on an active area of inquiry within the research community. Our findings ultimately imply that in the context of a set theory universe that satisfies the axiom that every infinite cardinal has a particular property, it is possible to prove the strong inequality $\aleph_n<2^{alef_n}$ in a way that aligns with this axiom's specifications. Our study also reveals a deeper relationship between the quantification of the size of sets of subsets as determined by the property of being closed under the operation of union and the property of being countable, which has significant implications for the understanding of the unique mathematical structure known as $\aleph_1$ in this setting. Our analysis highlights an intriguing dichotomy where the quantification of the size of sets of subsets that are closed under the operation of union requires the presence of $P$-points in general, whereas the quantification of the size of sets of subsets that are not closed under the operation of union can be achieved without the presence of $P$-points, which points to an inherent distinction between these two types of sets. In nuclear physics, a new class of collective states has been proposed, which
involves a specific pattern of nuclear rotations, denoted as R-negative states.
These states are thought to exhibit lower transition strengths to nearby positive
rotational states and are therefore expected to be more difficult to induce using
a photon beam. We will analyze the electromagnetic properties of a specific type
of nuclear collective states, namely the deformed proton spinors, using a precise
mathematical approach based on the Wigner-Dicke model. This study will provide
a detailed understanding of how electromagnetic transition strengths vary among
positive and negative rotational states, with a focus on the negative states.
Key features of the negative states include their generally weaker transition
strengths and the absence of certain specific types of transitions, which can be
referred to as E2 negative scissors. We will also examine and compare the
response of the R-negative states to the electromagnetic field in relation to
its counterparts, a type of collective states known as the positive scissors modes
. Through this analysis, we hope to gain a clearer picture of how these negative
states can be detected experimentally and what methods might be most effective. 
Furthermore, we will show how these findings conform to experimental data available
from the $^{194}$Os nucleus. Utilizing this knowledge, we will suggest which
other isotopes should be investigated in order to be studied using a photon beam
with higher energy. In addition, we will investigate experimentally how these
negative states can be polarized, in order to assess their magnetic properties,
and discuss how this research fits within the broader context of nuclear physics. 
Finally, future research directions are outlined.

Recent soft X-ray observations of high-mass X-ray binaries revealed the presence of fast variability originating from hot plasma near the acceleration zone, which displays significant coherence compared to harder X-rays. Notably, this coherence diminishes as the hard X-ray energy increases, suggesting that partial screening of the radiation field by the wind affects the observed variability. A study has now investigated the light curves and cross-spectral analysis of the O-type system Vela X-1, using data from its premier X-ray observation in 2020, alongside its second observation in 2021, during which frequencies up to $10^3$ Hz were probed. Results show a substantial drop in coherence ($\approx$20% versus $\approx$5%) between the 0.1-10 keV and 0.1-2 keV energy ranges in the later observation, indicating reduced variability persistence due to increased wind interference in the later observation. Furthermore, this increased screening is found to result in lower energy PeV-range photon production, which is consistent with earlier studies of these photon emissions. A companion paper will examine the variations in the primary variable observed in the 2020 data, using a detailed physical model. According to this model, the coherence gap in the later observation can be explained by an increased distance between the Earth and Vela X-1's acceleration zone during its inferior conjunction in the later observation. Nevertheless, this later position in the cycle presents an ideal time for observing the acceleration process. Consequently, we anticipate that future space missions will not only confirm but also intensify the currently observed patterns of variable behavior in the Earth-proximal PeV photon production in high-mass X-ray binaries. Moreover, we anticipate cross-spectral analysis to play a pivotal role in studying the effects of interstellar medium on these photon productions' variability. Ultimately, we advocate the implementation of targeted observation campaigns, centered around the acceleration zones' presence time in the binary orbits, to systematically examine the effects of wind on coherence levels in the light curves of these objects. By doing so, we will be well-positioned to capitalize on the arrival of space missions like Imager for Medium-Broadband X-ray Engineering (IMBIBE), the next-generation Chandra, and the future gamma-ray observatory, LUZAR, and thus significantly advance our understanding of the effects of wind on the coherence levels in the light curves of these objects. By doing so, we will be able to better comprehend the complex interactions between the flow and the acceleration of particles in the acceleration zones

Furthermore, the research suggests that the radial distance of these features increases with mass, but only out to a certain mass threshold. Below this threshold, the distance of these features remains consistent. Moreover, the study discovers that more massive galaxies tend to have tighter distributions of these features. Tidal features are less common in more massive galaxies, instead occurring more frequently at lower masses, and are less abundant in more massive halos, except for galaxies within a specific velocity range where they are less common at lower masses. These findings suggest a significant role for minor mergers in shaping galaxies up to a certain mass, but a lesser one in those more massive. Lastly, the study discovers that more massive galaxies tend to have older tidal features and features of more massive galaxies being older on average. These findings place stricter limits on the timescales involved in the minor merger process, at less than 6.7\% of a galaxy's mass per billion years. Current applications of deep learning in solid mechanics primarily focus on solving linear problems, whereas there's a lack of studies on modeling non-linear, history-dependent phenomena like plasticity using machine learning techniques that can continue learning. This research fills this gap by employing a new continual learning method calledodor memoryless learning to model the history-dependent plasticity. This technique is compared against a convolutional recurrent neural network and trained using data from a widely recognized non-linear test, the uniaxial low-cycle loading test on a univalent steel. The results of this study show that the proposed memoryless learning approach is able to keep up with a state-of-the-art convolutional recurrent neural network and provides a reliable way to model complex, history-dependent material behavior. Furthermore, this study highlights that memoryless learning's ability to spread out learned information over its entire training period could lead to more accurate predictions compared to other methods that tend to forget earlier learned information. On the other hand, challenges associated with applying this learning technique to 3D stress-strain paths, coupled with the issue of overfitting when training on such data, are also discussed. Some ideas for addressing these challenges are offered, including the use of principal components to represent complex 3D stress-strain paths and methods to correct the bias that arises from fitting curves to limited data. To demonstrate the potential of this technique in real-world applications, the ability of the machine learning-based model to predict material failure in a variety of scenarios is verified using a widely recognized failure criterion. Moreover, this study highlights that the predictions made by the material model, which employs a novel formulation that's compatible with the machine learning approach, match the results of traditional failure predictions and diffusion simulations. Some suggestions for employing this technique in large-scale numerical simulations are offered, including the potential to utilize this technique as an offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline offline failure predictor. The new model developed in this study has been shown to perform well both in a complex realistic scenario and in comparison to human experts, who have to accumulate extensive experience through years of work to develop their skills. Comparisons against human experts have also revealed that the new model developed in this study is more efficient in terms of the time it takes to complete tasks, especially when it comes to predicting material failure. The new model developed in this study has also been tested against traditional failure predictions and diffusion simulations and been shown to provide similar accuracy but employ a novel formulation that's compatible with the machine learning approach.

Deep neural networks that utilize quantized weights and activations, commonly referred to as quantized neural networks (QNNs), experience reduced computational and memory costs during execution but face increased challenges during training due to quantization. In our research, we introduce a novel end-to-end training approach for QNNs, dubbed AskewSGD. AskewSGD simultaneously applies the Askew mapping technique to gradients to counteract backpropagation errors and utilizes stochastic gradient descent to optimize model parameters. Our results demonstrate that this method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches involving the distributed stochastic gradient descent algorithm and achieves a 2.7 times faster training convergence time with minimal additional computational expense. AskewSGD was successfully applied to a variety of network architectures, including ResNet50, MobileNetV2, and NASNet, resulting in significant acceleration with the Tesla V100 GPU. Additionally, our method was used to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on the ImageNet dataset with the BNN-85 model, which features 85 multiply-accumulate operations per pixel. Notably, AskewSGD achieved a high top-1 accuracy of 75.6% at a low energy cost of 12 nJ per multiply-accumulate operation, resulting in an energy efficiency ratio of 27.86 GFLOP/s per dollar. Furthermore, our research involves a thorough comparison of the energy consumption and performance of the AskewSGD approach with other state-of-the-art training algorithms, including D-SGD. While D-SGD requires 0.53 watts to achieve a 75.6% top-1 accuracy on the same model, the power consumption is reduced to 0.0055 watts using AskewSGD. In contrast, D-SGD requires a 2.5 times longer time to complete the training process while using AskewSGD results in a 2.7 times faster convergence. By viewing natural language instructions as composite phrases, we can control the complexity of pre-trained language models and enhance their ability to accurately encode first-order logic assertions. Our method involves breaking down logical expressions into constituent parts and assigning them to separate model layers, allowing for an incremental verification process that begins with fundamental assumptions. Utilizing generative models in image editing has sparked controversy due to their reliance on unlabelled input data, which they use to learn the structure of an image domain. The problem with this approach lies in the models generating images of lower quality than what professional artists produce. A possible solution to improve the quality of the generated images would be to use videos of professional artists drawing instead of static images, as these videos can convey artists' styles more effectively. However, extracting frames from these videos results in significant motion in the background and foreground, making it difficult to distinguish between the artist and the background. Under these circumstances, training deep generative models using videos of professional artists drawing would be an impossible task without the models learning to mimic the extensive motion in the background. A novel framework has been introduced that leverages causal relationships inherent in video data to isolate the artist's motion from the background for use in generating samples of drawing videos. By using these generated videos as compact representations of artists' styles, the framework allows the training of a deep generative model that can learn to mimic the structure of a single image. A curation of these generated videos serves as a curation method for the model's latent space, effectively discovering and producing, at-will, images of higher quality than what professional artists produce. When applied to a variety of image generation tasks, this framework demonstrated its versatility by successfully transferring to the generation of images of higher resolution, as well as images obtained through other methods. Moreover, the framework introduced a new curation method that could be applied to the curation of unstructured, high-dimensional data, such as videos and images, as well as unstructured, high-dimensional data derived from them. Consequently, the framework introduced a new method for the training and evaluation of latent variable models, which relies on the causal relationships inherent in video data to isolate different factors of variation. By using this framework, the generation of samples of drawing images led to a new method for the evaluation of the quality of the generated images, as the separation of the artist's motion from the background allowed the identification of specific, precise strokes in the artist's style. We've investigated the dynamic properties of three acceptance rates in slice sampling: its basic form, as well as two adaptations – hit-and-run sampling and whitened slice sampling – which were introduced to outperform slice sampling. Our analysis shows that hit-and-run sampling maintains similar dynamics to slice sampling, whereas whitened slice sampling exhibits a distinct phase diagram. Furthermore, hit-and-run sampling's convergence rate in dimension $q$ is significantly higher than slice sampling, however lower than whitened slice sampling. Additionally, we've found in $q$ dimensional scenarios that whitened slice sampling yields a higher acceptance rate than hit-and-run sampling, however fail to outperform it in terms of efficiency as quantified by the mean acceptance rate over torus angles. We've also demonstrated that torus angles based metrics are more suitable for comparative efficiency analysis of these methods. Moreover, whitened slice sampling's efficiency surpasses that of hit-and-run sampling in lower dimensional scenarios up to $q=20$. In contrast, hit-and-run sampling outperforms whitened slice sampling in $q$'s range of $25$ to $40$. Lastly, we've found that torus angles based efficiency metrics are independent of the choice of major axis in whitened slice sampling. Our research was also accompanied by a complementary web tool for visualizing the phase diagrams of these methods. Created at https://smrt-energy.github.io/slice-sampling-phase-diagrams/. Developed using the same programming language and statistical computing platform as hit-and-run sampling achieves. Utilizing this tool enables users to freely adjust the parameters of the phase diagrams. In particular, varying the parameter values that define whitened slice sampling's optimization problem could potentially yield useful results in other applications. In an unexpected finding, cross-dimensional comparison revealed that hit-and-run sampling and whitened slice sampling exhibit a phase diagram shift at $q=20$. Such a significant dynamic change has not been reported in slice sampling in a cross-dimensional comparison. In order to further examine this unusual phase diagram shift observed in hit-and-run sampling, an alternative analytical approach was employed. Specifically, a multivariate random walk analysis was conducted. In the analysis it was determined that hit-and-run sampling's acceptance rate is influenced by the distance between the current point and the projection of the major axis along the direction of mean prior. As a result, when the angle between these two projections approaches $\pi/2$ the acceptance rate drops significantly. Our research demonstrated that whitened slice sampling does not experience this decline in acceptance rate in such a cross-dimensional comparison.

Using matrix product state simulations, we investigate the behavior of the Bose-Hubbard model when it's driven far from equilibrium, specifically within an area where the dissipative phase transition occurs, by monitoring how it evolves over time with the help of HBT correlation functions and their associated Fourier transforms. We find the Fourier transforms' patterns accurately predicting the features of the phase transition, while the HBT correlations themselves reflect the amount of dissipation in the system. When the system enters a state of order, characterized by finite momentum, the HBT correlation functions' behavior changes, being significantly lower than the system's overall amplitude. We identify a universal pattern in the HBT correlation functions' shapes, denoted as $\gamma(q)$, for different types of excitations and their corresponding momentum values $q$. This universal pattern can potentially serve as an indicator of finite momentum order in the system. Furthermore, we analyze the relationship between the HBT correlation functions' initial rise rates at low momenta and the types of phase transitions in the system. For the case of a second-order phase transition, the correlation functions' rise rate at low momenta is relatively slow and independent of the type of excitations, whereas for a first-order phase transition, the correlation functions' rise rate at low momenta varies according to the type of excitations, being directly proportional to the excitations' strength. We derive a general criterion, derived from the correlation functions' properties, to distinguish between first and second-order phase transitions in the system. We also demonstrate the significance of accurately modeling the system's initial states in the simulations in order to correctly capture the correlation functions' properties, specifically their initial rise rates, during the system's evolution over time. The findings from our study may offer a pathway to experimentally detecting order in the system by analyzing the shapes of the HBT correlation functions and their initial rise rates, thereby enabling the identification of ordered states with excitions having any type of momentum. The research may unlock a new pathway for identifying ordered states with excitations possessing finite momentum, a state previously unachievable through state-purification-based methods. The findings may also enable the distinction between first and second-order phase transitions in the system through experiments, providing multiple avenues for achieving this distinction. The research in principle can be expanded to analyze other types of dissipative phase transitions in quantum systems. The study's unique contribution lies in the fact that the HBT correlation functions' properties, specifically their shapes and initial rise rates, serve as universal indicators of ordered states in the system, a phenomenon previously

This article provides an overview in the realm of Dirichlet problems linked to linear elliptic equations, particularly those with smooth domains where the theory of weighted spaces plays a significant role. We will discuss an anisotropic sector of the half-space, a domain that has garnered recent interest. We will also examine a type of domain that, although slightly more complex, still enables effective problem analysis. These sectors are characterized by curved walls, differing direction sets for Dirichlet conditions across the walls, and direction-dependent coefficients. However, this analysis is simplified when certain conditions are met, such as minimal angles between direction sets, strong Dirichlet conditions on one wall, and certain requirements on direction sets and coefficients. Under these assumptions, weighted space properties in these sectors become more tractable. Consequently, these assumptions enable thorough an anisotropic estimate of the first Dirichlet eigenvalue, a consequence of which is a representation formula for the first Dirichlet eigenfunction. Specifically, this result states that the first Dirichlet eigenfunction can be expressed as a sum of weighted singular trigonometric functions, a type of function previously studied in classical trigonometric analysis and more recent weighted trigonometric analysis. The estimates and representation formula obtained are also valid for related problems, such as the Lp extremal eigenvalue problems and normalized eigenvalue problems in similar sectors. Although the proof processes share similarities, requiring corresponding adjustments to the proof of the representation formula, the estimates demonstrate a consistent trend of "better" results in lower-dimensional cases. The estimates and representation of solutions in sectors of the half-space rely heavily on the reduction of the given problem to a one-dimensional problem via a specific change of variables. The change of variables itself shares similarities with the classical polar coordinate change in Euclidean space but is anisotropic due to the direction-dependent coefficients. Consequently, this anisotropic change of variables is both necessary and essential for studying the problems in question. The estimates and representation of solutions in sectors of the half-space demonstrate that the theory of weighted spaces in one-dimensional problems is not only applicable to the studied sector but also sufficient for effective problem analysis. Furthermore, the sector of the half-space is a special case of the studied theory and theory of problems in general smooth domains, a fact reflected in the results obtained. The estimates and representation of solutions in sectors of the half-space are shown to be consistent with corresponding results in Dirichlet problems linked to linear elliptic equations in general smooth domains. We investigate the interplay between two mechanisms generating heat in a one-dimensional Bose gas.  The initial mechanism triggers non-linear reactions in the gas due to its interaction with a thermal bath, resulting in low-level dissipation.  The second mechanism, based on a theory first described by R. Blümel et al., utilizes periodic modulation to create high-frequency fluctuations in the gas.  When the gas experiences high stimulation, its behavior can be characterized as a closed system.  However, when the gas experiences low stimulation, its behavior can be explained using a linearized Floquet evolution equation.  By modeling the gas' behavior following a thermalization event, and assuming it exists in a local thermodynamic equilibrium state, we demonstrate that Floquet modulation enhances dissipation and shifts it toward lower stimulation levels.  The combination of these two mechanisms results in significant changes to previous research predictions regarding floquet-induced Bose condensation in one-dimensional Bose gas.  In particular, we have discovered that Floquet modulation greatly enhances dissipation and shifts it toward lower stimulation levels.  The interaction between dissipation and Floquet modulation leads to a unique phase transition in local thermodynamic system equilibrium, in which Floquet modulation alone induces Bose condensation in a system that otherwise experiences none due to dissipation.  The maximum threshold for photon count, at which Bose condensation occurs, is directly related to the balance between dissipation and Floquet modulation.  The phenomenon of Floquet modulation leading to Bose condensation opens doors for investigative research in other low-dimensional systems that experience Floquet modulation and dissipation.  The scope of applications extends to the study of Floquet modulation leading to ferromagnetic ordering in two-dimensional Bose gas.  The challenge of simulating Floquet-modulated magnetic ordering in two-dimensional systems using ultracold atoms lies in the complexity of linear Floquet evolution equation solutions, which necessitate the use of sophisticated methods for calculating high-frequency Floquet eigenstates.  The phenomenon of Floquet modulation leading to magnetic ordering in two-dimensional systems is, however, within the realm of experimental feasibility using ultracold atoms. Assuming $F$ and $G$ have continuous first partial derivatives, $G$ can be expressed as $F + L$, with linear growth, or $F + \log L$, with logarithmic growth, and we establish that $W^{1,p}$ regularity of $F$ implies $W^{1,p}$ regularity of $G$ under these conditions. We provide examples to demonstrate the validity of our findings. Furthermore, our results can be extended to any convex function with general growth conditions by applying an approximation method. We analyze a standalone optical clock based on a two-level quantum system and detect photons from its emission, finding that photo detection has a significant impact on the clock's performance. In contrast to previous research, we've discovered that photo detection, though detrimental at short timescales, ultimately improves the clock's accuracy in the long run due to a temporary slowdown in time measurement. This temporal delay is attributed to a temporary halt in the quantum dot's energy level shift caused by the photo excitation delay and reduced emission rate following each detection event. With the inclusion of photo detection, we've found that the optical clock's accuracy surpasses the conventional Sebastianelli standard after an elapsed time of around two and a half times the initial shift. Notably, we've identified an innovative method to enhance quantum metrology using a temporary optical clock 'pause' achieved solely through photo detection management. Photo detection triggers pauses that slow down the clock in a manner inversible to the average time shift, $\Delta t/\bar{t}$. In the long run, we've found that the optical clock with photo detection yields a precision that surpasses the traditional optical clock without detection. We've established a general formula for the optical clock's uncertainty: $\sigma_{\tilde{g}}^{-2}=\frac{4\chi^2\Gamma^2}{\langle\Delta N\rangle^2}\frac{\tau}{2\hbar^2}$. Here, $\tau$ represents the time, the photo detection rate $\langle\Delta N\rangle$, the  half-width of the energy level shift $\hbar\omega\tilde{g}$, and the emission rate $\Gamma$ are key factors. We've found that the time evolution of the two-level system can be described using the time-shifted standard deviation $\sigma_{\tilde{g}}$, which indicates the accuracy of the optical clock: $\sigma_{\tilde{g}}\approx\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\tilde{g}\sqrt{\frac{4\chi^2\Gamma}{\langle\Delta N\rangle^2}}$ at long times. Consequently, the photo detection has a positive impact on the optical clock's accuracy in the long run due to a temporary slowdown in time measurement. If a tensor network serves as its own erasure correction code using a single type of tensor, it must have specific contraction properties. This leads to a proof that such a tensor network has limited PEPS entanglement. Additionally, two corresponding proofs are provided: first, that maximal ERASE-correcting networks are restricted in their PEPS entanglement; second, that any tensor network capable of independent bit erasure has restricted PEPS entanglement. These findings imply that no tensor network with finite bond dimensions can act as its own independent bit erasure code. Furthermore, two potential implementations of quantum read-out errors in circuit models from the conjugated gauge freedoms are outlined. Firstly, two-flavor fermions in their physical space can represent the necessary erasure tensor component. Secondly, a simplified bulk circuit gate with an auxiliary qubit can act as the erasure tensor component. Importantly, both these representations must have limited bond dimensions.
