Two theories that attempt to explain the formation of these filamentary structures are the thermal instability triggered by the interaction of cosmic rays and cold gas in a magnetic field, and the shock caused by the interaction of protogalactic clouds in a cosmic web environment. Our research aims to provide numerical evidence to support these theories by studying the interaction of cosmic rays and cold gas in a magnetic field using a Monte Carlo technique. Through this research, we hope to gain a deeper understanding of the complex physical processes that shape these magnetized radio filaments. Our simulated models successfully reproduce the observed properties of magnetized radio filaments and provide valuable insights into their complex formation history. Our research reveals that early stages of filament formation may offer critical opportunities to study the dynamic interaction between cosmic rays, cold gas, and magnetic fields, enabling a deeper understanding of the regulatory role of magnetic fields in interstellar medium. Recent breakthroughs in neural language models have significantly improved the quality of text-generated outputs in dialogue tasks, enabling the creation of realistic fiction texts. However, these models often produce fictional information that is not supported by actual facts. To produce high-quality dialogue and narrative outcomes, we introduce a new theoretical framework for text-generation. This framework organizes existing knowledge into structured concept groups and establishes relationships between them using implicit and explicit attributes. A new generative approach, called Concept-Based Generation, utilizes this framework to produce text-based outputs. CBG employs a knowledge graph to first identify relevant concept groups for a given input and then generate concept-based sentences, using pre-trained surface form generators to finalize the text-based output. Experiments on Google Referral and T5 datasets demonstrate CBG's capabilities in generating accurate and detailed information. A live dialogue demo is available online. The framework and demonstration can be accessed at cbpgdemo.com. Both the framework and demonstration are open to the public. Since its inception in the early 1970s, quantum chromodynamics (QCD) has been the foundation for investigating aspects of strong-interaction matter. Despite significant advancements, questions regarding QCD remain largely unanswered, particularly at high temperatures and dense conditions that may have existed during the universe's early stages. The modern approach to this problem revolves around lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD), allowing researchers to compute properties using numerical calculations based on the principle of the path integral. Nevertheless, such computations remain challenging due to the complexity of QCD's action space. Furthermore, the large-scale numerical data generated often lacks clarity, causing difficulties in data analysis. This thesis delves into the potential of employing artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms to tackle these obstacles. Initially, the thesis explores the concept of Lissajous maps, which transform the action space into a more manageable, geometric form with linear properties, for applications in lattice gauge theories and QCD. Next, the thesis examines the utility of AI in developing an efficient coordinate transformation to simplify the QCD action space. Furthermore, the thesis presents studies on the geometry of the QCD action space and its implications for AI modeling. Finally, the thesis demonstrates the application of AI algorithms in lattice QCD, focusing on regression tasks. The results of these investigations are provided in chapters 5, 7, and 9 respectively. An overview of the research is presented in chapter 1, while chapters 3, 6, 8, and 10 contain the analyses of the findings, and an assessment of the related literature is provided in chapter 2. An in-depth explanation of the theoretical foundations and numerical implementations of the studies are contained in appendix 1, 2, and 3 respectively. Lastly, the conclusions of the research are concluded in chapter 11. This work, as outlined in the appendix, draws heavily from my doctoral thesis, titled "Artificial Intelligence in Lattice Gauge Theory: Geometric Exploration, Coordinate Transformation, Machine Learning on Gauge Configurations and their Applications to QCD", which was defended at the University of Barcelona on May 26, 2020, under the supervision of Dr. Pier Francesco Furlan. In our study, we have established a general upper bound for the R-nilpotency degree of any given group. In doing so, we have shown that our finding enhances a prior result specific to 2-group bases and also equals a previous result for Hamilton's nil-group-correct property. Furthermore, we have successfully determined the R-nilpotency degree for groups that are nilpotent of class 2 and for certain groups with a class equal to 3. In a secondary finding, we have established a connection between the R-nilpotency degree and the width of group factorizations. Our study has also revealed that our findings on the R-nilpotency degree can translate to bounds on the width of such factorizations. In particular, we have found new limits on the width for certain p-group factorizations. In a notable case, we have shown that the width for 2-group factorizations is capped at 2 times the group's nilpotent quotient rank, which effectively translates to a bound of 2 times the group rank in cases where the group is nilpotent of class 2. In another instance, we have found that the width for 3-group factorizations is capped at 8 times the group's nilpotent quotient rank. Lastly, we have successfully determined the exact R-nilpotency degree and width for Baudisch's example of a non-homologous group. We introduce an innovative inversion technique that retrieves complex temporal evolution of relevant experimental observables from experimental data contaminated with noise, given a specific phase space distribution. This noise removal approach can be applied to various ultrafast experiments, including strong field interactions, where it offers a significant advantage in noise-tolerant processing of noisy data, even when the signal is highly masked by noise. Leveraging the maximum likelihood principle, this method makes an optimal use of noise information to enhance the quality of data reconstruction. Additionally, we incorporate a novel strategy to optimize computational efficiency by applying a noise filtering procedure before data reconstruction. We validate the effectiveness and validity of this inversion technique by successfully reconstructing a phase space distribution from experimental data collected in a strong field ionization experiment. Notably, this inversion technique is capable of producing reliable results even when the signal is heavily obscured by noise, thanks to its incorporation of noise information during the data reconstruction process. Furthermore, we observe a consistent convergence of this inversion technique with respect to computational iterations, regardless of noise level. Consequently, this inversion technique provides a reliable tool for data analysis in ultrafast experiments, especially when the signal is heavily obscured by noise, while also making an efficient use of computational resources. We also anticipate that this inversion technique could be adapted and extended to a variety of ultrafast experiments, including X-ray pulses generated by attosecond oscillator and free-electron X-ray lasers. Moreover, we believe that this inversion technique has the potential to be further optimized by incorporating prior knowledge from theoretical models, similar to Bayesian analysis. Lastly, we anticipate that this inversion technique could be conveniently integrated into existing phase space distribution reconstruction codes, allowing for seamless incorporation into existing computational frameworks. This inversion technique is currently available for download at the public repository: https://github.com/ramirez-beraistorney/ML-Inversion. In conclusion, this inversion technique provides a noise-tolerant solution for reconstructing complex temporal and spatial evolutions of relevant experimental observables from noisy experimental data, while making an efficient use of computational resources. The integration of this inversion technique into X-ray spectroscopists' software toolkit is anticipated to contribute meaningfully to this field. The experimental data used in this study is openly available at the following link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsmrb.2022.102104. The COVID-19 pandemic worldwide has compelled nations to adopt various measures for tracking the disease, exemplified by the widespread use of contact tracing apps like France's StopCOVID, aimed at containing the disease's spread. Although these apps are suggested to be beneficial for public health, they also pose a risk of undermining individual privacy and facilitating a mass surveillance state. To explore the extent of data collection by such apps, we began by evaluating the data shared by StopCOVID's servers with third-party services. Our investigation revealed that nearly all these servers are hosted in countries with limited data protection, including those with data retention laws. Notably, a majority of these servers are managed by arms dealers and defense contractors, increasing the risk of data exposure and potential cyberattacks. In an effort to assess the severity of data exposure, we employed public tools to test the security of contact tracing servers and identified multiple critical vulnerabilities. Ultimately, our research uncovered a pattern of data collection by these apps, including sensitive data not only from users but also from their close contacts over a period. Our study highlights the potential for these apps to monitor the daily lives of individuals extensively. By demonstrating that data collected by these apps can be easily aggregated, we emphasize the urgent need for stronger data protection and user awareness regarding their data sharing preferences. In light of our findings, we recommend that users reconsider using contact tracing apps and instead advocate for policy changes drawing from lessons learned about the risks of surveillance technologies, such as those from the Caracal and BND/Airborne cases. Given the proliferation of these apps, we estimate that over 50% of the European population is participating in a massive biometric experiment with potential implications for civil liberties, data protection, and government accountability. As the unregulated nature of contact tracing apps raises serious concerns regarding data protection, we call for the swift introduction of regulations that can address these risks and mitigate them. Furthermore, the shared responsibility of tackling data protection risks among organizations, governments, and individuals is emphasized, leading us to propose the establishment of a data protection task force to monitor the long-term implications of these apps. In the face of ongoing pandemic discussions regarding the pros and cons of contact tracing apps, we argue that such a discussion should also incorporate the cons of data collection, ultimately influencing public perception and usage of these apps. Given our research conclusions, we anticipate that the COVID-19 pandemic will hasten a mass surveillance state, accelerating existing trends and data collection practices. This new discovery was possible after analyzing 16S rDNA sequences from six specimens, presumed to be non-human, which revealed that the genetic marker was not influenced by post-translational modifications or nucleotide variations. Subsequent phylogenetic analyses using plastid psbA and matK gene sequences as well as DNA barcoding data confirmed the relationship. Furthermore, one of the specimens, characterized as rich and diverse in flowering, was found to be the largest known in the family Solanaceae and was observed to be dioccious. Nonetheless, detailed autecology and breeding system studies are still required to thoroughly understand the newly discovered genus. Consequently, the proposed name, Iochromella, is suggested along with two preliminary species descriptions, Iochromella grandiflora and Iochromella ramosa. Additionally, multigene DNA sequences have been deposited in the GenBank database under accession numbers GSTC, GTC, and GTE. An accompanying epitypification is included as well as a detailed description of the material examined. Moreover, the proposal of two new species within the genus Iochroma is presented: Iochroma ramosum and Iochroma submontanus. Lastly, the distribution of genetic variation within the newly proposed genus Iochromella, closely related to the genus Iochroma, is examined through the AMOVA and PCoA analysis. An FST value of 0.0488 indicated notable genetic differentiation, suggesting unique genetic identities for specimens within the newly proposed genus Iochromella. Therefore, multigene DNA sequence data provide robust support for the new discovery. An original research article detailing the findings has been published in Bioinformation under the title "Unraveling the taxonomic enigma of Iochroma L.". Fairness assessment and enhancement in decision-making systems has become a significant concern, primarily due to increasing reliance on automated decisions that affect individuals' lives. Current research on fairness involves testing whether models demonstrate bias based on certain attributes, and if biased, how to rectify this through model adjustments or dataset alterations. Yet, existing fairness frameworks often overlook the intricate causes underlying decision-making outcomes. We propose integrating causal inference methods to investigate counterfactual fairness in classification issues, going beyond the scope of observational studies in causal inference. We developed methods for detecting causation and evaluating counterfactual fairness by utilizing data from decision-making systems, framing it as a problem of establishing causal relationships between decision-making outcomes and hypothetical, unbiased decision-making conditions. We further proposed a method for measuring fairness through counterfactuals and demonstrated a hypothesis-testing approach to assess fairness, complemented by a kernel-based technique for assessing fairness across different groups. We showcased these methods' applicability using real-world data, highlighting their added value in identifying and addressing bias within decision-making systems. We also presented a trade-off between achieving fairness through counterfactuals and maintaining accuracy, particularly in sensitive situations where deep learning models operate at a performance disadvantage. We concluded that incorporating causal inference methods offers a more comprehensive framework for fairness assessment and improvement in decision-making systems. With the growing emphasis on causal decision-making, it is likely that the distinction between black-box and white-box approaches will become increasingly obsolete. Next-generation radio telescopes will produce enormous amounts of data, necessitating local analysis to expedite findings and streamline global data sharing through peer-review processes, even before data are transferred to data centers for further examination. Unlike traditional single-dish observatories, interferometric arrays must synchronize data across disparate locations, further complicating data transfer processes. To address these challenges, we introduce the Data Integrate Analyze Share (DIAS) framework, a scalable, modular tool for processing and sharing data from large-scale interferometric arrays. The DIAS framework comprises four key components: data integration, data analysis, data management, and data distribution, which can be easily deployed on cloud platforms and scaled as needed. By leveraging containerization with Docker and orchestration with Kubernetes, DIAS ensures consistency and efficiency across data processing workflows, while its modular architecture enables simultaneous data processing by leveraging existing software tools tailored to specific scientific tasks, while the DIAS framework also includes features for data management and distribution. Furthermore, DIAS streamlines the data sharing process by providing a secure method for peer-review and facilitating data archiving, while also including important features for data access control and accounting. In addition, we outline future development opportunities and examine the efficacy of the DIAS framework by presenting a case study of its application to the Square Kilometer Array interferometric array. The results demonstrate that DIAS can reduce data transfer times by as much as 90%. By automating many aspects of the data processing and sharing process, DIAS can expedite the development of scientific research pipelines and streamline data analysis and sharing for future large-scale radio observatories, including the Square Kilometer Array and the Giant Magellan Array. Light field photography generates 4D images by capturing multiple 2D perspective images from a single capture point. These images are typically compressed using subband transform methods similar to those used in traditional image compression. However, the capture of a 4D light field inherently includes images that share perspective viewpoints, and compressing each separately inefficiently uses coding resources. Disparity information, a measure of perspective difference, can identify groups of similar images and facilitate shared data compression. This paper introduces a disparity-aided framework for light field image compression, utilizing inter-view prediction to reduce bit rates through shared data compression. Inter-view prediction is applied to image blocks with low disparity, identifying similarities among images. Block similarity measurement and prediction block selection are estimated from disparity data, and the proposed framework significantly compresses 4D light field data by 35%, outperforming state-of-the-art compression methods. Additionally, the proposed framework supports compression of hyperspectral light fields and captures core properties of image content. This information, though initially used for disparity estimation, is re-used for inter-view prediction, and the proposed framework demonstrates notable bit rate reductions when compared to established compression methods. Experimental results demonstrate significant bit rate reductions when the proposed framework is applied to hyperspectral light fields. This research highlights the potential for shared data compression in subband transform-based 4D light field and hyperspectral image compression, and the importance of accurately estimating disparity for improved image content representation. In order to enhance learning-based control algorithms' ability to generalize from data to operational scenarios, this study introduces an extension of reinforcement learning that incorporates multiple levels of abstraction. By leveraging lower-level policy data and an upper-level decision-making model, such an algorithm can prevent data collection risks and improve its performance in real-time. In comparison to traditional reinforcement learning techniques, our approach demonstrates superior performance and reliability in multiple case studies, including process control systems and vehicle trajectory planning. Furthermore, it is capable of producing results comparable to an optimal two-level controller under fully observable conditions. In addition to these benefits, our approach also offers improved safety guarantees through model-based data analysis. Moreover, by identifying safe states from data, our algorithm can recover the results produced by the optimal two-level controller, even in situations of partial observability. In a series of experiments, our approach was found to outperform existing learning-based control algorithms, including adaptive critic methods, in terms of performance, reliability, and controllability. Importantly, it was also found that our approach is relatively insensitive to data limitations, collecting only a small amount of real-time data compared to other techniques. In one such experiment, our algorithm successfully utilized approximately 15 seconds of collected data to produce results comparable to an optimal two-level controller, while other techniques required extensive data collection over a longer period of time. In conclusion, this study presents an innovative framework for leveraging data in reinforcement learning applications through the incorporation of multiple levels of abstraction, resulting in improved performance, reliability, controllability issues, and reduced data collection risks, thereby enhancing learning-based control algorithms' ability to generalize from data to operational scenarios. As such, our approach has significant practical implications and applications. In the future, our approach could be successfully applied in various data-driven reinforcement learning applications across multiple domains, including autonomous driving, process control systems, robotics, and the training of neural networks. In addition to these potential applications, our approach also offers theoretical benefits, including the ability to provide model assurance, estimate missing model parameters, identify optimal model structures, and analyze model quality. A dimensionality reduction technique called LS-SNE has been developed as a variant of the popular SNE technique found in most data analysis tools. SNE technique is widely recognized for its effective mapping of complex data onto lower-dimensional spaces, with t-SNE serving as an improved iteration of this process. LS-SNE focuses on two key aspects: first, local proximity is modeled using a log-normal distribution, differentiating it from the Gaussian distribution used by t-SNE; second, non-proximity is applied using an uniform distribution. By incorporating these elements, LS-SNE is able to maintain a constant scale and avoid the tendency of t-SNE maps to stretch or shrink. In contrast to other SNE techniques, such as CS-SNE which maintains proximity with a Cauchy distribution, LS-SNE is similar in that local proximity is still modeled using a non-Gaussian distribution. However, by incorporating an uniform distribution for non-proximity, LS-SNE is able to achieve more effective stretching or shrinking of its maps. This technique has been validated by its application to the Human Microbiome Project dataset, as well as other datasets. Results show that LS-SNE is able to maintain its scale consistency, achieve uniform stretching or shrinking of its maps, and facilitate accurate human-microbe representation. Consequently, it has also been able to recover valuable information on trichotomy co-evolution in microbial species. This technique has further demonstrated its generalizability by providing a more detailed comparison of modern mapping techniques, including UMAP, Low-Dimensional Embedding, LS-SNE, SNE, CS-SNE, Adversarial SNE, CS-Adversarial SNE, Linear Dimensionality Reduction, and Jensen-Shannon Divergence-based Low-Dimensional Embedding. Ultimately, LS-SNE has been found to outperform these techniques in terms of its effectiveness and efficiency. A computational approach has been employed to analyze the impact of weak electron-phonon interactions on polaron properties. Employing a systematically conserved, non-hermitian effective Hamiltonian, the complete set of fourth-order diagrammatic results for the polaron's mass, thermal energy, and entropy has been calculated. By comparing this outcome with the singly excited state model, it was found that the polaron's characteristic feature, the polaron 'Z' factor, shows considerable variation relative to the singly excited state model as the electron-phonon interaction strength intensifies. Moreover, the thermal energy and entropy of the polaron, with phonon degrees of freedom included, exhibit temperature-independent limits that match results from the singly excited state model. However, when the electron-phonon interaction is set to zero, the polaron's mass and thermal energy 'collapse' to their respective adiabatic limits at very low temperatures; these limits can be accurately described using a time-dependent perturbation approach. By utilizing a sophisticated control approach, the large robot is able to accurately track a pre-determined trajectory for hopping, with precise control of its movements despite its size and the unpredictable interaction with its environment. Our research reveals that a majority of these devices utilize the same firmware, yet current updating methods treat all devices individually, maximizing update success.  To address this, we're exploring Concurrent Transmissions (CT) as a strategy to enhance update reliability.  CT optimizes update rates by prioritizing devices with higher success rates, while also allowing wireless devices to jointly transmit firmware using correlated subcarrier channels. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for using concurrent transmission to improve firmware scalability, reliability, and efficiency, and identifies key challenges and opportunities in this area. This research utilizes the MUKI model, a power system optimization model that incorporates detailed short-term dispatch insights, to analyze the impact of temporal resolution on the economic costs of integrating new generation capacity. The study finds that improving the temporal resolution of the model increases costs associated with inefficient generation capacity utilization, but the benefit of enhancing resolution diminishes with increasing renewable energy penetration. Additionally, the research demonstrates that higher temporal resolution models reveal significant efficiency gains, specifically gains of 0.9-1.5% per hour, but the added value eventually reaches a saturation point, and the added complexity becomes excessively high. Conversely, the study finds that improving the model's spatial resolution does not exhibit such behavior, indicating that most efficiency gains occur early in the process and costs do not continue to drop uniformly. Further investigation involves examining the effect of hourly time steps on policy development and investment analysis using different power systems and various time steps reveals that models with higher temporal resolution advocate for earlier infrastructure implementation, greater renewable energy penetration, and increased storage needs. Nonetheless, the added value of such models diminishes rapidly, suggesting an investment cost threshold beyond which further refinement becomes excessively costly. This research suggests such a threshold for the specific case studied is around 15-20% of the total costs involved, amounting to $140-170 mllion. Ultimately, the study's results emphasize that even basic models with daily time steps can provide valuable insights crucial for investment and policy development decisions. Furthermore, the added value of models with higher temporal resolution accuracy comes at investment costs that might be hard to justify in light of the added value thresholds observed. Lastly, the study's research reveals the particular challenges of incorporating hourly time steps in models utilizing round-robin based methods for short-term dispatch operations, as evidenced by the significant computational requirements of such models, with added value thresholds exceeding $200 million. This paper addresses a persistent issue in autonomous driving - object detection using LiDAR data, despite potential errors or losses. Existing approaches rely on complete and error-free data, leading to a significant drop in performance when faced with losses. To mitigate this problem, a new framework called BEVFusion has been developed to combine information from multiple sources - both other sensors and nearby objects - to repair lost data and enhance object detection. The proposed network design leverages cross-beverage attention to identify valuable information from multiple sources, a 3D object beam-radiation mechanism to provide supplementary context from nearby objects, and an innovative reconstruction module to restore lost data and adapt to varying input lengths. The design captures both inter-beverage and point-interference relationships, utilizing cross-attention to align and integrate information from multiple sources. Comprehensive experiments show that BEVFusion significantly improves traditional methods in object detection, fixing losses in LiDAR data and advancing the state-of-the-art in single-moderate, single-missing, and multi-sensor object detection. The proposed method also demonstrates a significant 8.52 m AP increase in a moderate scenario with 10% point loss. Notably, the design of the object beam-radiation module surpasses current state-of-the-art single-point point target methods. Furthermore, experiments using simulated LiDAR noise also demonstrate the method's robustness to various levels of noise. The method's source code and trained models are publicly available on https://github.com/DanielValvani/BEVFusion. This research proposes a comprehensive framework that addresses these challenges by incorporating advanced techniques such as model ensembling, visual explanation, statistical analysis, and program synthesis to improve both design mining and program understanding. The study utilizes a Monte Carlo sampling approach combined with a genetic optimization method to generate and evaluate shape programs, and conducts thorough empirical studies to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. This research makes significant contributions to both design mining and program synthesis, opening new avenues for exploration. The complete framework, including all code and datasets, is publicly available for future research purposes. The study also includes a demonstration of the framework's potential to greatly aid large-scale quantitative studies in various application domains, and showcases its promising results in two distinct contexts: managing design data and facilitating scale-up. A significant challenge in completing data for video frames is addressing the shift in feature positions between frames. In this study, a low-rank tensor completion model combining streaming and structural priors is proposed to significantly reduce data acquisition costs and alleviate model training complexity issues. The model can be applied to video streaming in a online and interactive manner, enabling research into motion information without waiting for the entire series. The research reveals that conventional streaming tensor completion algorithms are severely hindered by motion between frames, highlighting a substantial performance gap of at least 40% or more for various motion levels. By incorporating structural priors, the proposed model can effectively utilize motion information, resulting in a substantial improvement in reconstruction quality of 2115 or more, especially under intense motion conditions, without compromising efficiency due to its online capability. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model matches or surpasses state-of-the-art performance for video tensor completion with a significant improvement of 0.55 or more, applied to video data, while offering online capability and robustness to diverse motion conditions. The research also shows that the model can utilize additional structure information, such as temporal homogeneity, to further enhance its performance by an absolute PSNR improvement of 0.09 or more. Moreover, the research indicates that the model can effectively tackle a range of challenges from sparse, over-observed, non-Gaussian data, all under intense motion conditions, without relying on probabilistic inference algorithms. The research reveals that the proposed model can successfully utilize structural prirors to produce robust estimations by adapting to outliers up to 30% with a significant improvement in reconstruction quality of several percent or more, especially under non-Gaussian data conditions, without relying on sophisticated loss functions or probabilistic inference algorithms. Experimental results of applying the proposed model to real-world applications demonstrate its potential by achieving a substantial improvement in object removal quality of 2.23 or more, applied to magic wand images, while efficiently handling intense motion conditions without relying on sophisticated panomax technologies. The research also opens new avenues for applying tensor completion to a wide range of video-based applications by achieving a substantial improvement in face swapping performance of 0.83 or more, evaluated using the L1 distance metric, without relying on sophisticated re-translation approaches or additional hardware infrastructure. Nichols algebras over classical Weyl groups are either infinitely dimensional when their 2-cohomology groups are non-zero or they are the free algebras. Therefore, it's reasonable to expect that Nichols algebras over other groups are either the same as their Weyl counterparts or they break new ground in algebraic structure. This article proves that Nichols algebras over any finite solvable group are indeed similar to those of Weyl groups in their braiding properties, which leads to the conclusion that their L-matrices must conform to a particular pattern. As a direct result, it follows that their Nichols algebras are either the same as free algebras or they can be stratified into successive free components. This article also explores the generic imprimitive case and identifies a fundamental characteristic, namely the stratification of crossed products by free objects. Furthermore, it shows that any Nichols algebra over any group can be stratified into either the same as its Weyl counterparts or the crossed products by free objects and thereby derives the necessary and sufficient conditions for stratification. Additionally, it outlines a clear distinction between the stratifiable and non-stratifiable cases, presenting an example of the latter. Lastly, it shows that any stratifiable Nichols algebra must either be the same as free algebras or it has infinite dimensions. This article aims to lay the groundwork for the final article in this series, which will classify stratifiable Nichols algebras. For simplicity, this article primarily focuses on the case of element 2, though it does address the case of element -2 in several theorems. Future articles will expand on these results in the case of element 2. The articles in this series rely heavily on free objects, which have already shown great potential in classification and recognition in the last two articles, and which will be further developed in the sixth and final installment of this series, along with the classification of asymptotic crossed products by free objects. This approach allows us to eliminate the need for pre-built databases, instead directly utilizing set signatures from subject and object modals to guide the parsing decision. This shift presents an evaluation challenge: how to effectively assess the accuracy of social media-based mental health diagnosis tools compared to in-person clinical assessments. To address this concern, researchers developed Q-MetaNet, a neural network-based system that utilizes data from individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia by clinical professionals and also present on social media platforms. This system demonstrates better performance than current leading methods, both general and mental health-specific, and indicates that estimating mental health via social media is comparable to clinical diagnosis. Furthermore, researchers tested the system's potential benefits and concluded that utilizing Q-MetaNet could positively affect both clinical diagnosis processes and social media-based mental health diagnosis. This research is significant as it establishes a benchmark for assessing the accuracy of mental health diagnosis systems utilizing social media data. Moreover, it highlights the system's vast applications which could utilize the vast amounts of available social media data to improve mental health diagnosis accuracy while maintaining user privacy. Finally, researchers demonstrated using Q-MetaNet's structure, meta features extracted from social media can significantly enhance the performance of mental health diagnosis systems that utilize meta features, such as decision trees, support vector machines, and recurrent neural networks. This research is an important first step in effectively assessing the accuracy of social media-based mental health diagnosis systems. Moreover, it provides practical solutions to overcome current challenges in utilizing social media data and presents a new, efficient method for improving mental health diagnosis accuracy. This research has the potential to significantly contribute to the advancement of digital mental health assessment using social media data. With continued advancements in AI technology, social media data sets, and psychological knowledge, mental health diagnosis systems utilizing social media data will increasingly approach the level of accuracy achieved by clinical professionals. Ultimately, this research could lead to the development of highly accurate, real-time, and automated mental health diagnosis systems using social media data. Such systems could provide valuable support to clinical professionals and help to address current shortages of skilled psychiatrists and psychologists. Although lockdowns significantly impacted daily life and economic activity, their effectiveness can be enhanced by the actions of hospitals, health care facilities, and individuals. To mitigate the spread of SARS-CoV-2, we have proposed a susceptible-infectious-recovery-quarantine (SIRQ) model that incorporates the actions of these institutions. By integrating the actions of these institutions into the model, we can assess their effectiveness and contribute to data-driven decision making for controlling the epidemic. Through the model, we found that a combination of lockdown measures and hospital actions can be crucial in controlling the SIRQ model. However, health care facilities' ability to contain the epidemic depends heavily on the efficiency of hospital operations. If hospital efficiency is high, contained outbreaks are possible even without quarantine measures. Conversely, if hospital efficiency is low, contained outbreaks require both hospital actions and quarantine measures. Furthermore, hospital efficiency does not directly affect death rates. By integrating economic data into the model, we found that an increase in hospital efficiency can lead to an increase in economic activity levels. If hospital efficiency is high, contained outbreaks on the basis of hospital actions can lead to higher economic activity levels. However, if hospital efficiency is low, contained outbreaks on the basis of hospital actions lead to lower economic activity levels. In an effort to minimize economic losses while controlling the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, we have proposed a multi-objective framework. By incorporating the concepts of Pareto-optimal multi-objective programming, we have framed the SIRQ model as a multi-objective problem, considering the trade-off between controlling the epidemic and mitigating economic losses. Through the model, we identified four distinct regions, each characterized by a unique combination of economic losses and control measures. The interaction between the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISGMR) and Isoscalar Giant Quadrupole Resonance (ISGQR) is studied in deformed atomic nuclei using a Random Phase Approximation (RPA) formalism. This combined RPA method is applied to nuclei across the two-nucleon drip line in Sn and Zr isotopic chains, using the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov method with Skyrme energy-density functionals. Our analysis reveals that the strong interaction between ISGMR and ISGQR coupling distorts their individual energy spectra. As a result, the energy structure of the ISGMR is shifted towards lower energies, while its peak strength is reduced. Conversely, the energy structure of the ISGQR is shifted towards higher energies, while its peak strength is increased. Additionally, the coupling distorts the energy dependence of the RPA response function, resulting in a peak broadening that is particularly pronounced in deformed nuclei and at lower energy excitation values below 40 MeV. This phenomenon is attributed to the RPA fluctuations induced by the coupled ISGMR and ISGQR states. Therefore, the influence of the coupling between these resonances should be considered in studies examining the energy dependence of the RPA fluctuation strength. Furthermore, the coupled RPA method presents a promising approach for controlling the impact of the interaction between low-energy collective states and the nuclear surface in flow studies. Furthermore, the study of the isoscalar E1 strength distribution, which extends far beyond the energy range of the isoscalar GQR, can be used to determine the isoscalar E1 strength more accurately. However, the influence of the coupling between the ISGMR and ISGQR on this isoscalar E1 strength distribution should be considered in such studies. Moreover, the observed coupling patterns in Sn and Zr isotopic chains are comparable to those in other deformed nuclei, indicating that the observed coupling phenomenon is associated with nuclear deformation. The study's findings are significant for understanding nuclear excitation across a wide range of nuclei across the two-nucleon drip line in Sn and Zr isotopic chains. Furthermore, the use of modern Skyrme energy-density functionals, like UNEDF1, yields accurate results for the isoscalar GQR in stable and unstable nuclei across the nuclear chart. However, the study's findings in very neutron-deficient and neutron-rich regions require verification with the use of a more precise beyond mean-field approach.

The success of recommender systems largely hinges on the understanding of user intent. Intention-driven recommendations not only boost user satisfaction but also streamline the user experience. Despite its significance, benchmarking an intent-driven recommender system poses a significant challenge. A key obstacle is the scarcity of publicly available data sets aligning with the system's requirements. To bridge this gap, we introduce a benchmark data set on movie recommendations, specifically designed to demonstrate intent-driven recommendations. The data set comprises a vast collection of movie titles and user IDs but differs from conventional recommendation data sets by lacking explicit ratings. Instead, the data set incorporates an explicit indication of intent for each user-movie pair, derived from a movie's scene description. This novel approach offers a unique method for teaching a model user intent and demonstrates its potential on numerous benchmark tasks including a contrastive self-supervised learning network. In recent years, PCA-based methods have been proposed for recovering low-rank matrices from massive underdetermined systems, often outperforming other techniques. These matrices can be seen as random reductions of the Toeplitz matrix, which encompasses various patterns, including shift-invariant patterns like the Hankel matrix. We found that PCA fails when applied to weighted Hankel combinations, ultimately leading to a suboptimal recovery of the original low-rank matrix. Building on this insight, we presented a family of algorithms grounded in shift-invariant transformations, which significantly improve upon PCA in terms of recovery quality and are robust to adverse weight distributions. Additionally, these algorithms possess shift-invariance properties and experimentally demonstrate superior performance across diverse scenarios and even withstand adversarial noise when applied to weighted Hankel combinations. Considering their versatility and reliability, we suggest using these algorithms as a starting point for recovering shift-invariant low-rank matrices in various real-world applications. Furthermore, we analyzed the theoretical performance of these algorithms and identified a lower bound on the recovery error, which was shown to converge at a rate of O(N^(1-2/m)) for matrices of rank m and size N. Although this result does not achieve the optimal, nearly-exponential convergence rate seen in other methods, the remaining gap highlights an intriguing opportunity for further research into algorithms that can more efficiently recover low-rank matrices from shift-invariant patterns. On a more practical note, our method's performance is comparable to or in some cases even superior to current state-of-the-art techniques, including LMaGG, L-SR, KKr, KKr-R, MedR, PNO, PNO-, LPT, LRT, FROST, and ISID in a diverse range of practical scenarios, which we will discuss in more detail later. As such, these algorithms are recommended as a sensible starting point for any real-world application involving low-rank matrix recovery from shift-invariant patterns. Bass algorithm successfully models the dynamic changes in various connected systems, from the behavior of data networks to the spread of infectious diseases. Its ability to describe complex dynamics is widely applicable, yet accurately modeling system growth requires precise parameters, especially the average number of connections. The development of efficient network controllers heavily depends on this parameter. To overcome this challenge, we propose an algorithm that utilizes Bass model predictions to enhance the performance of network controllers. By leveraging connections between Bass model predictions and control algorithms, we update the parameters of Bass models to improve our understanding of network behavior. Consequently, the parameter estimates improve the predictions and system stability. By testing the method with real data, we demonstrate its effectiveness in modeling and analyzing connected systems. The proposed approach can potentially expand to modeling other complex phenomena. In recent years, Automated Market Makers (AMMs), such as Uniswap, have become widely used platforms for conducting market transactions. These AMMs allow users to exchange cryptocurrencies by providing liquidity in exchange for fees. This study focuses on the price of "output" tokens when transferring "input" tokens, and how the curvature of the pricing curve affects surpluses and potential arbitrage opportunities. Surpluses are quantified by measuring the amount of output tokens that users can obtain with an extra input token, and this quantity is shown to be a decreasing function of the curvature for transactions involving three or more parties. Therefore, we found that the curvature of the pricing curves in AMMs creates opportunities for medium-scale arbitrage. This arbitrage involves a transfer of tokens to AMMs, followed by a transfer of output tokens to other platforms for a higher price, and this process is facilitated by a third-party bridge. To implement this arbitrage, we developed a simulation tool that utilizes optimal batch state transition strategies in Markov Decision Processes, and this tool is used to test the feasibility of the arbitrage. As a result, we demonstrated that the arbitrage can be successfully carried out, and this highlights the importance of considering arbitrage opportunities when evaluating the performance of AMMs. Additionally, we explored an extended version of the arbitrage opportunity that involves the transfer of three tokens, and we found that an modified version of Chebychev's inequality can be used to establish an upper limit on the minimum amount of output tokens that users can obtain with an extra input token. This extended arbitrage opportunity leads to the development of a strategy that transfers tokens from AMMs to other platforms for a higher price, and this process is shown to be feasible under realistic market conditions. To confirm the feasibility of the extended arbitrage opportunity, we conducted experiments under realistic market conditions and these experiments demonstrate that the extended arbitrage opportunity is medium-scale and large-scale as the output token price fluctuates. This study contributes to our understanding of the feasibility of arbitrage opportunities by providing a systematic approach to evaluating the curvature of pricing curves in AMMs and MMs. Furthermore, we extended the results to explore an additional arbitrage opportunity that involves the transfer of three tokens, and this future research direction may lead to the development of practical arbitrage strategies that can be utilized in real-world market transactions. Using LHCb's proton-proton collision data at 7 and 13 TeV, the researchers analyzed the production patterns of D0, D+s mesons from their decays into K+π- and KSπ-. They then derived the fragmentation ratios of D0, D+s, and various strange mesons created during the decays of D0, D+s, and their parent charm quarks. These fragmentation ratios of D0, D+s from their decays were found to be around 36.2% and 23.2%, respectively, which is lower than their counterparts for beauty quarks. The data also showed that strange mesons make up about 24.2% and 28.4% of the decays resulting from the D0, D+s decays, respectively. These results provide insight into the differences between the fragmentation of charm and beauty quarks. Furthermore, the data on fragmentation ratios at 7 TeV was used to calculate the cross-sections for the production of singly produced charm mesons, which were then compared with theoretical predictions based on perturbative QCD. The data on fragmentation ratios and cross-sections can be used to improve the calculation of fragmentation functions and reduce uncertainties in future analyses. These functions are essential in understanding various physical processes and can also be used to derive parton functions, which facilitate the calculation of inclusive quantities at the hadron level. These parton functions can then be used to optimize the design of detector acceptance in experiments, such as the LHCb. The analysis also demonstrated compatibility with theoretical predictions based on factorized perturbative QCD and estimated uncertainties based on non-perturbative fragmentation functions. This analysis represents the first experimental estimation of fragmentation functions for singly produced strange mesons. The data on cross-sections was consistent with theoretical predictions based on perturbative QCD within estimated uncertainties. However, the data on fragmentation ratios revealed discrepancies of 1.3σ and 1.6σ with various models based on different factorization schemes. The data on cross-sections was consistent with theoretical predictions based on perturbative QCD within estimated uncertainties. These results expand our understanding of fragmentation functions, providing new data on the production of strange mesons from charm quarks at high-energy proton-proton collisions. Python, Java, and C crypto libraries are misused in common programming tasks.

the library's API, with the Python crypto library being the most prone to abuse.

breaches. On the other hand, the Java and C crypto libraries have fewer issues,

design and potential security threats. We propose certain design principles,
like hiding sensitive code or implementing checks, that can decrease the risk of
potential security breaches. Ultimately, understanding the relationship between API
design and potential security threats can help developers create safer, more
secure crypto libraries that minimize the likelihood of potential data breaches.

In recent times, there has been growing interest in 3D data recovery using 2D imaging techniques.  The feasibility of 3D data recovery using 2D imaging has been established, yet predicting 3D data recovery accuracy based on 2D image volume has not been thoroughly addressed.  This research presents a quantitative framework for assessing the 3D data recovery capabilities of 2D imaging.  The proposed framework assesses 3D data recovery accuracy for large-scale scenarios based on the volume of 2D image data collected.  Analytical and computational results indicate that 3D data recovery accuracy is dependent on the 2D image volume and the data recovery process is optimized at a specific 2D image volume.  This optimal 2D image volume is found to be closely correlated with the data compression ratio for the 3D data recovered from 2D imaging.  This research provides a quantitative framework for selecting optimal 2D imaging strategies along with 2D image volume considerations to maximize 3D data recovery accuracy. Additionally, this research discusses design approaches to achieve high 3D data recovery accuracy using 2D imaging for large-scale scenarios. The analysis presented in this research is general and applicable to a variety of data types including surface, scalar and vector fields. The feasibility of 2D imaging for signless, positive or circular data recovery scenarios has also been addressed in this research. Computational results for a typical medical CT scan data set show that 3D data recovery accuracy greater than 90% can be achieved with 2D image volume of approximately 0.1 cubic centimeters. Additionally, we find that a lower bound for optimal volume is existent and the numerical value for this lower bound is calculated to be 0.042 in specific scenario of signless data recovery. This paper presents an optimized method for recovering underlying reflection coefficients in time-domain seismic data by employing a novel synthesis sparse model, which outperforms traditional methods by more than 10 dB in terms of data fitting. The proposed approach iteratively estimates reflection coefficients and velocities, using an alternating optimization process. By alternating between these parameters, we derive conditions for convergence and experimental results demonstrate significant accuracy improvements, especially for curved interface profiles, where our method yields a 5-fold decrease in minimum support compared to a conventional approach, resulting in data fitting improvements of over 15 dB. Notably, this method's efficacy is not limited to data fitting; reflection coefficient estimates also demonstrate substantial improvements, averaging 2-fold reductions in support for curved interfaces with data matching performance enhanced by nearly 20 dB. The proposed algorithm outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches in seismic reflection coefficient estimation, significantly improving data matching and reflection coefficient estimates. Furthermore, experimental results indicate that this method can successfully identify user-provided reflection coefficients, thus preventing interference from noise in reflection coefficients. Moreover, for the range $1 < p < 2$, it has been established that the compactness of $T_{g}$ (or $T_{g}^*$) implies the weak compactness of $T_{g}$ in BMOA_p. Subsequently, for the space Bergman-Poisson boundary, it has been proven that the unbounded linear operators whose symbols belong to a specific sub-space called VMOA_p for the range $1 < p < 2$ can be removed from consideration in context of weak compactness. Similarly, for the Bergman space, it has been established that the unbounded linear operators whose symbols belong to a specific sub-space called VMOA_p for the range $1 < p < 2$ can be removed from consideration in context of weak compactness. Further analysis reveals that the compactness of $T_{g}$ (or $T_{g}^*$) in context of the Bergman space or Bergman-Poisson boundary implies the boundedness of the Riesz transform $\mathcal{R}$ when considered in context of Haar series. We propose an efficient method for calculating the conformal data of quantum spin chains at low energy through overlaps of wavefunctions. Building upon this, we develop an approach to compute entire conformal data sets, including central charges, critical exponents, and dual structures, by relying on wavefunction overlaps and energy spectra. This method is successfully applied to various models such as the spin-1/2 XXZ Heisenberg Hamiltonian and the Kondo model. Importantly, our technique enables the determination of conformal data even for models lacking a clear Hamiltonian formulation, like the paired spin-1/2 fermions on a ring. Furthermore, we utilize our results to detect signs of conformal data "smearing" in an explicitly time-evolving scenario: the paired spin-1/2 fermions interacting with a chiral edge mode in a topological Kondo lattice model, during a quantum quench. In this case, the "smearing" originates from states with pair and solo-fermion symmetries that separate in the non-integrable situation. In contrast to the scenario of a quantum quench in an integrable system, the paired fermions do not exhibit entanglement "light speed" behavior. We display the associated time-evolving von Neumann entropy and explain its higher value compared to the case of pair-only symmetries through the emergence of string excitations. Lastly, our findings highlight the utility of wavefunction overlaps for analyzing the duality between target and source sides in CFTs and the resulting universality of target-side conformal data. Moreover, they reveal an intriguing connection between the CFT dual structure and the symmetry network of the original lattice model. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that the efficient computation of conformal data is within reach, even for systems not yet well-understood in the field. This research delves into the application of deep learning for the diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2, which causes COVID-19. Currently, deep learning methods that analyze lung CT scans alone or combine with clinical data are being tested for their potential to automatically diagnose the disease. To assess these models' performance when data is incomplete, the researchers developed a hybrid approach called the hybrid decomposition block, which ensures image and clinical feature importance are represented equally in the diagnostic prediction. Well-designed experiments indicate that this strategy enhances the sensitivity of the model. A degenerate version of the hybrid decomposition block, without considering clinical data, demonstrates improved robustness against image corruption. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method's efficacy and robustness was conducted using standard metrics and risk metrics. Testing the model on challenging datasets demonstrated its capacity to accurately differentiate between COVID-19 and fake positive lung CT scans up to 90%, whereas the model can reliably identify genuine lung CT scans contaminated with noise at a rate greater than 98%. Application of the hybrid decomposition block to real-world datasets demonstrated its potential to significantly enhance diagnosis by achieving an average increase of 10% in accuracy, 15% in precision, 10% in F1-score, and 10% in AUC-ROC compared to current diagnostic methods. Notably, incorporating clinical data into the diagnosis enhanced the model's sensitivity by 10% and accuracy by 10%. Therefore, this research indicates that combining image and clinical data is essential for the development of effective diagnostic models. It also suggests exploring multiple deep learning techniques to achieve more reliable machine-learned diagnostic models. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute positively to the fight against COVID-19. We apply the quantum $S$-matrix formulation to the Dreyer's model of black hole geometry. The approach involves selecting a specific spatial slice of the black hole, in this case the outgoing null slice, and defining the $S$-matrix on the hypersurface $\mathcal{I}^+$ formed by the axis of the black hole. However, the $S$-matrix formulation is limited in its ability to describe black hole quantities such as the entropy. But, when combined with the Hartle-Hawking isoentropic map, the $S$-matrix formulation enables us to compute the black hole entropy in a non-perturbative manner. Following this, we apply to Dreyer's black hole the approach developed by Alves, and previously used for the Doulgas-Schwartz black hole, that merges the $S$-matrix formulation with the expansion of the out-going null surface to establish a basis for the hyperdense matter. With these two methods, we confirm that the quantum $S$-matrix formulation is effective in dealing with black hole problems, and that the unified approach developed by Alves is a promising general strategy. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the unified approach has the potential to extend beyond application to Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker spacetimes. It is also noted that the work presented here represents the first successful application of the quantum $S$-matrix formulation to the thermodynamics of Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker spacetimes in two scenarios. In addition, our analysis brings to light a connection between hyperdense matter and the cosmological matter, and highlights the significance of the unified approach in dealing with matter at any point of the matter expansion. Ultimately, our results indicate that the unified approach developed by Alves is a versatile tool for addressing challenges in quantum gravity and cosmology. Furthermore, our analysis provides a clear demonstration of how the quantum $S$-matrix formulation can be used to make non-perturbative predictions based on the matter expansion, and how the phase space of the $S$-matrix can be used to establish a connection between the near and the far regions of spacetime. LitMind generates definitions that combine standard dictionary entries with literary flair, achieved by integrating the Mindspelling word-mutation algorithm with a dictionary of basic words and phrases. Interestingly, the results revealed that the definitions showed a significant stylistic similarity to the native English speakers who generated them, indicating that the LitMind algorithm is effective in capturing the style of different languages. While post-hoc explanations in recommendation systems are often required for transparency, their reliance on these explanations actually decreases the models' reliability. For instance, when explanations differ from the actual desired outputs, users may misunderstand their desired results. In this study, a framework for analyzing the accuracy of post-hoc explanations in recommendation systems has been created. The research demonstrates that explanations made by users that are not in line with the actual desired outputs by a significant amount negatively affect the results of subsequent recommendation model predictions. Conversely, explanations that closely match the actual desired outputs with little margin positively affects the results of subsequent recommendation model predictions. The research also finds that users not only provide explanations based on items they actually liked but also based on items they thought they liked. Consequently, recommendations based on these distorted explanations lead to items that are not genuinely liked by users. As a result, a multi-objective loss function framework has been proposed to break the reliance of recommendation models on distorted explanations. Through the use of an iterative optimization technique, the accuracy of prediction has been increased and the distortion in explanations has been decreased. Experiments conducted using a real-world dataset have shown the proposed method to outperform the current state-of-the-art methods. The research further reveals that distorted explanations brought about by post-hoc explanations may lead to recommendation models learning biased representations that reinforce and amplify this bias. Conversely, recommendations made by model predictions that take into account user-drawn explanations result in fewer items that are not genuinely liked by users. Consequently, a graph-based backpropagation technique has been proposed to address the issue of gradient vanishing when drawing post-hoc explanations. The research findings can be further applied to handle post-hoc explanations positively or negatively impacting recommendation model predictions depending on their level of distortion. This interaction between charged particles and radiation is a key factor in understanding phenomena such as radiation reaction and particle channeling. We have investigated this coupling using the Fokker-Bloch equations, focusing on how radiation interacts with an overdamped particle distribution. We found that the initial uniform motion of particles induces a radial density gradient in the distribution, which in turn causes radiation to slow the particles down through a process related to the Rayleigh-Taylor instability. We have further analyzed the effect of this process, referred to as warp-driven friction, and demonstrated its significant impact on the particle distribution, particularly in certain experimental setups where rapid quenching can produce a dense, anisotropic, and axially symmetric particle distribution. We have shown that conventional models of particle friction are inadequate under such circumstances and that the particle distribution becomes bipolar due to the emergence of small-density fluctuations. We have also identified the crucial factors that determine the efficacy of warp-driven friction, which includes the rate of particle quenching, radiation resistance, and the initial electron density in the drift space. We have verified the physical plausibility of these factors through detailed case studies. Notably, we have found that warp-driven friction can be substantial even when radiation field intensity is relatively low and that anisotropy in the particle distribution is a necessary condition for this effect to manifest. We have also observed that frictional behavior becomes nonlinear due to the auto-acceleration of particles resulting from their interaction with the warped distribution. This relationship is reminiscent of the concept of "magnetic mirroring" in particle confinement. In contrast to traditional methods, our MMRG algorithm produces generated data that's similar to the original minority class data, rather than the dominant majority class. Through thorough evaluation using a comprehensive set of imbalanced data sets, we've demonstrated the superior performance of our MMR algorithms compared to traditional methods, including AdaSyn. This research proposes a new approach to tackle the scalability issue in data-driven MPC for large-scale networks of cyber-physical systems. This enables the development of an optimized MPC algorithm, which uses spectral properties to derive an appropriate quadratic program for control decision-making. This paper develops an efficient temporal model that represents the variability of event intervals in temporal graphs. Unlike existing approaches, which model individual event occurrences independently, this method models the time gaps between events. The novel model uses a non-parametric Bayesian approach combined with a Griddy variational inference method to learn the distribution of time intervals in a collaborative fashion. This paper introduces a BLRM mechanism that utilizes Bayesian statistics to refine labels contaminated by training data noise, thereby enhancing the robustness of deep neural networks. BLRM's core component is a noise model based on the $l_1$-norm, which allows the algorithm to calculate the posterior distribution of each label via Bayesian inference and subsequently refine the label via optimization. The refined labels can then be fed back into the deep neural network, which is trained again using the updated labels. This process can be repeated multiple times. Moreover, BLRM comes with adaptive features, including the ability to determine its hyperparameters autonomously and only rely on task-specific inputs. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that BLRM achieves a high degree of adaptability and effectiveness. Moreover, compared to conventional methods, BLRM exhibits a notable ability to eliminate redundant data, achieve fast convergence, and maintain robustness in the face of data noise. Notably, BLRM's performance in robustness is comparable to or even surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, while its computational complexity is significantly lower. Moreover, the research shows that BLRM can be applied across a range of deep neural networks, including the ResNet, SE-Net, Wide-Net, and DenseNet models. Moreover, the refrubished labels generated by BLRM can be used in semi-supervised learning, which further validates the algorithm's effectiveness. A novel approach for precisely controlling light emission from molecules near optical nanoantennas is proposed and demonstrated, yielding tunable electromagnetic responses. 
The method leverages interference between the fields radiated by the nanoantenna and those confined within it, 
allowing the resonances' spectral positions and linewidths to be individually adjustable. 
This technique offers a means to optimize light emission in enhanced single-photon emission and highly efficient second harmonic generation applications. 
The independence of spectral adjustments enables the optimization of emission spectra in coherent light sources, 
whose resonances can be engineered to match molecular emission patterns to boost emission efficiency or the emission direction can be redirected away from the light source to improve detection capabilities without compromising the light source's properties. 
The presented concept is exemplified through theoretical modeling of different metal nanoantenna geometries. 
The results show that by tailoring the antenna geometry it is possible to achieve coherent light extraction of the molecule's emission while redirecting the light emitted by the antenna itself in opposing directions. 
This novel approach highlights the sophisticated light-manipulation capabilities of complex optical nanoantennas, 
whose custom design can be exploited to advance single-photon light sources and other coherent light applications. 
The demonstrated flexibility in EM responses can inspire the development of tailored light extraction strategies in real-world nanoantenna-based light emitters. 
The method presented in this work can be applied to different EM configurations and can be used to study electromagnetic responses in different material systems.

Amorphous and crystalline solids share many mechanical traits, yet their microscopic behaviors differ significantly. Amorphous materials are distinguished by their disordered molecular structures, which give rise to localized stress releases, known as plastic events. These events, analyzed through simulated digital models under increasing stress, have been found to happen in a seemingly continuous, steady pattern. A proposed explanation suggests these events result from localized molecular clusters that have reduced stability due to unfavorable bond orientations. Supporting this theory, this study demonstrates that introducing ordered regions within an amorphous material causes plastic events to occur more frequently, particularly in areas with higher bond angles. Consequently, this finding provides further evidence for the role of bond orientations in plastic events. Moreover, it highlights the potential use of ordered areas within amorphous materials as a means to manipulate their mechanical behavior. A deeper examination into the effects of ordered areas on plastic events may uncover new mechanisms underlying the combined strength and flexibility characteristic of many amorphous materials. For example, this principle could expand our understanding of how bone tissue adapts to varying loads. By investigating the mechanics of amorphous and crystalline solids at the molecular level, researchers may uncover novel means to enhance material durability in diverse applications. KNN, SVM, and neural network algorithms frequently encounter issues related to class imbalance, where one class has significantly more examples than others. Overfitting often occurs when these models are dominated by the majority class. In response, researchers have proposed the Total Loss Balance (TLB) method, which extends Overfitting Prevention by Adjusting Sub-matrices (OPAS) to address class imbalance for KNN and SVM. This approach involves adjusting the distance metric for KNN and reweighing classes for SVM. By focusing on in-class variations, TLB promotes inter-class variations, effectively addressing the challenges posed by class imbalance. In experiments, TLB demonstrated superior performance on real-world datasets, achieving improved convergence and accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, while also being insensitive to parameters. Furthermore, TLB's effectiveness was demonstrated even when the parameters were optimized using the conventional total loss, achieving a 25.6% improvement in accuracy for KNN and 9.6% for SVM. Interestingly, TLB's impact was found to be more substantial for KNN and SVM than neural networks. This research highlights TLB's efficiency in handling class imbalance without relying on data augmentation, semi-supervised learning, or curating data. TLB can be easily integrated into various algorithms as a loss function to prevent overfitting caused by class imbalance. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/Chengxiang-Du/TLB-IMBALANCE-Learning. Moreover, a comparative performance chart showing the impact of class imbalance on KNN, SVM, and neural networks is provided. Finally, TLB's applicability to deep neural networks is discussed, and future research aims to investigate this further. This study also reveals how class imbalance affects KNN, SVM, and neural networks, resulting in substantial disparities in performance. Moreover, a comparative performance chart showing the impact of class imbalance on KNN, SVM, and neural networks is provided. Finally, TLB's applicability to deep neural networks is discussed and future research aims to investigate this further. The discrepancy in performance under class imbalance is substantial, with differences of up to 60% observed in total loss and accuracy. Notably, neural networks exhibit relatively robustness to class imbalance compared to KNN and SVM. Several potential explanations for this phenomenon, derived from the theoretical analysis of neural networks' ability to tolerate class imbalance, are presented. Initially, neural networks' large capacity and difficulty in achieving maximum accuracy on majority class examples make them less susceptible to class imbalance.

This research assesses the level of COVID-19 related news coverage in multiple regions, utilizing data from online articles in five languages and 19 newspapers across Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, and Peru. A total of 65,728 articles published between 1 January 2019 and 30 April 2020 were analyzed, using 1,292 unique headlines and 11,839 article titles translated into English. A two-stage text mining approach was employed to categorize articles into ten COVID-19 related topics and five general categories. Findings indicate that larger newspapers dominated COVID-19 related news coverage and provided more in-depth analysis, while smaller newspapers focused on announcing auto-immune cases and highlighting government responses. In-depth analysis revealed that 56% of articles contained geographic information, with 71% being government sources. Human-centric entities emerged as the primary subject in article headlines (43%) and article bodies (51%). Additionally, it was found that 53% of articles included images, with 57% being photographs. Although there were significant differences in news coverage volume and content, all newspapers analyzed demonstrated some level of COVID-19 related news coverage. The study highlights the effectiveness of automated data collection and analysis in exploring large datasets, with implications for future research into news coverage and government communication during crises. The dataset and R code used in this study are available for public access. 

Keywords: news coverage, COVID-19, text mining, data analysis, machine learning, South America, coronavirus.

Gravitational field calculations in astrophysics and related fields pose significant computational challenges, particularly in large-scale simulations beyond O(N) magnitudes. To address these issues, finite difference methods were first used, followed by more advanced techniques such as Barnes-Hut and tree algorithms, which were later improved upon. The fast multipole method (FMM) emerged in the 1980s as a highly efficient approach for solving multiple systems of linear equations in linear algebra. Although FMM was initially developed for matrices representing Laplace and Helmholtz equations, its applications have expanded to support the Poisson equation and its derivatives, including gravitational forces. By adapting Korn's theorem, researchers have successfully incorporated force calculations into FMM. This framework has enabled the development of algorithms such as Korn's FMM, which we demonstrate through a series of numerical tests on a variety of tessellations. These tests show that Korn's FMM is accurate and computationally efficient, with time complexities of O(N log* N) in the near-field and O(N) in the far-field. Furthermore, it outperforms other state-of-the-art tessellation-based techniques in both computational speed and memory usage. Consequently, Korn's FMM may serve as a viable alternative to more complex cell-based approaches, such as POT and SkyTree, in future gravitational simulations. Moreover, our results indicate that Korn's FMM is adaptable to hierarchical tree data structures, making it a potential improvement over Potters' Tree (POT) algorithm. Although our implementation of Potters' Tree is less efficient than Korn's FMM, it is still a promising choice for future tree-based simulations due to its relatively simple design. To facilitate further research and development, both Korn's FMM and Potters' Tree have been made available as open-source software on GitHub.
