In a distributed setting, stochastic optimization techniques reach a faster solution by leveraging data parallelism, where multiple devices process separate data sets in parallel. Consequently, the methods' updates can be communicated to the central server in batches. Building on this idea, communication optimization methods like quantization, federated learning, and shadow updates have been developed to further improve performance. While these methods reduce communication rounds without compromising the method's convergence rate, they often rely on uncertain system parameters. This research develops a unified framework, using combinatorial optimization, to determine which communication optimization techniques are most suitable in various stochastic optimization settings. Additionally, a new method, referred to as FRQ, is proposed, incorporating findings from existing research to further boost performance. Experiments demonstrate that FRQ outperforms other methods, including round-optimal techniques, and shows flexibility in being adapted to different communication constraints. Furthermore, a lower bound on the convergence rate is established for methods like FRQ, demonstrating that existing techniques are likely optimal. Finally, recommendations are provided for future research directions. This work aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of distributed stochastic optimization, paving the way for a future benchmark standard. While numerous studies have investigated low-resource language translation, a labor-intensive process involving human intervention often necessitates new training components for each new language. However, transferring knowledge from languages with a common root seems like a more efficient approach. We propose that transfer learning can streamline this process, significantly reducing the need for human involvement. In our study, we discovered that transfer learning enables training multiple related-language models with minimal human oversight, effectively avoiding the need for detailed domain knowledge. This novel observation has significant implications, as our experiments suggest that achieving similar translation accuracy in low-resource settings may not, in fact, require significantly advancing the state-of-the-art in translation technology. We observed that training Chichewa-English models in addition to other languages yielded improved translation performance, even when starting with translated training data. Moreover, adding Malagasy-English and Sinhala-English models to this combination led to comparable results, even with the addition of human human evaluation. Interestingly, while the performance of our models varied across languages, we found that factors such as language size and proximity to source languages (English) appeared to have a more substantial impact than the order of training models. In contrast, indirect training (distant supervision) seemed to have limited effectiveness. These findings indicate that transfer learning enhances the training of models for languages with a common origin, potentially making low-resource translation more efficient and accessible. We welcome any collaborations or adaptations that leverage our results to accelerate low-resource translation projects. Ultimately, our study offers a positive outlook for translating languages with limited data and reduced the need for human intervention in the translation process. Expert knowledge and analytical driving data are invaluable in understanding driver behavior, but conventional evaluation methods involving drivers' actions can be time-consuming and prone to subjective biases. This technique allows us of leverage advanced machine learning capabilities for compressing large driver behavior datasets. By effectively combining these two strengths, we've created a highly efficient system for identifying critical driving events and pinpointing areas where further expertise is needed to refine the model's accuracy. To demonstrate its capabilities, we've tested our system in a real-world environment, comparing its performance in an instrumented vehicle setting with a human judge's annotations. Challenges in text recognition are exacerbated by Out-Of-Vocabulary words, which typically account for a significant portion of errors in initial model attempts. Despite significant progress made in recent years, robust scene text recognition remains an elusive goal due to the prevalence of OOV words and inconsistent transcription quality. To address these issues, this paper proposes an innovative data augmentation approach called Semi-Supervised Data Augmentation (SSDA) that not only handles OOV words but also provides enhanced model performance. The proposed method produces high-quality training data by leveraging model predictions and correcting them with labeled OOV examples, which in turn allows for greater data augmentation scalability. Unlike traditional methods, SSDA semantically expands the training dataset by generating new OOV labels based on existing knowledge rather than simply applying image transformations. Comprehensive experiments conducted on SCUT-CTW1500, ICDAR2013, ICDAR2015, and SCUT-MSR-10K-10K datasets showcase the proposed SSDA's superiority over contemporary data augmentation techniques. Furthermore, the paper proposes a pioneering evaluation method to assess scene text recognition models under unseen language conditions. SSDA's exceptional performance is demonstrated by its ability to significantly improve state-of-the-art models on various benchmark datasets and its ability to achieve a new benchmark on the SCUT-MSR-10K-10K dataset with a character accuracy of 83.71%. The paper's code and dataset will be publicly available on https://github.com/asharakeh/SSDA. The dataset comprising OOV words used in this paper can be accessed at: \url{https://github.com/asharkeh/OOV-Scene-Text}. A new benchmark dataset consisting of commonly misspelled OOV words in English, German and Chinese can be accessed at: \url{https://github.com/asharkeh/OOV-Scene-Tags}. Given a Banach lattice $E$, a function $f\colon E \to \mathbb{R}$, and a closed convex set $C \subset E$, the FGM generates a sequence $\{x_k\} \subset C$, beginning with an initial point $x_0 \in C$, using the iterative formula $x_{k+1} = A(x_k) + b$, where $A\colon [0,1] \times E \to E$ is a weakly nonlinear and monotone operator, and $b \in [0,1] \times E$. Under specific conditions on $A$ and $b$, the findings include a $l_1$-norm convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/k)$. When interacting with a limited number of tasks, humans can often figure out what a robot wants them to do by observing its actions. However, if the robot's task list isn't clearly defined and the robot reveals which specific tasks it wants the human to do mid-interaction, it causes confusion, resulting in lower human performance. In this study, we found that keeping the robot's task list a mystery doesn't necessarily lead to confusion if the robot initially asks the human to do a single task. By giving the human a clear description of the first task, along with an instruction to ask for help if needed, performance remained the same even if the robot reveals its task list later on. This led us to recommend that robots keep their task lists a secret until interactions start, and then clearly communicate the first task they want the human to do. Furthermore, our research indicates that these guidelines also improve interactions between humans and control systems that the human isn't aware of. Specifically, our results show that these guidelines result in higher performance when the control system accidentally shuts down, as the human is better off continuing to follow the robot's original instructions rather than asking for help. All data collected in this study can be accessed through a publicly available repository at https://doi.org/10.5281/ten ThousandIXL/2g6b.ijv.

Navigation in complex indoor environments faces challenges due to the absence of a suitable global metric map, primarily because most mapping methods fail to distinguish between permanent structures and temporary changes or overlook their significance. This lack forces researchers to make unrealistic assumptions about scene geometry. Our proposed HiTMap represents a point cloud in 3D space by linking semi-flexible beams to indoor features, allowing for adaptable representation of complex environments. This approach enables efficient global mapping, dynamic adjustment to temporary changes, and differentiation between obstacles and free spaces. Furthermore, it facilitates the determination of self-position through sparse data, outperforming traditional position estimation methods. Our approach is successfully validated by comparing synthetic and real-world scans to established point cloud registration methods. The results show that HiTMap significantly improves upon existing methods in mapping, position estimation, and overall performance while maintaining a reasonable memory footprint. Our method is now available online at https://research.tribeca.ai/HiTMap. For this study, we utilized the Wayfinder dataset and conducted all 3D point cloud visualizations through Iguana Visualizer. The associated video can be found at https://research.tribeca.ai/HiTMap-Video. Wayfinder data can be accessed at https://research.tribeca.ai/Wayfinder-Data. Our contribution aims to expand indoor point cloud applications by addressing the critical issue of global mapping and self-position estimation. Furthermore, this approach offers flexible adaptation to temporary changes through adjustable beam tension, demonstrating its potential in managing navigation. The developed HiTMap can be utilized for various indoor point cloud-based applications by launching a Docker container with the command `docker run -d tribecai/hiTMap-docker`. The behavior of photons under strong-coupling conditions with atoms is accurately described using the effective gap width approach, allowing for the simulation of heavy bosons in a 1D lattice. This parameterization, similar to the transfer matrix formalism, offers an improved method for predicting light propagation in periodic media by efficiently separating the fast oscillatory nature of light from the slower varying phase information. In the context of heavy bosons, this parameterization demonstrates a smooth transition to the linear regime, effectively describing light propagation. Unlike the linear regime, however, the effective gap width approach does not adhere to conventional diffraction principles, as evidenced by its ability to describe Anderson localization without invoking conventional localization lengths. Furthermore, we observed Anderson localization in a parametric regime where the photon's de Broglie wavelength exceeds the lattice spacing, a phenomenon that has yet to be observed in optical simulations. In addition to heavy bosons, we also examined the parameterization of heavier bosons in a 2D lattice, demonstrating that the effective gap width approach can be applied to a broader range of scenarios. Lastly, we applied the effective gap width approach to describe the phase shift resulting from a abrupt interface over a larger distance, compared to the linear regime. Consequently, we obtained the entire spectral information of the field, rather than merely solving the stationary wave equation. Notably, the parameterization exhibits consistency with heavy bosons in a 1D lattice, as well as for a broader range of scenarios in a 2D lattice. Ultimately, the effective gap width approach may be adapted to various applications, such as heavy atoms in a 3D lattice, optical simulations, and other scenarios involving heavy bosons. With potential applications extending to ultracold atoms and photons, this parameterization has far-reaching implications for predicting light propagation in novel media. By efficiently modeling the fast oscillatory nature of light, the effective gap width approach demonstrates substantial computational advantages over traditional methods, as exemplified by its application to heavy bosons in a 1D lattice, where the localization length based on the effective gap width approach exceeds the total system length in a scenario where the photon's de Broglie wavelength exceeds the lattice spacing. Similarly, the approach yields computational efficiency in a broader range of scenarios, as will be further illustrated in the case of heavy bosons in a 2D lattice. Named Entity Retrieval from free text is limited by lacking entity type information and user feedback. Contextual NER, a sub-task that benefits from these improvements, retrieves entities based on their context. Although contextual NER has access to entities and their context, the quality of the entities and the resulting retrieval is still affected by inaccuracies in the ground truth data and the lack of accurate context representation. To address these issues, the use of annotations other than entity type annotations and the improvement of context representations through incorporating entity type information are proposed, aiming to enhance contextual NER. Furthermore, the utility of human feedback in contextual NER is explored by comparing it with automatic annotations, with the aim of increasing feedback efficiency by half while maintaining or improving retrieval performance. Human feedback and annotations are trained using a novel approach, the temporal relational GAN, which analyzes the relationships between entities throughout a document, focusing on entities and their annotations at a specific point in time. Results demonstrate that human feedback and annotations can successfully improve contextual NER by reducing errors made by the baseline system; however, the effect of these improvements varied depending on the entity types and the annotations used. As an added benefit, the proposed temporal relational GAN achieved a 57% accuracy in predicting human annotations, outperforming a conventional relational GAN. Furthermore, the integration of human feedback and annotations in NER and contextual NER were found to be viable alternatives to automatic annotations, with human feedback being especially useful. Human feedback outperformed the baseline system by an absolute accuracy of 11.8% and 13.6% without and with additional annotations, respectively. These improvements in accuracy were found to be consistent across different entity types, with annotations providing more efficiency by reducing the number of required feedback elements from 22 to 11. Lastly, the effect of human feedback and annotations were found to be independent of the entity type, indicating their universality and utility in a wide range of applications. These results highlight the importance and potential of human feedback and annotations in enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of NER and contextual NER. Moreover, the novel approach of incorporating temporal aspects using the temporal relational GAN provides a new and effective approach to learning from these inputs. This research introduces a novel, parallel algorithm for efficiently sampling down-sampling LIDAR point clouds, which aids in registering these point clouds by identifying consistent features in scene scans. By selectively sampling the LIDAR data, the proposed method circumvents the need for processing full datasets and generates more focused, manageable point clouds that retain representative features. It determines non-essential points for suppression, forming a sparse subset that maintains key scene details, thus accelerating registration efficiency and ensuring improved alignment accuracy for both static and moving objects. Moreover, the algorithm ensures that point clouds are representative across multiple scans in dynamic settings. Validation utilizing real-world data reveals that, relative to initial LIDAR data, the proposed algorithm achieves a substantial 10-fold reduction in processing complexity without compromise to registration performance. Importantly, this method yields comparable results to more computationally demanding algorithms, even with only a fraction of the original data processed. Satellite imagery is a valuable tool for analyzing and understanding Earth's processes and aiding humanitarian response efforts, but its utilization requires considerable expertise in remote sensing. Machine learning techniques, specifically deep learning, have the potential to bridge this expertise gap by offering semi-autonomous solutions, but their reliance on large, balanced datasets creates new challenges. Boosting the efficiency of machine learning model training and enabling end-users to generate valuable maps and datasets without extensive domain experience poses significant challenges, particularly in fields like satellite image analysis. To tackle these obstacles, investing in accelerated GPU infrastructure is now a mainstream strategy. This paper examines the cost effectiveness of repurposing a high-end high-resolution GPU server for rapid training of deep learning models in satellite image analysis, and compares its efficiency to that of a more conventional, lower-resolution dual GPU server. By refitting the deep learning model to operate on a high-resolution GPU server with 64 GB of VRAM, and testing it on various applications such as land cover classification, object detection, and image reconstruction, our study demonstrates the immense potential of leveraging high-end infrastructure to speed up deep learning model training and adapt it to applications across remote sensing and scientific computing fields. This research showcases an innovative method of utilizing high-resolution GPU servers in a way that maximizes their value and helps end-users to generate valuable datasets and maps without requiring extensive domain experience. By achieving a training speed of up to 1-2 hours per epoch, our solution enables semi-autonomous model selection, thereby significantly enhancing user productivity. This research further distributes knowledge and resources equally to both developers and end-users, and presents an accessible, low-resource setup that consists of a combination of balanced training and iterative, semi-autonomous validation, thereby enabling end-users to select models in a semi-autonomous fashion. This research demonstrates the immense potential of leveraging high-end infrastructure to speed up deep learning model training and adapt it to a wide range of scientific and remote sensing applications. The study reveals that repurposing a high-resolution GPU server from other applications can substantially increase the value and efficiency of such infrastructure. This research offers an innovative method of utilizing high-resolution GPU servers in a way that maximizes their value and helps end-users to generate valuable datasets and maps without requiring extensive domain experience. The new low-resource setup reduces the need for extensive domain experience in end-users and saves valuable computational resources. The ability of enhanced second-harmonic generation in metallic systems to create electron hotspots heavily relies on non-linear changes in absorption. This concept is demonstrated within metallic nickel using a quantum-electrodynamics model. At low power levels, nickel's harmonic generation behaves symmetrically, but this symmetry is disrupted when power levels rise, caused by non-linear changes in absorption. Electron redistribution significantly contributes to this disruption, creating an inhomogeneous electron density that generates a magnetic field, reducing the axis symmetry of nickel's harmonic generation. When high fluences and power levels are combined, electron redistribution creates a local density that outweighs average electron movements, resulting in a nonlinear decrease in absorption, and subsequently, an observed conical beam becomes distorted. This beam distortion caused by electron-induced magnetic fields can help identify the electronic structure of a material. Using specific beam directions, this effect can be utilized to differentiate between various materials. Due to its reliability and precision, this method provides an alternative way to study the electronic structure of metals. This discovery has implications for the development of all-optical control over magnetism in metals in the future. Adversarial attacks on Deep Neural Network models have become a pressing concern, given the frequent failures when these models are exposed to slight alterations in input data. In order to counter such attacks, we suggest implementing a security system that integrates a generative adversarial network module. By deploying GANs within this system, it becomes possible for them to detect adversarial attacks by analyzing input data and categorize them using a detector module that distinguishes between legitimate and adversarial inputs. Furthermore, the outcomes generated by the GANs can be refined by a filter module, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the detector. Experimental evaluations conducted using the CIFAR-10 dataset demonstrated the capabilities of our proposed system, comprised of a FastGAN module and filter module, in improving the accuracy of the detector by approximately 5%. Additionally, by combining the outputs generated by the GANs with a tiny convolutional neural network, it became possible for the system to further enhance the detection rate to approximately 25%. In comparison to existing approaches such as Adversariae Detector Network and CleverHans, our proposed system, comprised of a FastGAN module and filter module, outperformed these competitors by 6% and 10% respectively, demonstrating its effectiveness and improved performance. The source code for our proposed system is available for public access at the GitHub repository https://github.com/asharakeh/GAN-Filter-GAN. Moreover, all the experiments performed using this code achieved consistent results, thereby affirming the reliability of the obtained findings. The investigation into different GAN models, such as InfoGAN and ALI-GAN, is also presented in this study, highlighting their relative shortcomings in comparison to FastGAN. Ultimately, the integration of a GAN module and filter module in the proposed system enhances security while minimizing computation overhead, thereby making it a dependable solution for safeguarding DNN-based systems against adversarial attacks. Automatically labeling Multiple Sclerosis lesions in MRI scans across various hospitals proves challenging due to uniform data utilization. Leveraging a experiences archive, we attain ground truth for novel hospital data through a multi-step process involving segmentation, water and iron content analysis, and pathological examination. Pathology-driven comparison of recent iterations of our segmentation algorithm reveals that experience replay enhances the algorithm's performance. Moreover, incorporating our custom-designed distance measure and multi-scale, multi-path convolution architecture enhances segmentation results. When fine-tuning the algorithm with single-path, single-scale models and experience-replayed data from Montpellier University Hospital, the performance further improves. Official evaluation metrics indicate that our approach surpasses human expert standards in lesion segmentation. Furthermore, in a collaborative effort with neurologists, we developed a system that assigns a likelihood value to each MS lesion, based on characteristics such as water and iron content, size, location, and sequence. This probability value corresponds to the patient's likelihood of suffering from an MS lesion, as verified by a single neurology exam. Finally, we developed a method to highlight regions of uncertain diagnosis in anonymous MRI scans for subsequent expert analysis by neurologists, and demonstrated its effectiveness using a dataset from WU WU "doubtful" scans. Multiple hospital diagnostics were simulated by integrating data from the CHU and Montpellier University Hospital. Our uncertainty detection approach achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.85, and showed that experience-replayed data significantly improved the model's diagnostic accuracy for rare MS lesions. Overall, our study demonstrates the potential of leveraging experience archives to tackle data heterogeneity across various hospital settings. This research also showcases a minority-class specific approach to diagnostic enhancement, and highlights the importance of incorporating uncertainty analysis in medical imaging for more reliable diagnostic decisions. Experience-replayed data contributed notably to the model's ability to distinguish rare MS lesions, and this knowledge can be applied to other minority-class data analysis issues throughout the medical and vision communities. The development of massive stars is a widespread phenomenon, yet the initial stages of these stars' formation remain poorly understood. Investigating how massive stars are formed in giant molecular clouds is crucial to understanding their birth process. We utilized data from the Submillimeter Array to observe six cores in the RC1 region of these clouds, which is known to contain several high-mass protostars. By analyzing 12CO, 13CO, and C18O emissions in three wavelengths, we found that the cores' 12CO emissions significantly exceed their thermal values, indicating a CO abundance increase. As a result, the cores' central stars' temperatures and densities are no longer stable. Furthermore, the 12CO emissions' rapid decay in lower wavelengths suggest that a significant amount of 12CO is being converted to CO, either through the action of X-factors or chemical reactions. Notably, the decay in the RC1 core, which is known to contain a massive star, exceeds its neighboring cores by over 50%, indicating a potential X-factor trigger. By modeling the CO snow line's effect on H2CO, CH4, and other molecules, we found that the decay in the 12CO emissions in higher wavelengths can be attributed to the central stars' increasing mass. Based on these results, a possible scenario for massive star formation in the RC1 region involves the peaceful coexistence of massive stars and low-mass star-forming cores, which eventually share the same mother core. It is predicted that, over time, the low-mass core will undergo a similar mass increase as the other cores, potentially becoming one of these massive stars. Consequently, a graph showing the relationship between mass increase and formation rate in molecular cores versus their initial masses indicates a potential link between core mass and formation rate. If verified, this link could explain the observed patterns in core mass distribution, as well as the prevalence of massive star formation in giant molecular clouds. Future observations focusing on lower-mass cores in these clouds could confirm the link and shed more light on massive star formation, which is currently poorly understood. When assessing the impact of network expansions, a common issue is to determine how to measure the benefit of adding a single new element to an existing set. We have observed that the dynamics of silicon dioxide nanograins during liquid-to-amorphous solid phase transition, induced by heat transfer in an experiment, follows a specific rule. This rule, called "scaling," was initially used to study the cooling of supercooled liquids and was later applied to analyze the transformation of silicon dioxide nanograins. This observation led us to reevaluate the theory of glass formation, linking it to the thermal conductive process and suggesting a new method for studying how temperature affects the transition. Moreover, we found that this thermal conductive process can produce "ideal" glasses, which have previously been difficult to create experimentally. Ultimately, our study highlights the utility of observing the cooling of supercooled liquids at a constant temperature of the surroundings, rather than the usual method of gradually reducing it. Recent advancements in transformer-based models for natural language inference rely heavily on syntactic augmentation techniques. However, standard augmentation methods might not effectively address "weak" forms of negation, thereby underperforming in real-world applications. This research proposes a novel method of "semi-synthetic" augmentation tailored to handle negations, achieved by reversing sentence components in pairs while maintaining original word order. The approach also introduces new forms of negation by combining original and reversed components. Evaluations across two datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this method in enhancing performance for semantic matching tasks, with notable improvements of up to 3.2% in F1-score on the SICK corpus and 1.3% in F1-score and 1.1% in F1-score on the MultiSICK. Moreover, analysis of the dataset indicates that this method is particularly beneficial in tasks involving "weak" forms of negation, such as contrapositive and double negations, where improvements are seen to stabilize as the proportion of these negations increases. The method also exhibits stability in enhancing performance across various task-specific models when tested on the SICK corpus, with notable enhancements of up to 3.3% in F1-score and 1.4% in F1-score, respectively. The code and dataset are publicly available on GitHub. The dataset has been updated to include the original SICK dataset with negations restored and a new dataset, MultiSICK-Neg, which includes both original and reversed samples paired with different forms of negations. The new dataset demonstrates higher task difficulty with higher negation rates and was found to have more diverse transformation types in semantic augmentation. The method was also tested on more complex tasks, including classification and ranking, and was found to have more consistent and adaptable performance in these settings. The results demonstrate the potential of the novel semi-synthetic augmentation method in enhancing the performance of transformer-based models, particularly in tasks involving "weak" forms of negation, and suggests the creation of a new dataset to evaluate their performance in these tasks. We analyzed the diffuse gamma-ray background observed in the Fermi-LAT data above 100 GeV using two methods, in conjunction with gamma-ray spectra generated from simulated galaxy clusters. Our simulation of the cosmic diffuse gamma-ray background revealed that it can be fully explained by the cumulative effect of galaxy clusters throughout the universe's history, using observed constraints on the extragalactic gamma-ray background. Additionally, we compared the observed upper limit on the diffuse gamma-ray background at high energies with various models of galaxy distributions. Our study indicates that models proposing significant diffuse gamma-ray emission from galactic halos or magnetic fields in galactic nuclei cannot explain the observed cap at high energies. In contrast, models attributing diffuse gamma-ray background to radiation produced within galaxy groups and clusters are consistent with the observed upper limit. We also found that the gamma-ray spectrum of the galactic center can be accounted for by the contribution of galaxy clusters, and that the observed reacceleration of cosmic rays in the galactic center may not be necessary to explain the observed gamma-ray spectrum. Therefore, our study supports the idea that the gamma-ray background is predominantly a result of hadronic interactions within galaxy clusters, with an estimated contribution of approximately 60%. We utilized the SPT catalog to estimate the hadronic interaction cross-section, which was found to be $\sigma_{\rm Canesvena}$, within the range of typical cluster magnetic fields. Furthermore, our study yielded an lower bound of $10^{-16}$ cm$^{2}$ when considering the SPT catalog, and an even tighter bound of $10^{-17}$ cm$^{2}$ when utilizing the more recent catalog of galaxy clusters detected by Planck. We discovered that the diffuse gamma-ray background observed at high energies could be significantly altered if there is an increase in the typical magnetic fields within galaxy clusters. For example, a doubling of the fields would result in a nearly two-fold enhancement in the predicted gamma-ray background. In contrast, a decrease in the fields by half would result in a nearly ten-fold reduction in the predicted gamma-ray background. In conclusion, our study provides strong evidence that galaxy clusters are a dominant source of gamma-ray emission contributing to the observed diffuse gamma-ray background at high energies. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of cluster astrophysical magnetic fields in shaping the observed diffuse gamma-ray background, suggesting potential avenues of investigation into their effects. Ultimately, the agreement between our findings and observations reinforces the validity of simulations used to predict galaxy distributions and the structure of the universe's large-scale architecture. For a closed linear operator A generating a $C_0$-semigroup, the given formula calculates the Lyapunov constant $\omega_1(A)$ in terms of graph norms, which is pivotal in evaluating the boundedness of the resolvent and left invertibility of the semigroup. Building upon the theory of $\gamma$-well-posedness, this paper defines the Lyapunov inequality numbers $\gamma_+(A)$ and $\gamma_-(A)$ and derives them using the computed $\omega_1(A)$. The study establishes that these numbers represent upper bounds for the Gruber numbers $\gamma_1(A)$ and the maximal growth numbers $\gamma_0(A)$. Furthermore, it is proven that strong stability is equivalent to $\gamma_-(A) = 0$ and the closed operator A is densely defined. The paper also obtains relationships between the numbers and the well-posedness criteria for A, as well as its relationship to the resolvent and inverse C_0-semgropt. It is also noted that practical calculations of these numbers can be challenging when the resolvent is not compact, but it is shown that $\gamma_+(A)$ has a simpler expression, which is linearly dependent on $\omega_1(A)$. Therefore, this number may serve as a useful indicator of well-posedness for operators in abstract spaces. The findings are substantiated with several examples that illustrate how the numbers can vary, specifically in relation to A being densely defined, as well as differences between regular and singularly perturbed operators. It is shown through direct computation that the numbers can reach any non-negative value. Last, this paper presents a new criterion for exponential stability by applying the numbers and discusses their use in testing the stability of closed operators. It is shown that strong exponential stability implies $\gamma_-(A) = 0$ and the operator A is densely defined in the space. Upon finding suitable numbers for an arbitrary stable operator A, this paper develops conditions under which the generated C_0-semgropt is norm-to-norm bounded. Consequently, this result extends and generalizes previously established theorems, including those for sectorial and bounded Hille-Yosida operators. It is also shown that this theorem represents a comprehensive summary of the established stability criteria in this paper. Finally, this paper presents several examples demonstrating the practical application of the established criteria to concrete differential operators. These examples highlight the usefulness of the numbers in determining the well-posedness of differential operators

The strong star-forming activity and the widespread presence of dust in Green Pea galaxies make them ideal subjects for studying the formation of metals in the early universe. The analysis of spectroscopic data from five of these galaxies, observed using the OSIRIS instrument on the GTC, reveals the kinematic structure of their interstellar medium. The data, acquired in the 2019-2020 period, include integral field unit observations taken at a high resolution and show that four of the galaxies feature a symmetrical, spiral-shaped structure, while the remaining one exhibits two distinct rotating cores separated by a significant gap in the gas. The galaxies' line profiles demonstrate high rotation velocities outside the core regions and decreasing velocities towards their centers, indicating either the breaking of rotational symmetry or an irregular separation between core regions. Additionally, the data reveal varying levels of uncertainty in the gas velocity, possibly due to minor errors in the final calibration or the presence of small flows within individual fibers. The data show that the OSIRIS observations can accurately determine the velocity dispersion within individual structures, better than previous studies using long-slit spectroscopy, and highlight the benefits of using the OSIRIS under these observation conditions. When utilizing a Retrieval Augment Generation (RAG) architecture as the model, fine-tuning presents distinct challenges due to its dual encoder architecture. RAG's lack of compatibility with standard autoregressive training techniques and the availability of a labelled dataset that covers all possible scenarios that the model might encounter during training hinder its optimisation. As a result, its training cannot be treated as a typical supervised learning process. Instead, its parameters need to be simultaneously updated while generating output for multiple tasks in a sequential manner, and this process requires defining task-specific or shared embeddings that reflect the outcomes of multiple tasks in a labelled dataset that the model is not trained on in an autoregressive fashion prior to its fine-tuning. Furthermore, the updates to the model need to be limited in scope in order to prevent degradation in performance. In order to address these challenges, the authors introduce a novel approach to fine-tuning RAG models that involves training the model in an autoregressive fashion using a dataset of task-specific or shared descriptions in an augmented form and limiting the scope of updates to the model. Through evaluating the model on various question-answering tasks, the authors demonstrate that fine-tuning based on task-specific descriptions significantly improves the model's performance relative to the baseline model and that the model's performance is comparable to that of a model that was trained on these tasks in a supervised manner. In addition, the authors observed that fine-tuning based on shared descriptions also improves the model's performance but to a lesser extent. Finally, the authors observed that the model's performance in an augmented setting outperforms its performance in a non-augmented setting. In conclusion, the approach presented here offers a novel methodology for fine-tuning RAG models in a novel manner. extract information from text more effectively. However, to further improve these
tasks, having accurate labels is necessary. Unfortunately, manually labeling data
for complex tasks is time-consuming, costly, and often impractical. To overcome
this challenge, we have created a qualification pipeline that helps produce high-
quality annotations by filtering out irrelevant data. Our pipeline consists of
steps that utilize natural language processing techniques to identify qualified samples
for labeling. By doing so, it reduces the need for human intervention during the
annotation process. In this paper, we describe how to develop such a pipeline for
temporal information extraction and present its components along with experimental
results. Furthermore, we demonstrate that using our pipeline can produce high-
quality annotations as well as improve a model's accuracy in a sequence labeling task
without further training. To support future research, we have made our pipeline's
code and a dataset of annotated temporal information extraction examples available
online. The dataset can be accessed at: https://github.com/magdeldar/tae-dataset.

Text-video retrieval has garnered significant attention in recent years, and current methods focus on matching frame-level representations with text embeddings through a dense prediction framework. However, conventional representations are insufficient to capture the underlying semantics of videos as they fall short in capturing long-term semantic patterns. To address this limitation, this work introduces TS2-Net, a two-stage dense prediction framework that leverages spatial and temporal contexts to derive more expressive video representations. Specifically, TS2-Net comprises RGB and motion streams that capture contextual information across frames, followed by a semantic mapping stage that aggregates features to represent semantically meaningful units within videos. The derived units then drive a retrieval framework consisting of dense labeling, transformation, and pooling stages to facilitate transformation-invariant learning. Through extensive experiments on MSRVTT, MSVD, DiDeMo, and TSVT datasets, TS2-Net has demonstrated superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, including the application of pre-trained models like ResNet50, LRCN, and VGGish. Furthermore, TS2-Net has demonstrated generalizability and robustness in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by adversarial testing. The project's source code and video samples are available on GitHub. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a foundational understanding of video semantics, leading to improved performance in text-video retrieval tasks. It is anticipated that this knowledge will enable the development of more robust visual representation learning methods, ultimately enhancing the state-of-the-art across multiple vision applications. A paper detailing this work has been published at the 2022 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. In the rapidly evolving field of the Internet of Everything (IoE), the possibility of multiple devices operating simultaneously at the same technology is high, which may result in a decrease in signal quality. As a consequence, single-technology interference has the potential to mislead the signal identification process. To address this challenge, a robust machine learning method based on deep learning for signal detection is proposed in this paper. The method compares the Mac IDs of known signals with those of signals in the environment through a natural language processing technique. The method was tested using 80 s long signals from the IEEE 802.15.1, IEEE 802.15.8, IEEE 802.11b/g/n, IEEE 802.15.6, and IEEE 802.11a/n/b/g/ac/m/ax standards, mixed in same-technology and cross-technology pairs. The results indicate that the method achieves a high signal classification accuracy of 98% in cross-technology scenarios and 99% in same-technology scenarios with a database of 1000 IDs. The method shows resilience to partial overlay of cross-technology signals, achieving a classification accuracy of 98% even when there is a 50% overlap. The method also demonstrates the ability to detect the technology of the dominant signal even when it is weaker by up to 10 dB. The method's efficiency was further validated by analyzing the time complexity, space complexity, and accuracy in relation to signal duration. The method was found to perform well across various signal durations, with the ability to identify signals as fast as 10 ms for 1 s signals and an increasing accuracy with longer signal durations. The method's complexity was observed to be inversely proportional to the number of IDs in the database, with the ability to identify signals in proportional time complexity and space complexity. The method's accuracy was found to be proportional to the number of classified signals, demonstrating the influence of the number of signals on signal detection. To validate the practical applicability of the method, a prototype was developed on Raspberry Pi 4 using Raspbian OS and tested in real-world scenarios. The results of the prototype's testing revealed the prototype's effectiveness in identifying signals from cross-technology and same-technology interference with high signal classification accuracy of up to 100%. The study's insights provide a foundation for evaluating the significance of test smells in terms of their practical impact and can guide developers and maintainers in identifying priority refactoring goals. Ultimately, the distinction between minor quality defects and critical system failures is revealed through the developers' eyes, and it becomes evident that while test smells may have a minor impact according to empirical metrics, they are considered highly critical by practicing developers. The study also underscores the necessity of developing practical methods for identifying and eliminating test smells based on actual developer experiences and guidelines that factor in developers' perspectives on quality criteria. Lastly, the study highlights that developers' perceptions on test smells can change over time, and future research may uncover similar shifts in their views on other software defects and imperfections. Accurate detection of heart rate variability (HRV) via inter-beat intervals (IBIs) is essential for diagnosing autonomic nervous system disorders. A new IBI estimation method focused on enhancing the visibility of Q, R, and T waves in noisy ecological settings. Utilizing deep learning, the approach combines QRI-net and TRI-net to identify Q and T waves, and R-Net to determine the heart rate interval, while suppressing noise via a learned division strategy. Experimental results indicate that this approach achieves mean absolute errors of 20, 43, and 67 milliseconds in the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia, Harvard STanford-Biomedical, and ecological contexts, respectively. When applied to the IEEE Data Portals' extensive ecological database, the proposed method outperforms existing approaches, demonstrating its real-world relevance and substantial potential to improve time-series diagnostic accuracy in noisy ecological settings. Embedding graphs dynamically has proven more challenging due to static graph embedding limitations. One major issue is dealing with changing node and edge relationships, where traditional methods often overlook how these changes affect the structure of the graph. To address this, we can think of developing dynamic graph embeddings as a continuous process that takes into account the direction of change. However, current methods primarily focus on whether edges have appeared, disappeared, or remained the same, and overlook the direction of change. As a result, embedded representations of nodes often fail to predict whether edges have moved in a particular direction. To mitigate this, we've introduced a new dynamic graph embedding approach called TE-GEE, which takes into account both the creation and deletion of edges, as well as how existing edges have moved in a particular direction. This approach involves combining the predictions of multiple autoregressive models, utilizing both node attributes and the embedded node representations from previous time steps. TE-GEE dynamically adjusts its focus on different aspects of the graph by combining the predictions of multiple autoregressive models, and through soft-sharing information across time steps. TE-GEE embeds each node as a combination of its current features and changes over time, and can be used for various tasks such as predicting new edges, recognizing nodes, and detecting changes in the graph. Thanks to advances in deep networks, state-of-the-art performance has been achieved on large-scale visual classification tasks such as image retrieval and person re-identification. However, the quality of the learned embedding is yet fully understood. We introduce a novel approach to directly measure how effectively an embedding separates classes in an unknown dataset. This measurement, called Deep Class-wise Discrepancy Loss (DCDL), forces the network to learn distinct, class-specific features. By utilizing class labels instead of pair-wise labels, our method alleviates the need for extensive data collection. We test DCDL on person re-identification and demonstrate its efficacy by surpassing the current best results when incorporated into the widely-used Siamese and ResNet architectures. Moreover, we develop a model selection technique based on class discrepancy that enhances the network's generalizability. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/leverone/classwise.

Deep learning techniques have successfully trained end-to-end camera calibration networks, but prior approaches relied on limited, annotated datasets. In contrast, traditional calibration methods utilize vast amounts of unlabelled data and are therefore more efficient, despite similar direct regression approaches being explored. This research justifies the use of direct regression with minimal calibration data by providing a novel, geometrically-constrained regression loss function derived from the essential matrix's fundamental matrix. In comparison to previous deep learning methods, our results indicate a significant reduction of at least 2000 parameters on typical 2D-to-3D reconstruction datasets, and our loss function outperforms those previously used. Additionally, this study calms concerns surrounding overfitting in direct regression by revealing it's not a primary issue and instead results from a suboptimal loss function. Finally, our direct regression approach is successfully applied and outperforms previous methods in demanding 6DoF pose and extrinsic calibration tasks. Recent advancements in this area centered on Reinforcement Learning methods incorporating an adversary as an environment, simulating the adversarial attack. These methods utilize a policy network responding to adversary actions as inputs, aiming to enhance robustness. This work challenges the necessity of an adversary network, proposing a simpler alternative that achieves similar robustness by directly perturbing input images. Experimental results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets confirm that our method successfully replaces the adversary-intensive training required by existing RL-based techniques. In information retrieval, canonical mapping is a method used for source identification, where a query with precise coordinates is matched with a target by the same authority. While commonly applied in astronomical databases, its effectiveness drops when the query's coordinates have errors or minor authority variations. To counter this, a proposed method integrates query photometry into comparison metrics, leading to improved source association. Testing this method on ZTF data targeting the M31 galaxy showed a 22% increase in transdimensional acceptance rates when compared to traditional canonical mapping, specifically in cases involving 1-2 magnitude photometry. When the photometry added was less reliable, the method still exhibited benefits but in a lesser degree. The method also includes a model-based component that forecasts the expected photometry of the target source, making it more resilient to photometric inaccuracies. As a result, the method now includes an added robustness of 25% when the photometric uncertainty exceeds 1% magnitude. Finally, the method remains computationally efficient with a processing time of less than 0.1 seconds for individual matches. With its potential in various fields like Mira variable identification and transneptunian binary systems analysis, the method remains fast and efficient. The method's full implementation is available online at https://github.com/LoicDaures/canonical-mapping. Further research will involve extending the method's application to other fields. Analysis times may vary depending on the dataset size and computer specifications. The version of the implementation used in the study was version 0.1 of the canonical-mapping python package. Visualizing complex ontology structures can be challenging due to the 2D representation, which often results in confusing and link-heavy layouts. To address this issue, we have developed OntoPlot, a new visualization tool that employs a hierarchical graph layout to simplify understanding. By dynamically adjusting the main categories, OntoPlot creates a hierarchical breakdown of the ontology, making it easier to analyze. The tool also allows for the classification of entities and classes, enabling users to input specific annotations or rely on the auto-classification feature. Finally, OntoPlot presents its findings in an interactive 3D layout that is easily interpretable. In contrast to existing recursive and 3D visualizers, OntoPlot offers a simplified and centralized view of the hierarchy. Our experiments demonstrate that, on standard ontology datasets, OntoPlot surpasses state-of-the-art 2D visualizers while maintaining comparable runtime efficiency to existing recursive visualizers. Notably, OntoPlot exhibits comparable accuracy to expert-hand curated classifications, achieving a high accuracy of 0.884 on the NCBITax dataset. Compared to the application of additivity-based methods, such as those used in our previous work, the application of CycleGAN maintains artificial flavor while significantly reducing the computational burden during the process of de-noising and color enhancement. This results in a significant 12 times decrease in processing time when applied to a dataset of 22851 colorized images. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is verified through user studies which reveal that it achieves a higher score for color articulation and overall visual appeal compared to other methods. Our investigation into the thermal diffusion coefficient under conditions of strong temperature fluctuations focuses on how the movements of molecules affect the coefficient. We found that enabling molecules to bend and rotate relative to each other significantly alters the coefficient in a variety of gas mixtures, leading to direction-based variations. In contrast, this effect is minimal in dense fluids where molecules are closely connected. The importance of molecular flexibility in this context is most pronounced at temperatures where molecules have some but not full flexibility. The impact of molecular flexibility increases as the ratio of temperature fluctuations to average temperatures also increases. The effects observed in mixtures where lighter species dominate, such as in air, differ from those in mixtures where heavier species dominate, such as in carbon dioxide and oxygen. The experimental methods used to measure thermal diffusion in these systems do not account for the observed direction-based variations, which may lead to discrepancies between experimental and calculated results that vary by order of magnitude. Specifically, in mixtures of carbon dioxide and oxygen at standard temperature and pressure, taking into account the observed direction-based variations reduces discrepancies between experimental and calculated results from 30% to 10%. The experimental methods used for lighter mixtures, such as in air, do not in fact underpredict thermal diffusion, indicating that flexibility does not contribute to observed discrepancies in such cases. The direction-based variations in thermal diffusion also occur at higher temperatures and pressures, suggesting that flexibility may contribute to discrepancies in predictions in such cases as well. The contribution of molecular flexibility to thermal diffusion may need to be considered in thermal diffusion models to minimize discrepancies between experimental predictions in such cases. The research also indicates that flexibility may lead to additional direction-based variations in other factors such as heat conductivity and viscoelastic properties. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly enhanced the quality of music restoration. This paper presents an innovative method combining techniques from low-rank regularization and deep learning to restore degraded music recordings. Our approach utilizes a two-stage framework, leveraging a Convolutional Neural Network to remove noise from a low-quality music recording and a second CNN to retrieve the original signal from the noise-removed input. Noise reduction is achieved in a second stage by extracting low-rank features from the noise-removed input and applying a Weighted Sparse Overlap-and-add operation. This two-stage framework is capable of retrieving the original music signal, with experimental evaluations confirming the effectiveness of our method in music restoration applications. Furthermore, we successfully competed in the 2020 Challenge on Auditory Source Separation and Music Restoration, securing 4th place in the single-channel track of the IEES task. Creating convincing throwing motion animations in animation and special effects requires a thorough understanding of physical laws and human impressions of reality. In this research, we applied machine learning to generating throwing motion animations, starting by gathering a vast library of actual throwing motions captured through motion capture technology. Subsequently, we created a formula-based model to describe these motions and used it to generate new motion trajectories when a user specifies a throwing style. To increase the new animations' realism, we included random variations in the timing and intensity of these motions, drawn from a distribution based on the actual motion data. A user study demonstrated that the random variations enhanced the realism of the throwing motions, and our research was found to create animations at least as realistic as, or up to 23% more engaging than, animations generated through other methods. The technical aspects of this research are documented in a paper titled "Throwing Hacks: A Machine Learning Approach to Impostor Physics", which is available online. To facilitate the use of our discoveries, we have created a software tool called MimicThrow that allows for the creation of customized throwing motion animations. Our research is an significant contribution to the field of computer animation, as the design of its underlying physics is public for the first time it can be shared openly without compromising trade secrets. Our work opens the door to the use of machine learning in physics-based computer animation, and our code is available online at https://mimicpath.github.io/MimicThrow/ under a permissive open-source license. we've developed an attention model that integrates syntactic cues at the source level, 
accounting for sequence reordering in translation. This novel model can be used in two ways: 
1) as a post-net for enhanced fluency or 2) as a syntax-aware reordering mechanism. 
In experiments, the proposed model demonstrated superior effectiveness, surpassing state-of-the-art models 
in translation quality, specifically in fluency and reordering, for both general-purpose and machine learning-based language models. 
Our research also demonstrates the transferability of the syntax-aware attention model to other NMT applications, 
such as translating rare or out-of-vocabulary words, highlighting its versatility. 
Furthermore, analysis of the proposed model's attention patterns and their correlation with sentence syntax 
confirms the incorporation of syntactic information and provides valuable insights for further optimization. 
One notable outcome of this research is the significant improvement in translating sentences with numerous jumps 
in attention patterns, thereby validating the potential of using disentangled syntactic information in deep sequence-to-sequence models. 
This new understanding may pave the way for the development of new techniques to handle complex attention patterns 
related to sentence structure and promote the creation of more accurate and fluent machine translations. 
Ultimately, the proposed model has potential not only for further improvement but also for application in other NMT-based applications. 
Our research also compares the performance of low and high memory-footprints, demonstrating that the syntax-aware attention model can be efficiently used with limited computational resources. 
To facilitate comparison and reproducibility, the source code and pre-trained models for the proposed approach have been made publicly available on GitHub, specifically within the fairseq open-source project. 
This public release also facilitates future research opportunities to investigate the proposed model. 
In the future, the proposed approach can be extended to other language-related applications, such as text classification and summarization, providing valuable insights and enhanced performance. 
Furthermore, the integration of the proposed model in neural sequence transduction applications is feasible, 
potentially leading to significant advancements in related technology. 
Ultimately, the proposed approach has the potential to produce significant, meaningful improvements in machine translation.

Typically, the outer disc's volatile content is assumed to remain solid, but newly discovered processes could potentially release volatiles. We conducted a study to determine how gas released from icy solid evolution affects Snow-Line locations, protoplanetary core compositions, and their respective growth patterns in disc environments. We employed multiple simulations utilizing the Adaptive Simulated Nebula code, taking into consideration varying binding energy values representative of the outer disc's newly released volatiles. As binding energy values decreased, the Snow-Line shifted towards the disc's outer edges, depending on the gas density. With lower binding energy values, Snow-Line locations deepened in the disc's outer regions, but gas densities had a negligible effect in the disc's inner regions. We analyzed how varying Snow-Line locations impacted growing planetary core compositions and its potential effects on water enrichment. With lower binding energy values, Snow-Line locations moved deeper into the disc's outer regions, resulting in planetary core compositions with lower water mass fractions and increased enrichments of heavy elements. As a result, planetary core masses within a 0.1 M_Jupiter mass range, formed between 1 to 10 AU, increased due to gas accretion in locations beyond the Snow-Line. Conversely, planetary core compositions with higher water mass fractions and reduced enrichments of heavy elements resulted from lower gas accretion rates in locations below the Snow-Line. These gas accretion patterns were consistent with planet formation models of the Earth and other terrestrial planets. Ultimately, the release of volatiles from icy solid evolution leads to diverse Snow-Line locations, planetary core compositions, and growth patterns in disc environments. These diverse planetary formation pathways could contribute to the diverse diversity of planetary masses, compositions, and sizes observed in the known exoplanet population. Future observations of volatile species, Snow-Line markers, and planetary mass-radius relationships could further distinguish between these planetary formation models. We explore the complexity of learning an unknown quantum state $\rho$ given access to it and measurements of associated expectation values $F(\rho)$. We consider two primary problems: 
1) Determining the minimum number of samples required to accurately calculate $F(\rho)$ up to a certain degree of precision using a given number of repetitions.
2) Identifying the optimal approach for estimating $F(\rho)$ using a specified number of samples and repetitions.
For both issues, we identify multiple categories of states where the required complexity is well-defined and can be quantified.
These findings align with long-standing theoretical assumptions in a related area of research known as quantum complexity theory. Furthermore, they have practical implications in a diverse set of applications, including state learning and quantum compilation. 
To derive these results, we establish a connection between quantum complexity theory and a related area of research and utilize previously developed lower and upper bounds on the complexity of optimization problems.
These bounds are then extended to analyze the complexity of estimating expectation values $\mathbb{E}[\phi(\rho)]$, where $\phi$ represents an arbitrary unitary operation. 
As a result, we derive new lower and upper bounds on the complexity of optimization problems as a byproduct. 
Specifically, we examine the complexity of maximizing a given function $f(\rho)$ subject to constraints $g(\rho) \leq b$ where $\rho$ is a state in the set of all density operators. 
By applying our analysis, we also look into the complexity of maximizing a quantum advantage in specific quantum metrology scenarios where multiple copies of an unknown state are available for measurement purposes. 
In another application, we use our analysis to derive lower and upper bounds on the complexity of estimating $F(\rho)$ when $\rho$ is symmetric. 
Application of these results to random circuits reveals an interesting connection to randomized quantum computation, and it appears that randomized circuits can sample from a circuit family that is computationally difficult to sample from exactly, yet sampling from it is feasible with any reasonable probability.

This modified theory can provide a trade-off between the required number of samples and estimation precision, and it offers both tight and tight-lower bounds on the complexity of estimation.

Significant progress has been made in semi-supervised learning (SSL) techniques,
which can effectively utilize unlabeled data in addition to labeled data.
Although most current SSL methods are designed for label prediction, they do
not consider the scenario where class labels change over time. In this study,
we focus on transmuting the class labels of base classifiers using unlabeled
data, which can significantly boost the performance of prediction on new, as
well as past, data. Two transmutation methods based on graph-based and
consistency-based ensembles were developed and demonstrated to be more
effective than traditional SSL methods in evaluating various datasets.
Additionally, our research indicates that incorporating transmutations does not
necessarily increase computational costs compared to the required predictions.

In the classic setting of multi-task linear regression, we examine how algorithms can learn quickly from data, taking into account a large number of tasks. Notably, existing methods face two major obstacles: how to handle a substantial number of tasks when the number of observed samples is limited, and the challenge of competing tasks influencing each other's predictions. To address these issues, we are proposing a new approach called "Task-Conditioned Noise Reduction" that improves the efficiency of learning in such scenarios. This method revolves around a novel framework called the "Task Linearized Regression" (Task-LR) problem, allowing us to break down the complex multi-task problem into simpler components, each of which can be learned quickly. Furthermore, we have developed a strategy to consolidate these learned components and re-introduce them into the original problem, effectively overcoming the limitations of earlier methods. In our model, Task-LR not only offers an analytically scalable solution to the multi-task problem, but it also highlights the connection between our method and existing techniques that require much broader assumptions. Notably, Task-LR reduces the challenge of competing task influences during the learning process. In particular, we demonstrate through empirical analysis that Task-LR achieves a significant reduction in influences from competing tasks among a range of algorithms, from a minimum of 50% decrease in influences learned by the MultiTaskNet model to a 99% decrease influences learned by the FedPer model. Concretely, Task-LR yields an improvement in sample efficiency of at least two orders of magnitude for the MultiTaskNet algorithm, and a sample efficiency improvement of three orders of magnitude for the FedPer algorithm. Overall, our method addresses the two major challenges of learning in multi-task linear regression, namely the limited availability of samples and competing task influences. Task-LR offers an analytically scalable solution to the multi-task problem that requires much broader assumptions than existing methods, while also providing sample efficiency improvements of at least two orders of magnitude over the MultiTaskNet algorithm. Task-LR achieves an adaptable sample efficiency profile that is comparable to the MultiTaskNet algorithm, and a highly robust performance against influences from competing tasks among a range of algorithms. Finally, we propose a new path for learning to adapt to novel tasks through online learning, taking into account a substantial number of tasks. Quantization and knowledge distillation are widely used methods for developing efficient, high-performance deep learning models. Their effectiveness has been extensively evaluated for English data but their performance in less resource-rich languages remains unclear. In this research, we assess the effectiveness of post-training quantization and knowledge distillation across eight languages, using English models, knowledge graphs, and labeled data in various languages. Our findings show that post-training quantization produces more consistent results than knowledge distillation, and that while both methods can accelerate inference without sacrificing accuracy, they impact training differently. Training with larger models produced using knowledge distillation significantly outperformed quantization-based models, highlighting a potential speed-accuracy tradeoff. Automated detection of pneumonia from chest X-rays using machine learning is crucial, particularly during crises such as the COVID-19 outbreak. The need for large, annotated datasets poses a significant obstacle to deploying such systems in real-world settings. To address this issue, we present an end-to-end, transfer-learned CNN model that is capable of performing pneumonia detection using minimal supervised data. The proposed method involves utilizing image augmentations to substantially reduce the necessity for labeled data while achieving comparable diagnostic accuracy. Moreover, the approach includes means augmentation to decrease the impact of variations in data collection procedures among different datasets, thereby facilitating domain adaptation. The efficacy of the proposed method is evaluated by integrating three publicly accessible pulmonary image collections, including a joint evaluation on two major pneumonia datasets (RSNA-Pneumonia Detection and COVID-19-CHASER). The results demonstrate outstanding performance using a small portion (10% of total data) of the RSNA-Pneumonia Detection set, with high AUC values for both validation sets. The the proposed method's potential in real-world applications is further assessed through performance testing using a small subset of the COVID-19-CHASER set, with a focus on different implementation scenarios involving varying amounts of labeled data. The findings suggest that the need for labeled data can be significantly reduced to as low as 3% when applying a combination of data augmentations. The source code for the proposed method has been made publicly available on GitHub. The paper includes an additional discussion on the potential applications of the proposed method in outbreak scenarios, along with a study on its performance characteristics using limited data from the COVID-19-CHASER dataset. To facilitate replication of the study, the paper includes included included included a supplementary appendix providing detailed information on the dataset splits, hyperparameter settings, and technical specifics. The corresponding doi addresses are provided for the RSNA-Pneumonia Detection: 10.1055/s0039-16299-8 and COVID-19-CHASER: 10.1007/s00521-020-00453-1 datasets. Our findings highlight the need for a more nuanced and context-dependent assessment of contrastive causation. The proposed matching and retrieval strategies are evaluated within a zero-shot and few-shot speech translation framework, and results indicate significant gains over traditional methods, with latent speech outperforming acoustic speech. A self-supervised approach to pre-training latent speech is also explored, resulting in further performance enhancements over methods relying on token retrievers. The notion that knowledge-assisted learning is a pioneering concept in artificial intelligence is somewhat of an understatement, yet the effective incorporation of known information into black-box learning methods remains a mystery. Typically, existing techniques either crowdsource knowledge from biased human sources or derive knowledge from pre-existing datasets, neglecting the wisdom of experts. When knowledge is incorporated, it typically involves modifying data features, applying performance metrics, or both. However, the common assumption that including knowledge is always beneficial is questionable - the answer may depend on the specific dataset and task. Our research introduces a systematic framework that utilises structured knowledge in a more controlled manner by accounting for its potential effects on model performance. Leveraging the expertise of domain specialists to define problem-specific features is a more efficient source of knowledge. Our method iteratively evaluates knowledge modules (expert inputs) to determine which to include, when to include them, and what impact they will have, ultimately providing a comprehensive performance assessment. Our experiments across multiple datasets reveal various real-world scenarios where incorporating expert knowledge is beneficial and informs task formulation. The domain-specific nature of our method makes it suitable for tasks involving limited data such as drug response prediction, drug profiling, and target identification. Our method's efficacy is evident in datasets where traditional feature engineering struggles to produce meaningful results. Furthermore, we propose a novel method that estimates how much each knowledge module will contribute to performance when incorporated. Our approach is versatile and adaptable to various tasks, including those with distinct modalities and formats of incorporated knowledge. Our method's potential is further demonstrated in experiments involving distinct modalities, where the incorporation of sequences and the utilisation of self-attention mechanisms facilitates the prediction of drug responses from sequence-based features. Our results illustrate that incorporating expert knowledge through our method enhances black-box learning. Our approach stands out from existing techniques by providing a more controlled incorporation of expert knowledge to inform task formulation and better performance. Our method's efficacy in diverse real-world scenarios makes it an attractive solution for distinct modality formats. Our research highlights the necessity of developing methods that can effectively incorporate expert knowledge to inform task formulation and better performance. Our approach successfully addresses key questions surrounding the incorporation of expert knowledge, including its potential effects, optimal inclusion points, and adaptation to distinct tasks and datasets. Our method's adaptability to distinct modalities and formats of incorporated knowledge makes it an attractive solution. Our approach effectively addresses key challenges in drug response prediction. We introduce an innovative approach to recognizing vertebrae and obtaining their exact positions in Spine MRI images. Based on 3D multi-scale convolutional neural networks, our method focuses on analyzing three-dimensional vertebrae column columns rather than individual two-dimensional slices. Furthermore, we created a comprehensive public dataset, referred to as SpineMRI, containing 40 MRI scans with corresponding ground truth, ensuring accurate analysis. A comprehensive evaluation of our method in comparison to existing techniques demonstrates a substantial increase of 10 to 20% in vertebra identification rates and minimal position error rates. For instance, the CENPSL method's error rate decreased from 3.73 vertebrae centimeters to 1.19 centimeters, allowing our approach to outperform the CENPSL method, which had previously achieved the lowest positioning error, by a significant margin. that electromagnetic fluctuations are significant in quantum systems. In our 
investigation, we examine how these fluctuations impact the properties of polariton 
emitted from a two-mode cavity containing two nonlinear mediums separated by a layer 
with restricted thickness. By solving the Heisenberg equations, we demonstrate that 
quantum vibrations of the electromagnetic field contribute to polariton instability, 
resulting in an elevated level of entanglement between the laser emitters in the cavity 
and a characteristic "bunching" effect of photon correlations during polariton 
emission. Furthermore, our findings indicate that modifying the cavity's parameters 
can optimize polariton properties and help in observing and studying their complex 
behavior. These results offer potential applications in generating entangled states of 
light and observing novel quantum phenomena. In particular, they have implications 
for observing quantum vacancy effects in atomic systems with two highly interacting 
levels. The associated project involves exploring vacuum-related effects in quantum 
systems with attractive interactions between emitters in the cavity and co-operating 
emissions from coupled quantum systems. The potential for practical applications 
includes enhancing coherent emission, improving light directionality, and developing 
light beams with minimal energy. Moreover, our study contributes to an advanced 
understanding of quantum critical phenomena, such as phase transitions in quantum 
systems represented by level shifts in coupled emitters in the cavity. The associated 
technical report provides supplementary information on this topic and includes a 
generalized description of quantum critical phenomena in systems with repulsive 
interactions among emitters. In the case of specific cavity conditions, we found 
that quantum critical phenomena can occur when the emitters' levels are far apart

such as polariton bifurcations and the merging of polariton eigenvalues as external 
parameters are varied. The associated project involves studying these phenomena 
using an advanced mathematical framework in the case of unidirectional emission

parameters in the cavity. The results presented in this study represent a novel 
approach to understanding quantum critical phenomena in complex quantum systems.
